How better ways of screening drugs could soon lead to thousands fewer animal tests

New Scientist September 15, 2026

As many as 190 million animals are used in biomedical research around the world every year. But after centuries of experiments, controversy and countless life-saving benefits, science may finally be approaching a point where animal testing is no longer the default option.

Until recently, that idea would have sounded implausible. Modern biomedical research has relied on animals almost since its inception, using them to study disease and test new medicines before they ever reach people. But over the past few years, that assumption has begun to shift.

Efforts to replace animals in science have the firmest backing yet from policy-makers and regulators. In April 2025, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) published a five-year road map to reduce animal testing in drug-safety studies. Months later, the country’s National Institutes of Health (NIH) stopped requiring animal models for many of its grants. Late last year, the UK launched a similar plan to phase out animal testing, and the European Union followed suit in June.

Advertisement

We may finally have a cure for many different autoimmune conditions

These initiatives largely seek to make more widespread use of better alternative methods. A sliver of plastic no bigger than a microscope slide threaded with human liver cells can now identify toxic drug effects better than using rats. Lab-grown cells are sparing rabbits from once-indispensable tests that screen medicines for contaminants. And AI models are identifying potential drug targets at record speeds, without using animals.

“The science has reached a point where there is a much better evidence base to support the fact that phasing out much animal testing might be possible,” says Celean Camp, head of the UK campaign group Replacing Animal Research.

Animal experimentation dates at least as far back as the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle, who dissected dozens of animal species to better understand anatomy. But modern systematic use of animal experiments didn’t start until the mid-1800s. Then, and now, advocates for using animals argued that many of them have bodies similar enough to humans to justify tests on biological mechanisms and drug effects, thus informing science and improving healthcare without injuring people.

Pushback started almost immediately. Public horror at some of the Victorian physiologists’ methods prompted the UK to pass the world’s first animal testing law in 1876, which ensured it was done only by licensed scientists.

Yet, as generations of scientists have repeatedly said, nobody really wants to run animal experiments. They are slow, expensive and come with significant paperwork – and that is before everyone involved weighs up the ethics of deliberately inflicting pain on animals, including dogs, pigs, monkeys and, yes, guinea pigs.

But, as distasteful as it might be to some, animal testing has let researchers probe biological processes and screen experimental medicines. It has facilitated monumental breakthroughs, from the discovery of insulin and antibiotics to the development of pacemakers and covid-19 vaccines.

Most modern regulations on animal testing rest on a 1959 concept known as the 3Rs: replacement, reduction and refinement. “Replacement” means replacing animals with computer models or bacteria where possible; “reduction” is using as few animals as possible; and “refinement” is minimizing pain and distress. Countries often vary in how they apply the framework. Rules in the UK and the EU, for example, cover all vertebrates, but the US excludes mice, rats and birds bred for research, which constitute the majority of test animals.

But there are still a lot of animals used in research (see box below). About half of animals used in scientific tests these days are involved in basic research – the kind done at universities to uncover how biology functions and fails. The other half is split roughly between testing new drugs for side effects and setting safe exposure limits for chemicals, such as pesticides.

With some exceptions, public and political opinion has largely tolerated that trade-off. But there are signs of waning support. In 2001, most Americans believed medical testing on animals was morally acceptable. By 2025, fewer than half did. The most recent UK survey, from 2018, found support holding steadier at about two-thirds – but also a growing appetite for alternatives, especially among younger people.

“The public has always been somewhat supportive of animal research where there is no alternative,” says Camp. But new techniques now lessen the need for an increasing number of animal tests, and scientists haven’t caught up with that, she says. “There’s more and more evidence that the regulatory mechanisms to check that there is no alternative have not been functioning as well as they could,” says Camp. “So that assurance on which the public trust and the public support stands is a little shaky.”

Earliest use of anaesthetics uncovered in Chinese doctor’s tomb

Regulatory agencies are now trying to accelerate the transition to non-animal methods – and have been for a while. “The whole push towards more non-animal models isn’t recent,” says Ivan Rusyn, a toxicologist at Texas A&M University. Instead, he says, the recent proposals result from a “perfect storm” of political, scientific and regulatory activity over more than a decade. For example, back in 2013 the EU banned animal testing on cosmetics, proving regulators could force the issue and that industry would adapt.

The recent UK and EU road maps aim to build on this progress and develop more non-animal regulatory tests. The US approach is slightly different and aims to replace animals in scenarios where they are notoriously poor models – such as for testing monoclonal antibodies, a treatment that mimics the immune system.

Neither transition intends to be a wholesale replacement, as none of the alternatives can fully recreate a whole-bodied animal. But used in the right context – replacing an experimental method here or a safety check there – the technologies can meaningfully reduce animal testing and even produce better results.

So, what actually are the alternatives? One of the most established is cell cultures, which let researchers expose living human tissue to chemicals. These can replace some mandated drug and chemical toxicity tests, but a flat dish of cells is a poor substitute for the changing environment of a working organ.

Devices called organs-on-a-chip try to close that gap by recreating some of that dynamism. Roughly the size of a USB stick, they house cells on a flexible scaffold lined with tiny fluid-filled channels that supply nutrients and remove waste.

Organs-on-a-chip have a significant leg up on animal models when it comes to testing drug safety. More than 90 per cent of experimental drugs that appear safe and effective in animals don’t receive regulatory approval, largely because they turn out to be toxic to humans.

In 2022, biologist Donald Ingber at Harvard University and his colleagues at the biotech company Emulate, which he co-founded, built and tested the toxicity of experimental drugs using a liver-on-a-chip. It identified nearly 7 out of every 8 drugs that proved toxic in clinical trials despite appearing safe in animal tests. “People are ignorant about how far this field has progressed,” says Ingber.

The chip, which is now in the final stages of FDA approval, has already made its way into labs. The pharmaceutical company Moderna has used it in place of primates to screen compounds used in mRNA vaccines for liver damage.

Ingber’s lab also builds chips to mimic other organs, including the cervix, lungs, kidneys and intestines, and wires them together with artificial blood vessels. “We have, like, a human body-on-chips,” he says. Mounted on a scaffold, they can physically flex to mimic breathing or gut motion, addressing one of the oldest complaints about cell cultures: that real tissues never work in isolation.

Even more complex are organoids, self-assembling blobs of human cells that mimic organs. Rather than growing cells on an engineered scaffold, as chip-builders do, organoid researchers stimulate stem cells – which can transform into other cell types – into miniature, three-dimensional tissues. The resulting “mini organs” capture more of a tissue’s structure and cell variety.

Hans Clevers at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, a molecular geneticist who pioneered organoids, argues the technology can already outperform animal models for some human conditions, including cystic fibrosis. “We have animals that beautifully mimic the symptoms, but they typically don’t have the underlying cause,” he says.

That distinction matters because laboratory animals have always represented a compromise. Scientists can coax mice to develop cancers, inflammatory diseases and neurological disorders resembling human illness, but such conditions often arise through genetic engineering or artificial intervention, rather than the biological processes that make people sick. Clevers says his team developed an antibody to treat a head and neck cancer called squamous cell carcinoma entirely in organoids, with no conventional animal testing. The drug is now in phase III trials.

Organoids and organs-on-a-chip also open a door to personalised medicine in a way that animals can’t. Researchers can grow them using a patient’s own cells and then test candidate drugs directly on tissue sharing that patient’s biology.

Other animal alternatives don’t involve biological material at all; they run on computers in what researchers call in silico models. AI systems trained on genetic, chemical and clinical datasets can flag potential drug targets and predict toxicity. One problem, though, is that models don’t always explain how they generate decisions, which makes regulators cautious about relying on them to judge safety.

Molecular docking software goes further and simulates how a potential drug physically fits and binds to its target protein, letting chemists screen thousands of compounds on a laptop. Then there are pharmacokinetic models, which divide the body into mathematical compartments – liver, kidneys, bloodstream – to predict how they absorb, break down and clear drugs. The approach could help estimate safe doses in groups of people rarely included in trials, such as children or pregnant women.

None of these tools alone gives the complete picture of a drug. But together, they can help researchers zero in on compounds most likely to succeed and then investigate them further with organoids, organs-on-a-chip and remaining animal tests.

In practice, it can still take years, or even decades, for non-animal methods to be widely adopted. Take fever tests, a widely used way of checking whether drugs contain contaminants. For more than a century, regulators have mandated injecting new drugs into rabbits to see if they cause the animals to develop a high temperature, signalling an infection – simple, effective and unpleasant for the rabbit.

Alternatives to using rabbits have existed for decades. For example, a screening test using horseshoe crab blood, which clots on contact with bacterial toxins, dates to the 1970s. Then, a non-animal test emerged in the 1990s: a human blood test that measures immune responses to contaminants.

Yet, it took until this year for the rabbit test to be officially phased out, and then still only in Europe – it is ongoing in some countries, including the US.

Some of the lag comes down to understandable caution. “The regulators say they can only make judgements on whether the data is adequate once people submit it to them,” says Camp. “And the companies are saying, well, we’re only going to submit data that we know the regulators are going to accept.”

The new road maps are attempting to break this impasse by validating non-animal models and creating guidelines around their use in drug development.

It can also be challenging for career scientists to move from familiar territory. “Academics generally tend to do incremental stuff, and it’s very hard to learn a whole new methodology,” says Ingber.

There are some signs of movement, however. A 2024 analysis of research on breast cancer, lung disease, blood cancer, heart disease, neurodegenerative disease, diabetes and toxicology found that by 2022, publications using only non-animal methods had overtaken those using animals in all seven areas. That could be due to a rise in tests developed as a response to the EU cosmetic-testing ban.

Eye implant that restores vision lost to age approved for use

Government money may also accelerate the shift. China launched a project in 2024 to speed up the development of lab-grown human tissue models. In the US in 2025, the NIH opened its first organoid-development centre, while halting funding for research using only animal models. In Australia, the New South Wales government allocated $4.5 million in 2024 for a programme to reduce and replace animals in medical research.

None of this is to say that animal research will ever be phased out entirely. “It’s animal research that gives us an understanding at the organism level that all of this in-vitro stuff, including organoids, do not,” says molecular and cell biologist Michael Hadjiargyrou at the New York Institute of Technology. Delete a gene from cells in a dish, and the consequences are often minor. Delete it from a living animal, and it can reshape their physiology.

“We need to educate Congress. They need to know how critical animal research is to scientific discovery,” says Hadjiargyrou.

Rusyn thinks political rhetoric on reducing animal testing has occasionally run further than the evidence justifies. He is particularly unimpressed by a US Environmental Protection Agency’s pledge to drop mammal testing requirements for pesticides by 2035. “It is completely bonkers, in my opinion, as a toxicologist,” he says.

Free newsletter

Because cell cultures are often more sensitive to chemicals than an intact animal, they risk banning substances that would otherwise be harmless at the doses people encounter. Even committed opponents like Camp accept that some animal research will always be necessary. It is difficult to see how research into psychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases, for example, could proceed otherwise, given the complexity of the central nervous system and the brain.

But there is some evidence that the regulatory drive for replacements is having a positive impact. In its first-year progress report, the FDA announced that a change to primate toxicity testing for certain immune-based therapies had saved hundreds of non-human primates and that there is “potential for [saving] thousands more animals as methods expand”.

But while the shift to alternative methods may be a long and laborious process, there are at least 190 million reasons to keep trudging ahead.

Roman roads weren’t so straight after all

New Scientist September 15, 2026

Roman roads weren’t as uniformly straight as commonly thought, according to a digital reconstruction of the vast ancient road network that challenges centuries-old assumptions.

“All roads lead to Rome? They are all straight? We still walk Roman roads in the region today? These are widely held assumptions, even among academics,” says Tom Brughmans at Aarhus University in Denmark.

We’re finally reading the secrets of Herculaneum’s lost library

While observations from archaeological digs and surveys have sometimes dispelled these assumptions, Brughmans says it was unclear how accurate they were at the full continental scale of the Roman road network, which connected Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and parts of western Asia.

Advertisement

Last year, Brughmans and his colleagues used topographic mapping, satellite imagery and historical sources to create a map of roads throughout the Roman Empire in AD 150, totalling almost 300,000 kilometres in length – more than double what previous data suggested.

The team has now used the map’s dataset to analyse the topography and structure of ancient roads in terms of their slope, elevation, orientation and straightness, to answer key questions about the Roman road network’s structure. The results were then compared with the modern transport network.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The analysis revealed that Roman roads were mostly straight, but generally only in places where the landscape permitted, such as lowland regions in western Europe and North Africa. In mountainous regions, roads were less straight than modern roads, probably due to topography and technology limitations. Major modern roads tend to be straighter than ancient roads, the study shows, since they are designed to facilitate faster travel by car.

Brughmans and his colleagues also found that around 90 per cent of Roman roads were built with a slope gradient that could permit the passage of animal-driven carts and wagons – including through the Alps. “This suggests that the Romans were dedicated to maintaining and improving overland accessibility and connectivity on an empire-wide scale,” says Brughmans.

Meanwhile, Rome wasn’t as central as the medieval proverb “all roads lead to Rome” suggests. Provincial capitals consistently served as key crossroads, mediating overland communications in their respective provinces. Major public and military roads served as crucial communication arteries, facilitating the flow of goods, people and ideas on the provincial level, according to Brughmans.

Pompeii’s streets show how the city adapted to Roman rule

While some post-Roman cultures kept the same roads and routes into modernity, others didn’t, the study found. According to Brughmans, the reasons for this variability could be massive, such as the industrial revolution, or dependent on local decisions, for example, a town opting to not have a railway station, causing gradual depopulation and decreased investment in road infrastructure. “Our results suggest there are thousands of these stories to be told,” says Brughmans.

“Interestingly, the correlation between the ancient network and the modern network shows that, in some ways, the Romans created the future geography of Europe,” says Ray Laurence at Macquarie University in Australia. “The key limitation to this approach is that the road network was formed over 600 years, but little account for temporal differences has been included in the study.”

Nature Communications DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75453-3

LSD could be approved for anxiety in the US in 2027

New Scientist September 15, 2026

LSD could be approved for treating anxiety in the US as soon as 2027. This expectation comes after a landmark trial showed that a single dose of the psychedelic drug eased the mental health condition without severe or lasting side effects.

“It’s a milestone,” says Greg Cooper at University College London, who wasn’t involved in the trial. “It looks fairly likely that approval from the [US Food and Drug Administration] will happen in the next year or two,” he says. “That would set a precedent for approval elsewhere, such as the UK and Europe.”

The 3 best ways to tackle anxiety, according to a leading expert

“It seems likely that LSD will get FDA approved in the next 12 to 24 months,” says Jules Evans at the Challenging Psychedelic Experiences Project in the US, which researches difficult psychedelic experiences.

Advertisement

The trial was made up of people with moderate or severe anxiety who had tried a range of standard therapies. An approval will therefore probably apply to these groups, says Cooper. But people with milder anxiety would probably be able to access it at their doctor’s discretion, he says.

It is important that people don’t self-administer LSD for anxiety, says Cooper. “The results don’t mean that LSD is safe or effective to try at home,” he says. “An LSD [trip] can last for 6 to 12 hours and can sometimes cause intense fear, panic, confusion or frightening experiences.”

In the trial, Robert Barrow at Definium Therapeutics in New York and his colleagues recruited more than 200 adults across the US with moderate or severe generalised anxiety disorder. This affects almost 3 per cent of adults each year in the US and involves worrying excessively about a broad range of things, such as work and relationships.

The team tapered the participants off any anxiety medications before randomly assigning them to either take tablets adding up to a 100-microgram dose of LSD or placebo pills. A third group took 50 micrograms of LSD, a dose that has mind-altering effects, such as hallucinations, but didn’t substantially reduce anxiety in a prior trial. This was to overcome a common problem in psychedelic research, where participants can usually gauge whether they have taken a drug, impacting the placebo effect.

Free newsletter

Three months after the dosing day, those on the higher dose had experienced a 9.8-point reduction in their anxiety levels, on average, out of 56 on a commonly used anxiety scale. In comparison, the placebo group’s score dropped by 4.7 points, on average, according to results announced by the company.

A reduction of 9.8 would noticeably improve someone’s quality of life, says Cooper. “It is certainly meaningful,” he says. None of the participants experienced severe or lasting side effects.

“In a disorder with high prevalence, high burden, high unmet need and no innovation in decades, a single dose of [LSD] has shown a rapid and durable effect,” said Barrow, speaking during a press briefing in August on a prior trial that found similar results when comparing only 100-microgram-dose LSD with placebo.

Unlike most trials into psychedelics for mental health conditions, the participants in the Definium ones weren’t offered psychotherapy in the weeks following the dosing day. Instead, they received limited psychological support on the day itself, although those already on psychotherapy were allowed to continue having it. “We stripped everything back and tried to show, to the extent we were able, the drug-only effect,” said team member Dan Karlin, also at Definium Therapeutics, at the briefing.

How do we deal with anxiety generated by ever-accelerating change? Sam Conniff and Katherine Templar-Lewis’s The Uncertainty Toolkit sets out to empower us, but it’s a flawed read

Adding regular psychotherapy would probably make the intervention more effective, says Evans. LSD is thought to work partly by boosting the brain’s ability to rewire itself and alter thought patterns, which psychotherapy also aims to do, he says.

In rare cases, LSD can cause psychosis and suicidal thoughts and behaviour. In the latest trial, only people without a history of these behaviours were included. “People were screened extremely carefully and given the drugs in an extremely well-controlled and safe and well-considered environment,” says Cooper. Such careful screening is needed, alongside long-term monitoring, if LSD is approved, says Evans.

Other psychedelic drugs like psilocybin and MDMA are already used to treat particularly severe cases of depression and post-traumatic stress disorder in some countries, such as Australia and Switzerland.

A new biography of Stephen Hawking gets to grips with a complicated man

New Scientist September 15, 2026

Hawking Graham Farmelo (UK: John Murray, out 24 September; US: Bantam, out 24 November)

Is there anything new left to say about Stephen Hawking? The world-famous physicist, who died in 2018, has been the subject of multiple books, documentaries and films, as well as penning dozens of his own tomes. In Hawking by Graham Farmelo, we now have the first authorised biography, and with it access to previously unpublished material from the Hawking family and others. Despite this, his family life is probably the least interesting part of the book – the really compelling stuff is in reassessing his later life.

Part of this is down to a problem common to almost all biographies: people and their families don’t tend to do anything interesting before they become famous for the thing you actually want to read about. The first five of 17 chapters cover Hawking’s life in extensive detail, thanks to detailed documents written by his parents Frank and Isabel, including an unpublished autobiography by the former. But what do we actually learn?

Advertisement

The best new popular science books of September 2026

Unsurprisingly for someone born in 1942, Hawking had a fairly typical middle-class post-war childhood. His father enjoyed DIY and sharing a telescope with Hawking, while his mother was in charge of the bulk of the childcare. The family had a near-miss with a Nazi V1 rocket. They grew their own vegetables to supplement meagre rations. All of this is documented and footnoted by Farmelo’s impressive scholarship, and a figure like Hawking is certainly worthy of such historical investigation, but a thrilling read it is not.

Material on Hawking’s diagnosis with motor neuron disease and his family’s reaction to the news that he would likely be dead within in a decade unsurprisingly pulls much harder on the heartstrings, as does his growing romance and eventual marriage to his first wife Jane. But yet again, I couldn’t help feel that all of this is well-trodden ground, particularly from Jane’s autobiography and the film it spawned, The Theory of Everything, in which Hawking is played by Eddie Redmayne.

It is only around a quarter of the way into the book, when Hawking becomes a jobbing scientist, that my interest began to pick up. The physics landscape of the late 1960s and early 70s was very different to what it is today, and Farmelo does a fantastic job of immersing you in this world. Black holes, which while still puzzling to us today are mostly uncontroversial, were thought of by many as “the cosmic counterpart of the Loch Ness Monster”, Farmelo writes – meaning Hawking was really sticking his neck out in working on them.

It is here that a distasteful recurring thread first emerges – Hawking’s frequent oversight in acknowledging collaborators. At multiple times during his work in the 1970s, Hawking published papers without naming researchers who, under typical scientific norms, should have been co-authors. Farmelo highlights this, but doesn’t seek to examine the psychology behind it, despite the fact there is a clear throughline with the fame and adoration Hawking sought and enjoyed in later life. Still, the fact that Farmelo resurfaces these forgotten disputes, once papered over in Hawking’s route to fame, as part of an authorised biography should be applauded.

Farmelo’s isn’t the first revisionist take on Hawking – Charles Seife got there first in 2021 with Hawking Hawking, a book which examined the making of his celebrity and failed to attract a UK publisher, perhaps because it was felt too controversial in his home country. As Hawking’s life passes further into history, I imagine we can expect more.

Gravitational waves finally prove Stephen Hawking’s black hole theorem

Certainly, Hawking had some truly ground-breaking ideas about black holes in the 1970s, most notably Hawking radiation, the idea that black holes can actually emit particles and eventually even evaporate. We are still yet to detect Hawking radiation, despite most physicists believing that it exists, which is why he never won a Nobel prize – something that Farmelo explains was clearly a sore spot for Hawking.

But after that, when he catapulted to fame with the famously unreadable A Brief History of Time? As the decades wore on, Hawking’s scientific ideas were increasingly pedestrian or indeed flat-out wrong. As Farmelo points out, he frequently lost scientific bets, most strikingly that the Higgs boson didn’t exist – a view Hawking advanced when appear as himself on The Big Bang Theory in an episode that aired just months before the particle was actually discovered. Like many of his contemporaries in the 1990s and early 2000s, Hawking was enamoured with string theory and its variant M-theory, a framework for understanding the universe that increasingly appears today to be a dead end.

My own experience of reporting on Hawking’s research near the end of his life bears this out – he would frequently come out with grabby-sounding headlines, but physicists would politely tell me off the record that they didn’t feel the work was particularly new or detailed enough. Farmelo goes some way to acknowledging this in his epilogue, but doesn’t dwell on why Hawking worked in this way. I think it is probably time we did. Was it down to a lack of original ideas, his penchant for fame-seeking, or his difficulties in communicating as his condition worsened, making it harder for him to publish traditional scientific papers? My honest answer, though it feels impolite to say so, is probably all three.

Where does that leave Hawking, rather than Hawking? If you have already followed his life in detail, I’m not sure you have much to gain from this book. If you only know Hawking as a celebrity scientist, Farmelo’s book gets you closer to the man underneath, though I would argue Seife did it better. If it is 2042 and you’re writing a centenary retrospective of Hawking’s life, Farmelo’s scholarship is a fantastic place to start, but I’m hoping between now and then we can continue to decipher Hawking. When speaking of a man who famously held a party for time travellers (an incident strangely not mentioned in the book), I see no reason to constrain my recommendation to the present.

How I made a slime mould the protagonist of my new sci-fi novel

New Scientist September 15, 2026

I never start writing a science fiction book without first asking scientists a lot of extremely strange questions. My next novel – A Wall Is Also a Road, which comes out on 6 October – was a particularly tough case. I decided that my main character would be a cellular slime mould who is also a graduate student. Why not? I certainly spent most of graduate school feeling like an amoeba.

Why it’s high time we stopped anthropomorphising ants

Gardenpath, the slime mould in question, is studying environmental science at a university that floats high above our galactic plane in a gaseous region known as the circumgalactic medium. You may not have heard of it, but this roughly spherical space is where the Magellanic clouds orbit – two dwarf galaxies near the Milky Way – along with rogue stars, planets and other chunks of random crap squirted out by Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy. It’s full of all kinds of stuff that could support an advanced civilisation, from metals to water.

Before I could even begin to imagine what Gardenpath looked like, I needed to understand where they live. So I called up Molly Peeples at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Maryland, whose lab made stunning simulations of the circumgalactic medium (you can see them on the web at foggie. science). She gave me a tour of this distant region, which is full of spots where the swirling gas is warmer or colder, almost like weather.

Advertisement

I decided that the slime moulds would experience the circumgalactic medium the way humans experience the atmosphere on Earth. Their single-celled bodies could be absolutely enormous in this low-pressure environment full of diffuse gases. Living in this region of space would affect the slime moulds’ understanding of what is scientifically possible, too. That’s why Gardenpath’s fellow scholars think the galactic plane – where we live – is utterly lifeless and uninhabitable. Who could possibly survive in that radiation-saturated gravity well?

Gardenpath literally fumes when their professors scoff at their proposed area of study: a little planet inside one of the Milky Way’s spiral arms. But they don’t express rage by emitting sound waves that agitate molecules in a soupy, thick atmosphere like we do. Instead, they spurt electrons, hormones and other chemicals, opening receptors in their membrane to receive answers. On Earth, we call this cellular signalling. To Gardenpath, it’s just talking.

Wesley Swingley, a molecular biologist at Northern Illinois University, spent a long afternoon with me on a video call brainstorming about what kind of culture would develop among polymorphous people who communicate by swapping smells through apertures in their skin. A diffuser would be like a megaphone, I suggested, and a specific gas like methane could serve as a question mark. Swingley added that the slimes would need an organelle for storing memories, which I dubbed a gnosome. Because their membranes are permeable, Gardenpath’s professors can actually reach inside their body to probe their gnosomes during a test, which is just as creepy as it sounds.

Cells have many single-purpose receptors, which led us to think about something I called an “oath receptor”. Think of it as a biological friendship ring. When Gardenpath’s classmate Oriel wants to become BFFs forever, the two of them reach inside each other to create special receptors that can only receive their friend’s signals. It would be as if your bestie gave you a set of custom ears that can only hear their voice.

New Scientist recommends Togetherness, a radical new view of life

What else do slime mould graduate students need? A way to publish their findings, of course. The slimes store data inside fungi, so their libraries look like nurseries packed with containers of mushrooms. Want to send some data over the network? Plug your fungus notebook into a vent and release a bunch of spores that will bring your information to its destination.

I also created slime mould body language. These blobby little guys get bumpy when they are nervous and stretch up tall to laugh. They sprout more eyestalks when something intrigues them and dangle an extra-long arm to add a sarcastic edge to whatever they are emitting.

This makes things especially weird for Gardenpath on Earth, because humans look like people who are laughing sarcastically while paying very little attention to anything with their paltry two eyes. Still, they manage to find a friend among these weird creatures, a woman named Murtis who lives in a city called Pompeii, at the foot of a very intriguing volcano.

Don’t worry – I talked to a lot of archaeologists to get ancient Roman culture just right. Thankfully, Pompeii expert Eric Poehler at the University of Massachusetts Amherst walked me through Pompeiian plumbing and told me about the famous “prosciutto sundial” discovered in Herculaneum, a site nearby. If you want to know how that fits into the story, you’ll have to read it!

One of the fundamental forces is stronger than we thought

New Scientist September 15, 2026

One of the universe’s fundamental forces appears to be stronger than we thought, a finding that could lead to the discovery of new particles.

The electroweak force unifies the electromagnetic and the weak nuclear forces. Under ordinary conditions, the two forces are distinct and play a role in different processes, such as the weak force being part of radioactive decay and the electromagnetic force affecting charged objects. But at very high energies and temperatures, like as seen in some stages of the early universe and in particle colliders, the two forces combine.

Alessandro Conigli at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz in Germany and his colleagues have now calculated several properties that capture the strength of the electroweak force with unprecedented precision and found a discrepancy with past calculations.

Advertisement

Calculating details of nuclear forces is notoriously difficult. For decades, researchers could only do so with “phenomenological methods” where they could not solve equations exactly but had to include inputs from experiments. This made it more difficult to say whether the best theoretical predictions agreed with experimental findings or not, as the two approaches were mixed.

Lost quantum traces could reveal dark matter at the Large Hadron Collider

In 2024, the phenomenological method was called into question when an experiment involving particles called muons appeared not to match theoretical calculations. However, when researchers refined these calculations using a new technique called lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD), everything worked again.

Conigli and his colleagues used this same technique to calculate two numbers that capture how quantum pairs of virtual particles and their antimatter “antiparticles” affect the strength of the electroweak force at different energy levels.

Across two studies, the team found that the lattice QCD results differed from the phenomenological calculations by around 1 per cent. While small, this discrepancy is significant because the researchers managed to halve the errors in their calculation. This level of precision is crucial for unravelling several mysteries that currently plague our understanding of particles.

Specifically, it will help in the search for phenomena not contained in the standard model of particle physics, which tabulates all known forces and particles, including the electroweak force. It is a remarkably well-tested theory of the world, yet it currently doesn’t explain important phenomena such as dark matter, which is very abundant in our universe.

The mystery of nuclear ‘magic numbers’ has finally been resolved

The properties that the team calculated are badly needed to aid experimental searchers of new particles, says Colin Morningstar at Carnegie Mellon University in Pennsylvania. “I applaud the work very heartily,” he says.

Krishna Kumar at the University of Massachusetts Amherst says the biggest implications of the work will be for particle colliders that are yet to be built, such as the proposed Future Circular Collider, which will surpass the precision of existing experiments. “If you build a new collider, the question is, will you have the theoretical prowess you need to interpret the measurements?” says Kumar.

Conigli says that the new work ought to serve as an encouragement and a reason to keep building better and better colliders. “We truly believe that this could be a game changer,” he says.

Physical Review Letters DOI: 10.1103/r2cx-tl7s

Physical Review D DOI: 10.1103/bk78-wtvd

Reading for pleasure boosts memory, empathy and mental health

New Scientist September 14, 2026

Whether it is a novel by Charles Dickens or Jackie Collins, reading for pleasure is good for brain health. Regularly enjoying a good book has been linked to improved memory, empathy and mental health, among other benefits. This may be through its effect on brain structure or by building cognitive reserve.

“Reading is like a cognitive workout,” says Falk Huettig at the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics in the Netherlands, who wasn’t involved in the research. But reading for pleasure has plummeted over the past 20 years, which may partly be due to us spending more time on social media.

Is reading always better for your brain than listening to audiobooks?

In the latest research, Barbara Sahakian at the University of Cambridge and her colleagues pooled evidence on the effects of reading from pleasure from five surveys and eight long-term studies, with tens of thousands of participants between them.

Advertisement

Many of these linked reading to greater volume of grey matter – part of the brain that supports thinking and memory – and stronger communication between brain regions. This may be how reading builds cognitive reserve, says Sahakian. This is the brain’s ability to defend against ageing and adapt to damage, which is heavily shaped by our lifestyle.

Free newsletter

Reading was also repeatedly linked to improved mental health. One study found that children who began reading for pleasure early in life had moderately larger brain surface areas and volumes in regions linked to emotional control. This feels particularly important amid evidence that youth mental health is worse today than it was decades ago, says Sahakian.

Overall, the team linked reading for pleasure to reduced stress, greater empathy, enhanced wellbeing and reduced loneliness. In childhood specifically, reading was associated with better attention, memory, executive function, academic achievement and fewer mental health problems. Among older adults, it was linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline.

Growing evidence reveals that creativity is one of the best-kept secrets for boosting your health. From live theatre to a quick crafting break, here’s how to harness the power of art in your everyday life

Reading fiction may be particularly important by exposing us to narratives that allow our brain to practice how we might respond to life events, improving its predication abilities. It may also make us feel connected to the characters, reducing feelings of loneliness.

Non-fiction may stimulate different parts of the brain, says Sahakian. But what is important is that you “read for enjoyment, as you will read more often and longer”, she says.

Psychological Medicine DOI: 10.1017/S0033291726105625

Brain implant lets people with paralysis speak and gesture at the same time

New Scientist September 14, 2026

A brain implant has enabled people with paralysis to speak while gesturing, such as nodding or waving. These sorts of exchanges, done via an avatar, could help them communicate with more nuance.

“In our everyday life, gestures play an important role in communication,” says Samantha Brosler at the University of California, San Francisco. “Saying ‘maybe’ and nodding your head has a very different connotation than if you shake your head.”

‘Fusogenic’ neurosurgery let paralysed pigs walk again – are we next?

Experimental brain implants have boosted the ability to either speak or move among people with paralysis, but attempts to do both simultaneously haven’t been very successful. To achieve this, implants need to cover a large part of the sensorimotor cortex, a brain region involved in speech and movement, says Brosler.

Advertisement

Now, Brosler and her colleagues have tested an iPhone-sized implant in this part of the brain in two people with paralysis. The first participant, who the researchers call Bravo-1r, became paralysed after a stroke, while the second, Bravo-6, had amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the most common form of motor neuron disease.

Both participants had lost almost all movement in their limbs. They also couldn’t speak and could only make unintelligible sounds.

Free newsletter

First, the team recorded the participants’ brain activity while they repeatedly attempted to say 10 phrases – such as “hello”, “nice to meet you” and “how’s it going?” – or perform 10 gestures, like waving, clapping and shaking their head. In some cases, the participants attempted to do these separately, while in others they tried both simultaneously.

The team then used each of the participants’ brain recordings to train customised machine learning models to predict their intended phrases and gestures.

To put the models to the test, the participants attempted to repeat various pairs of phrases and gestures that were displayed on a screen. The models interpreted their brain activity and used that to control the movement of an avatar resembling the participants, while the speech predictions flashed up on the screen.

The team chose to use avatars, rather than attempting for the individuals themselves to speak and gesture, because this offered a relatively simple way to prove that both actions could be simultaneously decoded from brain activity, says Brosler.

Keith Thomas, a man in his 40s with no sensation or movement in his hands, is able to feel and move objects by controlling another person’s hand via a brain implant. The technique might one day even allow us to experience another person’s body over long distances.

Bravo-1r’s intended gestures and speech were predicted with 88 and 84 per cent accuracy, respectively, while Bravo-6’s were predicted with 66 and 70 per cent accuracy. “If those models were operating on complete chance, the accuracy would be like 9 per cent,” says Brosler. “It was really exciting.”

“It’s a very nice piece of work, with robust results,” says Henri Lorach at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland. But it’s based on a very limited set of phrases and gestures, and these still need improving, he says. “For daily use without frustration, there needs to be higher accuracy.”

Brosler says the team is working to address this by further training the models and tweaking the algorithms. She also says that future models could move a person’s own body – if their joints and muscles are in a good enough condition – and produce a synthetic voice, rather than having to do this via an avatar.

Nature Neuroscience DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02446-2

Jet-powered drones pose a new threat to Ukraine – can they be stopped?

New Scientist September 14, 2026

A new generation of faster and deadlier attack drones is being launched against Ukraine, forcing engineers to develop more advanced interceptor drones to take out waves of Russian attacks.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, says four new devices are in testing that will help to tip the balance, as the country suffers a surge of attacks from the new drone models on targets such as petrol stations.

Since the start of the conflict, Russia has launched daily strikes using Shahed drones powered by petrol engines similar to those in motorcycles. Ukraine relies on layers of air defence – including fighter jets, machine guns, missiles and interceptor drones – to try to bring them down before they hit civilian or military targets. But the latest jet-powered models are harder to shoot down, sparking a hasty research-and-development effort.

Advertisement

How Ukraine became a drone factory and invented the future of war

On 30 August, Zelenskyy said that over half the drones deployed by Russia are now jet-powered Geran-4 models. The attack drones were originally designed by Iranian company Shahed Aviation Industries but were licensed to Russia, which manufactures them under the name Geran. They are known colloquially in Ukraine as Shahed.

A spokesperson for the Ukrainian government defence innovation department Brave1 told New Scientist that the problem is speed. Older Shaheds used to fly between 100 and 150 kilometres per hour, but the jet-powered updates can reach 500 kilometres per hour.

“The existing copter-type drones cannot always catch up with such targets, which is why jet-powered interceptors are a necessary technological response,” says the spokesperson. “It also represents a major engineering challenge, because the high speed compresses the time window between initial detection and target strike. Russia is constantly experimenting and adapting its Shaheds to make them harder to intercept.”

Free newsletter

One new trick is an updated jet engine that shrouds its heat signature, making it harder to detect for certain countermeasures that home in on hot objects. New types of electronic-warfare devices are also being built into Shaheds, and some even have rear-facing cameras to detect interceptor drones and trigger evasive manoeuvres.

To tackle this new threat, Ukraine will need to develop a new generation of interceptors, capable of speeds of at least 450 kilometres per hour and fitted with AI control.

Brave1 is working closely with the Ukrainian air force to develop and test a fleet of more capable, but still low-cost, interceptors. Four varieties are currently under consideration. One type will be winged drones with jet engines similar to the new Shaheds, another will have an impeller for propulsion, and a third will be familiar quadcopter drones with extremely advanced motors and batteries and some aerodynamic tweaks that allow them to reach the needed speeds.

“Across all these platforms, the key capability is the ability to detect, track and engage a target autonomously at very high speeds. This requires advanced terminal guidance using optical, thermal or other sensing methods, with as little reliance on human reaction time as possible,” says the spokesperson. “The main difficulty lies not in developing the physical hardware, but in developing automation, artificial intelligence.”

Fully autonomous drones have killed human soldiers for the first time

Kyiv resident Olexandra Shekhireva tells New Scientist that almost all Shaheds targeting the city are now jet-powered models. “Just this morning, two Shaheds flew near my house,” she says. “I heard one of them dive down and the sound is really different than the old Shaheds. It’s noisier, louder – not like a conventional motorcycle engine, more like a plane. They’re obviously faster.”

“In recent weeks, the guys who kill drones have been working incredibly hard. In general, their skills are changing and developing a lot, and they are able to quickly adapt to new tricks. The methods and tactics of attacks change literally every two weeks,” says Shekhireva.

She packs a bag and organises a change of clothes before bed, and has timed the journey to different shelters – 46 seconds from her building lobby to a nearby one, and 5 minutes to a better one up the road. She can then decide which to go to based on the type of alert. “I try to sleep until the last minute, which isn’t smart, but it’s simply impossible to not sleep for a week,” says Shekhireva.

But despite the danger posed by the new jet drones, Shekhireva is more concerned with ballistic missiles. “I’ve seen the results of both on my own street. A year ago, a drone hit the residential building next to mine and it destroyed a couple of flats, but the other people in the building still live there. But when a Zircon [ballistic missile] hit my residential building, the shockwave destroyed almost all windows in the district, and the whole building and a couple nearby are condemned,” says Shekhireva.

A judge cleared a court today after loud outbursts punctuated a brief hearing in which a man denied killing two people in Wattle Downs.

The defendant, a 30-year-old from Drury, has interim name suppression.

However, suppression has lapsed for the two people who died: Keagan Desmond Bell and Elaine Beatrice Rudolph.

An elderly man yelled abuse at the defendant as he entered the dock this morning for his first appearance in the High Court at Auckland.

A woman next to the man in the courtroom gallery placed her hand over the man’s mouth as the outburst attracted Justice Michele Wilkinson-Smith’s attention.

“You are entitled to be here,” the judge explained. “I do not want to close this court. If you want to see what happens, you’ll have to be able to calm yourself.”

Justice Wilkinson-Smith took not guilty pleas to two counts of murder through defence lawyer Bradley Moyer and set a trial date for September next year before remanding the defendant back into custody.

“That’s enough,” the judge told the gallery, as verbal abuse erupted as the defendant left the dock.

She ordered the court cleared, but those in attendance for the appearance were already leaving.

Outside the courtroom, the crowd of onlookers could be heard yelling at each other: “Get f***ed” and “F*** you”.

Police found Bell and Rudolph dead at a Gambare Place property in Wattle Downs on August 27. Authorities had received reports of a person armed with a handgun at the property.

Both deceased had fatal gunshot wounds, authorities later reported.

“I can confirm we are speaking with a 30-year-old man who is currently in custody,” Detective Inspector Tofilau Faamanuia Va’aelua said in a statement to the media the day after the shooting.

The man was charged with two counts of murder four days later.

The defendant’s name was suppressed at his first appearance in Manukau District Court earlier this month.

Tributes for the victims have been posted online describing Rudolph as a “beautiful soul been taken too soon” and “so talented, funny and straight up”.

Bell grew up in Māngere, where one mourner described him as “mischief, sporty and a cool bro in our youngin/ teenager days”.

National leader Christopher Luxon and finance spokeswoman Nicola Willis are set to make a “significant” policy announcement, understood to be related to supermarkets.

It comes as Labour rushes forward its own announcement promising to outlaw price gouging if elected.

A spokesperson for the National leader’s office has informed journalists of a “significant” policy announcement about 10.30am in National’s caucus room at Parliament.

A livestream of the announcement will be played at the top of this article.

Labour was expected to unveil its own policy later this morning but has published it earlier than anticipated.

Labour’s policy would make it illegal for large companies with significant market power, such as supermarkets, to charge excessive prices for essential goods and services, or to pay unfairly low prices to suppliers.

The party also wanted to embolden the Commerce Commission to investigate price gouging and support consumer groups and suppliers to do the same.

Companies found to be price gouging would be forced to pay penalties and “hand back every dollar of excess profit”, Labour’s policy states.

New policies are coming thick and fast from political parties as they prepare for the election campaign, which will ramp up after the House rises next week.

Yesterday, Willis hinted the National Party would campaign on another round of income tax cuts.

Speaking on a panel at BusinessNZ’s election conference in Wellington, Willis was asked about bracket creep, the phenomenon by which a person’s income tax burden increases thanks to inflation pushing more of their income into higher tax brackets.

She said National had a “track record” on bracket creep, having been the only party to re-set tax thresholds in 14 years. She said National would try to pull the same trick again.

“If elected again, our position is if we can keep to our Budget Responsibility Rules. [It] is essential that we return the books to balance and get the debt curve ending down.

“Then priority should always be always to adjusting tax settings so that working people on average wages aren’t being slapped with bigger and larger effective taxes every year.”

She said National would have more to say after Treasury opens the books at the Pre-Election Economic and Fiscal Update on September 29.

National campaign chair Simeon Brown, also the State-Owned Enterprises (SOE) Minister, told the Herald yesterday that National was ”not going to the election campaigning on asset sales”, although no formal policy has been released.

Meanwhile, Act promised to freeze the adult minimum wage for three years if elected and make it more difficult for unions to collect membership fees from workers.

The party also promised to introduce a training wage set at 60% of the adult minimum wage for workers under 20, available for their first 12 months with any employer.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins says companies found to be price gouging would be forced to pay penalties and “hand back every dollar of excess profit”. Photo / Anna Heath

Chris Hipkins says that the Labour Party will outlaw price gouging if elected to Government after November’s general election.

The Labour leader is expected to officially unveil the election policy at a convenience store in Wellington this morning, saying a handful of big companies are ripping off households, and there is currently no law preventing it.

The policy would make it illegal for large companies with significant market power to charge excessive prices for essential goods and services, or to pay unfairly low prices to suppliers.

The party also wants to embolden the Commerce Commission to investigate price gouging and support consumer groups and suppliers to do the same.

Companies found to be price gouging would be forced to pay penalties and “hand back every dollar of excess profit”, Labour’s policy states.

“Nearly one in three New Zealand households couldn’t afford enough food last year. Since National took office, the price of butter has gone up 58%, bread is up 45%, and mince is up 30%t,” the party’s commerce and consumer affairs spokeswoman, Arena Williams, said.

She said growers and suppliers were also doing it tough, and that the party intends to target the few “big players”.

“It won’t touch the 97% of New Zealand businesses that are small, like your local dairy or cafe.

“It also only applies in markets for essentials, like food, power, fuel, transport, telecommunications, banking, and insurance.’

Williams said Prime Minister Christopher Luxon promised to fix the cost of living, but said he is “too out of touch to realise that families can’t even afford the basics under his policies”.

Labour has been teasing the policy since the Green Party announced earlier this month its own policy to nationalise 120 pre-existing supermarkets to create a new Government-owned supermarket, “KiwiMart”.

Co-leaders Chlöe Swarbrick and Marama Davidson said the new nationalised supermarket chain would have a mandate to prioritise affordability, and would help break up the power of the current duopoly.

National’s finance spokeswoman Nicola Willis said the Green Party’s policy was reminiscent of communism.

One of New Zealand’s most prolific serial burglars is back in the community after serving his most recent prison sentence in full, despite authorities assessing him as a high risk of reoffending.

Lexington John Lewis has amassed more than 450 convictions, including at least 200 for burglary, and spent more than 30 years behind bars, earning a reputation as one of the country’s most persistent property offenders.

The last judge to jail him for breaking into the homes of unsuspecting New Zealanders described Lewis as having “one of the worst criminal histories I have ever seen”.

“It is fair to say, you have more burglary convictions than any other defendant that I have come across in recent times, if not ever,” she told Lewis when sentencing him in 2023.

A thief’s tale: Lexington Lewis - one of NZ’s worst burglars - is back behind bars

One of NZ’s most prolific ‘institutionalised’ burglars, Lexington John Lewis, back to prison after 4-month crime spree on parole

Lewis has served sentences in prisons across the country and offended extensively in both the North and South Islands.

Police sources have previously described him as one of New Zealand’s most prolific burglars.

In 2019, Lewis was jailed for four years and eight months on seven charges of burglary, among other crimes.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

At sentencing, the judge described Lewis as “a spree burglar” and “clearly a recidivist” who committed offences with “regular abandon”.

“You are a recidivist burglar, beyond doubt – and also a spree burglar,” he told Lewis.

“You are an incorrigible burglar, undeterred by prison,” he said.

Lewis was released on parole in March 2022, but after a few months he cut off his electronic monitoring bracelet and went on a “four-month spree of offending” across Auckland’s North Shore.

He later pleaded guilty to 19 charges including six burglaries by night, and was jailed for a further three years.

Lewis waived his right to appear before the Parole Board a number of times.

On August 8, Lewis’ sentence ended and legally he had to be released. In late July, the Parole Board imposed a raft of release conditions that will remain in place until February.

Judge Jane Lovell-Smith said Lewis completed treatment in prison in May 2025 and had “good” engagement with a psychologist.

He received “a considerable number of positive file notes” about his behaviour inside, was working as a cleaner and undertaking guided releases.

However, after returning a positive drug test in January, a further visit outside the wire was declined, and he lost his job.

Judge Lovell-Smith said Lewis had been assessed by Corrections as a “high risk of reoffending”.

There were also concerns about his “impulse control issues in a stressful environment, and poor problem-solving skills under stressful circumstances”.

“Mr Lewis has previously said that he finds prison life easier and safer than living in the community,” Judge Lovell-Smith said in the parole decision.

“Mr Lewis will be released on his statutory release date on standard and special conditions to six months past the sentence end date. The board is satisfied that each condition which has been proposed by Corrections is a reasonable, necessary and proportionate response to the risk posed by Mr Lewis, and is also the least restrictive means available.

“The board’s paramount consideration, however, remains community safety, balanced appropriately with the offender’s rights.”

The conditions include Lewis living at an approved address, not consuming alcohol or drugs, and attending any psychological assessment and counselling as directed by his probation officer.

Lewis’ troubles seemed to begin not long after his birth in 1969.

Documents obtained from courts around New Zealand reveal he had a “traumatic upbringing”.

By the age of 5 he was “passed around” foster families and boys homes, repeatedly abused along the way. He later sued the Government for the abuse and received a payout.

As a teenager, Lewis was placed with a foster father who did not abuse him, and things were looking up - until the relationship met an “untimely end”.

Lewis arrived home one day to find the dead body of his foster father, with a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head.

He left school at 15, struggling with post-traumatic stress disorder, and began offending soon after.

Between the ages of 17 and 40 - when he was sentenced by Judge Bruce Davidson - he spent just three Christmases out of prison.

“I normally only last two months,” he told the report writer of his prison releases.

His criminal history backs that up, showing incarcerations coming soon after each time his liberty was restored.

As a result of his time behind bars, Lewis became institutionalised.

When out of prison, he relied on the unemployment benefit, but was supplementing the payments by regular offending.

By 2009, he had more than 300 convictions - mostly for burglary, theft and other dishonesty crimes.

But peppered among the stealing was violence - assault with intent to injure, assaults on police, assault with a blunt instrument - and unlawful possession of weapons including firearms and knives.

He escaped and failed to stop for police, routinely drove while disqualified and even managed a prison break in October 1993 while on remand at Hawke’s Bay Regional Prison facing burglary charges.

In 1999, Lewis also made headlines in the Herald when he admitted burglaries in the Cambridge and Whitianga areas.

He pleaded guilty to burgling 39 homes and breaking into 14 cars.

Police believed at the time he was responsible for burgling up to 100 homes while occupants slept.

“Mr Lewis admitted that his past burglary convictions were similar in nature, in that he would enter the property at night while people were home and take their bank cards,” the pre-sentence report said.

He admitted he was institutionalised and preferred prison to the free world, stating people behind bars “cared” for him.

“I have brothers in here, staff care about me,” he told the report writer.

Anna Leask is a senior journalist who covers Christchurch issues and national crime and justice. She joined the Herald in 2008 and has worked as a journalist for more than 20 years with a particular focus on family and gender-based violence, child abuse, sexual violence and homicides. GDT: Dairy prices fall 1.1% as butter slumps, whole milk powder eases

New Zealand Herald September 15, 2026

The GDT index fell 1.1%, with butter down 5.7% and cheddar up 16.5%. Photo / Devyn Staines

The Global Dairy Trade (GDT) price index fell 1.1% at the latest auction overnight, reversing some gains recorded at the previous event.

The result follows a 0.1% increase at the previous auction two weeks ago, when strong demand for proteins helped counter seasonal increases in supply.

Whole milk powder, which has the biggest influence on Fonterra’s farmgate milk price, fell 0.8% to US$3565/MT.

Skim milk powder, Fonterra’s second-largest reference product, edged up 0.1% to US$3689/MT.

Butter dropped 5.7% to US$4760/MT, while anhydrous milk fat fell 3% to US$5739/MT.

Cheddar bucked the downward trend, rising 16.5% to US$4075/MT.

Among other products, buttermilk powder eased 0.5% to US$4549/MT, lactose fell 4.3% to US$1794/MT, and mozzarella declined 6% to US$3992/MT.

A total of 42,444 tonnes sold to 126 winning bidders across 18 bidding rounds, with 155 participants taking part.

On July 13, Fonterra revised its 2026/27 farmgate milk price forecast to $9.25/kgMS, within a range of $8–$10.50, down from the opening forecast of $9.75/kgMS and a range of $8–$11 announced in May.

For the 2025/26 season, which ended on May 31, the co-op narrowed its forecast range to $9.60–$9.80 per kgMS, from $9.40–$10, while keeping the midpoint unchanged at $9.70/kgMS.

That compares with the record $10.16/kgMS paid for the 2024/25 season.

Woman falls through glass shower after fainting with flu

New Zealand Herald September 15, 2026

By RNZ Digital reporters

This story contains a graphic image of an injury.

A woman who fainted through a glass shower door while sick with Influenza A is urging others to take the flu seriously, as a doctor warns hot showers can trigger fainting.

Kat Murray was 26 when, two years ago, she suffered multiple deep cuts in her back, with the glass narrowly missing a critical nerve that could have left her paralysed.

Hospitalisations from flu and flu-like illnesses have been in the “very high” category for weeks, according to data from PHF Science. In Auckland they were at 10-year highs.

When Murray woke up feeling unwell she assumed it was a cold and took the day off work, but the next day she felt worse.

“I felt really cold so I took a hot shower to warm up. While I was in the shower I was hit by overwhelming nausea and instinctively tried to make it out to avoid being sick in the shower.”

Murray remembered leaning towards the window before passing out.

“I fell backwards into the shower glass and went through it ... there was blood everywhere, glass everywhere. I didn’t know my name, the day of the week, anything.”

Murray said her partner helped get her to a local A&E, where she sat in a blood-soaked jersey for four hours.

“It was scary – I had a big gash from my shoulder blade leading towards my neck and all the way down my back. I had eight stitches in one gash and the majority taped up so they couldn’t split.”

While there, Murray did a swab test to rule out Covid-19 and was told she had Influenza A.

“It took three weeks for all the stitches and the scabbing to heal and another three weeks to kind of normalise all the scar tissue. I’ve got a good handful of scars on my back still.”

Murray said it was important for people to take having the flu seriously and to be more aware that it wasn’t just a standard bug.

“We treat the flu like a minor inconvenience rather than the aggressive systematic threat it is,” she said.

“Young people often feel invincible, pressuring themselves to keep working, moving and functioning when they need rest and proper medical care.

“Stay home, get checked by a doctor and take your health seriously.”

Medical director at Tū Ora Compass Health, Dr Louise Poynton, said anyone could still get unwell with the flu and it could be serious and needed to be treated as such.

Poynton said anyone who was unwell with a fever or dehydration had a higher chance of falling as it could lead to a drop in blood pressure.

“Hot water can cause blood vessels to relax, which can also cause a drop in blood pressure.”

For anyone with the flu it was important to stay hydrated and take care when moving from sitting to standing, as well as giving the body time to adjust before moving around after standing, Poynton said.

Jumping into a hot shower when feeling dizzy or light-headed could increase the risk of fainting.

She said even someone who was otherwise fit and healthy, would normally need between seven and 10 days at home to recover – and some effects of the flu could last several weeks.

“Anyone who has had it will take it seriously,” she said.

While the number of cases this season seemed to be slowly easing, there were a lot of cases around and doctors were seeing people with complications of the flu.

“Stay home if you’re unwell, wear a mask, keep your house well ventilated ... more broadly stay healthy – eat nutritious food, sleep well and stay active.”

She also urged anyone who hadn’t had a flu vaccine this year to get one.

Central Hawke’s Bay cattle stud secures $50,000 bull, breaking Angus New Zealand record

New Zealand Herald September 15, 2026

Jeremy Cullwick (far left), owner of Tapahia Angus Stud, bought yearling Angus bull KayJay Captain W901. Also pictured are Sam Kjestrup, Rodney Kjestrup, Joan Kjestrup and Neil Kjestrup of the Wairarapa-based stud KayJay Angus.

An Angus New Zealand yearling bull sale record has been broken after Central Hawke’s Bay cattle stud owners Jeremy and Kate Cullwick bought a “chunky” one for $50,000.

The couple, who own Tapahia Angus Stud at Wanstead, bought the yearling bull, KayJay Captain W901, at the KayJay Angus auction in the Wairarapa on September 10.

Jeremy Cullwick said that with the bull insured and due to arrive on the farm in the next couple of weeks, there were already plans to collect his semen to be sent to Australia.

“There is an Australian stud who have been in touch and they are securing the Australian semen rights for him as well.

“That will help contribute to paying the price of him.”

Cullwick said the 1-year-old animal was chosen for his ability to “take the stud forward”.

He said there were certain physical and genetic traits that he desired and found in Lot 2 which made him perfect to cross with his “fantastic line-up of yearling heifers”.

“He is a cracking bull; he’s well rounded with many good attributes; he is thick, solid and chunky.

“He has got a great set of feet and really good back legs and moves really well, so that great conformation combined with a great set of EBV [estimated breeding values] made him a standout.”

Cullwick said the animal’s structure was important in the selection process.

“You don’t want them to break down on the hills ... we need our animals to last.”

Cullwick said they didn’t set out to break any records.

“You always do have a maximum figure of what you are prepared to pay, and we were very close to that.

“We were very keen to get him.

“His genetics are going to influence our stud for years to come.”

Cullwick said kudos should be given to the Kjestrup family for their breeding.

Jane Allen, the general manager of Angus New Zealand, a member-based organisation with a “Bred for Balance” focus, said Hallmark Angus near Tutira previously held the record of $29,000 from a 2025 sale.

Allen said the sales record price signalled “significant confidence” in Angus NZ members’ genetic programmes.

“Beef farmers are investing to ensure there is financial deliverable bred for performance and profitability within their herds.”

Roddy Kjestrup of KayJay Angus said they were happy the bull was “heading to a great home at Jeremy and Kate’s”.

“Lot 2 was a quality animal right from a young age.

“He displayed real sire appeal and had a presence about him from day one.

Kjestrup said the animal was a heifer’s first calf, weighing 27kg at birth, 335kg at weaning and 578kg on sale day.

“Captain W901 has a great data package showing calving ease, short gestation, growth, high fats and IMF [intramuscular fat], combining with his raw power, where he is packed with heavy muscle and bone, which sets him apart from other calving ease sires.

“He’s a bull with real substance and great shape.”

He was the top-priced bull in the sale, with another Captain selling for $22,000.

Michaela Gower joined Hawke’s Bay Today in 2023 and is based out of the Hastings newsroom. She covers Dannevirke and Hawke’s Bay news and loves sharing stories about farming and rural communities.

While parts of the country have been treated to warmer springtime temperatures, snowfall is still in store for the bottom of the country.

A road snowfall warning is in place for the Crown Range Rd from 3am this morning until 3am Thursday.

Snow is expected to drop to 500m early Wednesday afternoon, and 3 to 5cm of snow may accumulate above 700m, with less at lower levels.

The heaviest falls are likely between midday and 8pm Wednesday.

Motorists have been reminded of the ongoing closure of SH6 between Lake Hāwea and Makarora due to slips caused by recent weather.

Weather permitting, the road will reopen daily for three convoys.

Southbound convoys leave Makarora village at 7.15am, 12.45pm and 6.15pm and northbound convoys leave Isthmus Peak carpark at 8am, 12pm and 5.30pm.

There is also ongoing stabilisation work underway on the zig-zags down from Crown Terrace to SH6 near Arrowtown, with a one-lane closure in place 24/7 for several weeks, operated by traffic lights.

Motorists are advised to allow extra time, especially at peak travel periods.

MetService has issued a heavy snow watch for Central Otago, Southern Lakes and the Mackenzie Basin from Wednesday 4pm until Thursday 2am.

Heavy rain watches have also been issued for Fiordland from Tuesday 6pm until 10am today, and the ranges of Westland District from Wednesday 6am until midnight Thursday.

Temperatures should begin recovering after Thursday, with Christchurch forecast to reach about 16C on Friday.

The wintry turn comes just weeks after New Zealand recorded its third-warmest winter on record, with only one winter since 2000 colder than average.

By Kate Green of RNZ

Wellington Hospital’s emergency department has closed off part of a corridor this week to accommodate extra beds as patient numbers remain high.

Health NZ acting interim group director of operations for Capital, Coast and Hutt Valley Robert Blaikie said: “At times when there is high occupancy [in ED], steps are taken to temporarily increase capacity by placing up to four beds in a corridor outside the ED observation unit for stable patients awaiting admission or discharge.”

That was the case on Tuesday.

“A nurse is assigned to this area for monitoring,” he said. “To minimise disruption and create privacy for these patients, access to the corridor is temporarily restricted.”

This winter had brought a significant increase in presentations to emergency departments across the country, he said.

This flu season, a particularly contagious strain of influenza, coupled with already high occupancy rates in hospitals, was contributing to high levels of stress across the health system nationwide.

Alongside steps to temporarily increase capacity, Blaikie said Health NZ was prioritising acute care, increasing temporary capacity in wards, freeing up more inpatient beds by frequently reviewing ward patients to assess if they were ready for discharge, and using additional community support, such as early supported discharge.

It was also ensuring suitable ED patients were being seen in alternate primary care places, outside of EDs.

Blaikie said it reinforced the importance of work underway to relocate and expand the ED and increase capacity in acute services.

On Wednesday, nurses at Tauranga ED, through the NZNO union, declared a “state of emergency” themselves, with staff there also being asked to assess and treat patients in corridors due to a lack of space.
