A student-led survey of nearly 600 students has found most oppose the Government’s proposed social media ban for under-16s.

Respondents argued that platforms play an important role in communication, connection and support.

The survey, conducted by 15-year-old Ōtūmoetai College student Liam Howard, attracted 596 responses from students across New Zealand, including 549 from the Bay of Plenty, mainly from Ōtūmoetai College.

On August 24, the Government introduced the Online Safety (Minimum Age and Child Safety Risk Assessment) Bill, which would ban under-16s from social media and require technology companies to protect children online.

Under the bill, platforms including Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook would have to take reasonable steps to verify users are aged 16 or older.

Companies that fail to comply could face penalties of up to 10% of their global revenue.

The survey was distributed through school networks between March and June.

Respondents, from Years 9 to 13, completed it anonymously and were required to log in through Google to prevent multiple responses.

The questionnaire included multiple-choice and written-response questions about students’ social media use and attitudes towards the proposed ban.

“I didn’t see anyone talking about what youth were thinking on the subject,” Liam said.

“I saw on the news it would be all about the parents, whose perspective is important, but I just felt odd they were leaving out information on the people the ban is literally about.”

He said if no one else was going to collect the information, he would do it himself.

“I should at least try get the data and try to get it out there so people know what we [teens] think about the subject.”

According to Liam’s survey, 65.8% of respondents said they opposed the proposed ban, while 21.9% supported it.

The survey asked students how much time they spent on social media each day, what they used it for, whether they believed it did more harm than good, whether they supported the Government’s proposed social media ban for under-16s, and what their biggest concern would be if a ban was introduced.

Eighty-five per cent of respondents identified social media as a major tool for communicating and socialising with friends.

More than 60% said they were highly concerned about losing contact with friends and family if a ban was introduced.

But 11.5% of surveyed students said social media was doing more harm than good, while nearly two-thirds said it was not.

Liam said the results showed social media was used to connect with family and friends.

“Which I found really wholesome. People weren’t talking about it in terms of entertainment; they were actually talking about real uses for social media.”

He said respondents had raised concerns that the ban could leave young people less willing to speak up if they encountered unsafe situations online.

“If they manage to get onto social media and they end up in an unsafe situation, they’re not going to feel like they can talk about it because they’re not supposed to be on social media.”

Liam said the Government should introduce a non-partisan youth committee so young people could have a stronger voice in decisions affecting them.

“The harms outweigh the benefits and students need a voice. They need to be heard right now.”

He plans to make a submission to a select committee as the bill progresses.

“I know that I want to get into politics so that I can try to help people and defend against a policy like this. I know I could provide a fresh voice.”

Netsafe works with individuals, families, schools and communities to address online harm, promote digital wellbeing and encourage safer use of technology and social media.

Chief executive Brent Carey said the “real test” of the legislation would not be simply how many social media accounts were removed.

“It will be whether fewer young people experience harm.”

He said parents and governments had become “increasingly frustrated” by the gap between the influence platforms had over young people’s lives and the accountability companies faced when harm occurred.

“Age restrictions offer a clear and easily understood response. Their growing popularity also reflects a loss of confidence that voluntary measures alone will deliver adequate protection.”

Education Minister Erica Stanford said she regularly visited high schools and made a point of speaking with students about their social media experiences.

Asked how the Government had engaged with young people on a social media ban, Stanford said she regularly asked students about what they were seeing and experiencing online.

“Recently I sat down with a group of 13 young people and talked to them about how their experiences of social media had impacted them.”

She described the discussion as “enlightening and concerning” and said it had made her “committed” to ensuring the Government moved ahead with measures to reduce online harm.

Ōtūmoetai College principal Russell Gordon said he “strongly” supported giving students opportunities to have their voices heard in important community conversations.

“Young people are living with these technologies every day, and their experiences and perspectives should be part of the conversation about how we respond to them.”

He said social media had “clear benefits”, but warned it drew teenagers into a world dominated by platforms designed to keep them engaged, sometimes to the “point of addiction”.

“If our experience with the cellphone ban is anything to go by, younger students may benefit from being given a break from the relentless demands that social media, whether deliberately or unwittingly, can place on them.”

Kaitlyn Morrell is a journalist for the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post. She has lived in the region for several years and studied journalism at Massey University.

Wild, profane and heartbreaking: A guide to Anthony Bourdain’s best TV

Sydney Morning Herald September 16, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

In the parlance of the business in which Anthony Bourdain made his name, the film Tony is the first course in an extended tasting menu. It’s the appetiser of a degustation menu that will run over many servings and involve many ingredients and helping hands.

The film, which is now in cinemas, is a coming-of-age drama about a restless, angry and punch-drunk teenager (played by Dominic Sessa) on a summer-season bender of rebellion, booze, unrequited first love and soul-searching. It’s the origin story of the man who decades later would become executive chef of a feted Manhattan restaurant, a bestselling author and a frighteningly prolific TV presenter.

The film foreshadows the book that propelled chef Bourdain’s meteoric second act in 2000, when Kitchen Confidential: Adventures in the Culinary Underbelly (it’s worth remembering the book’s full title) became a global bestseller. It kicks off with this memorable passage from the book’s opening chapter. “I was … a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless young lout, badly in need of a good ass-kicking”. His words.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

2:25

Trailer: Tony

This new film gives a glimpse into a young Anthony Bourdain's first steps into the restaurant industry.

It vividly pinpoints many of the qualities that would make Bourdain one of the unique, original and treasured figures TV has ever known. He was a mercurial and mouthy personality who wore his heart on his sleeve, ever inquisitive, with a yen for adventure, food, pleasure and companionship, and a well-documented taste for drugs and addictive behaviours. Bourdain died by suicide in 2018, reportedly after the breakdown of a relationship, though the toxicology report indicated he wasn’t taking drugs at the time.

It’s not entirely surprising nor unexpected that Tony has also renewed interest in his TV shows.

It was here, Bourdain’s third act, as a TV presenter after quitting professional cooking following his book’s success (and revelations of the restaurant world’s unglamorous secrets), where the magic really happens.

First came A Cook’s Tour (SBS On Demand, Tubi). Made for the US Food Network between 2002 and 2003, it has Bourdain visiting the world’s “foodie” hotspots (Sydney and Melbourne included), eating in starred restaurants and local greasy spoons, meeting with food-scene celebrities and what would decades later be known as influencers. It’s very much in the boilerplate format of food and travel shows, and the least interesting of his TV work. The middling quality of the video has certainly not helped its longevity.

It was in No Reservations (2005-12, Amazon Prime Video) and Parts Unknown (2013-18, Amazon Prime Video, 7Plus, 10Play) that Bourdain, his crew and creative partners took flight. They invented a format and style that transcends most if not all the norms of the food and travel genre. These shows aren’t about plugging destinations or theme parks, or even to paint a rosy picture of a place.

In the Beirut episode of No Reservations, for instance, Bourdain and his crew arrive the day before war breaks out. From their luxury hotel they keep the cameras rolling, ever aware that despite their safety and boredom the rest of the population is in peril. The episode ends with this heartbreaking passage: “Maybe in the real world, the one without cameras and happy food and travel shows, everybody, the good and the bad together, are all crushed under the same terrible wheel. I really hope I’m wrong about that.”

These are shows that use travel and food as their starting points, but are mostly about people living in diverse parts of the globe, their cultures, habits and histories, their dreams, disappointments and hopes.

They are also about how Bourdain saw himself. The shows are opinionated, brash, wild and profane, as well as tender and occasionally heartbreaking – much like Tony in the film. In many episodes of No Reservations and Parts Unknown, Bourdain openly and unsentimentally discusses his depression. In Tony, the character finds salvation in the kitchen after a particularly dark and unpleasant night on the town by learning how to cook and then observing the joy that brings to diners. He also finds companionship among the fellow dirtbags toiling in the kitchen’s insufferable conditions (shout-out to Stavros Halkias as Dimitri, a character who also appears in Kitchen Confidential).

Just as Kitchen Confidential lifted the lid on the dirty secrets of the hospitality trade, Bourdain’s TV shows are no less scathing of food porn and fame, not to mention his role in the dog and pony circuit of book signings and celebrity-chef talks.

“Look at me now travelling the world like a Borscht Belt comedian,” he says while visiting a food festival in New Zealand in No Reservations. The willingness to make himself the butt of the joke is evident in Tony too.

It’s hard to fathom the scale of Bourdain’s output: 104 episodes of Parts Unknown and 142 episodes of No Reservations. Bourdain died during filming of Parts Unknown, leaving a few episodes without his narration (there’s also two posthumous tribute instalments). Each episode has its own unique flavour and style, invariably shaped around a destination’s depiction in popular culture, such as a movie associated with that place. Apocalypse Now for the Congo, Mad Max for “the arse end of the world”, Australia.

The final course of the Bourdain feast is arguably the most challenging. It’s the little seen 2021 feature-length documentary Roadrunner: A Film About Anthony Bourdain (Apple TV, Amazon Prime Video). It’s a difficult and painful reckoning by those who intimately knew Bourdain, focusing largely on his globetrotting, TV career after Kitchen Confidential and how his life unravelled in the months leading up to his suicide.

2:39

Official Documentary for Anthony Bourdain's Roadrunner

The Official Documentary for Anthony Bourdain's film Roadrunner.

Many of the people that director Morgan Neville interviewed in Roadrunner appeared in one or more episodes of No Reservations and Parts Unknown. Bourdain’s TV family included chefs, artists, filmmakers, musicians and writers. There’s a lovely nod to that in Tony, in a pivotal scene where the charismatic French chef Eric Ripert has a blink-and-miss cameo. Ripert frequently appeared in the shows and his presence is a touching reminder of how loyal people were to Bourdain.

In many ways Tony and Roadrunner are perfect bookends of Bourdain’s career and life. They shine a light on the unique talent he brought to his still luminous TV shows.

All supporting acts withdraw from Ed Sheeran’s tour in solidarity with Macklemore

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 21:47:16 GMT

Three openers and live band for Sheeran’s tour depart after removal of Macklemore over ‘free Palestine’ comments

All four supporting acts for upcoming dates of Ed Sheeran’s Loop tour have withdrawn in solidarity with fellow opening act Macklemore, as backlash grows to his removal from the tour over onstage comments in support of Palestine.

Finneas, the singer who was scheduled to open for Sheeran on six South American dates in November, withdrew from the tour on Tuesday afternoon, hours after Sheeran posted his own lengthy statement to Instagram explaining pressure from venue owners to remove Macklemore for pro-Palestine comments made during two shows at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium.

In a two-minute speech on 4 September, the Grammy-winning artist told the audience he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”, along with the words “free Palestine”. The remark prompted a petition calling for Macklemore’s removal from the tour from the Israeli American Council and the opposition of some venue owners – including Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and a prominent donor to Israel.

“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneas wrote on social media. “I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people.”

The decision came shortly after Aaron Rowe, an Irish singer who opened for Sheeran in Australia earlier this year and was scheduled for the 10 remaining dates in North America, announced his own withdrawal from the tour. “I don’t take the decision lightly,” he wrote on Instagram. “Ed has been a friends to me and has changed my life, I could never thank him enough for this.

“But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation. I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children. I would lose all respect for myself to carry on as normal.”

The Irish band Beoga shortly after joined Rowe in departing the US tour to protest the “silencing of Macklemore by zionist lobbies”.

“We are a traditional Irish band who never saw ourselves playing in stadiums of that size and that opportunity is not lost on us,” they wrote on social media. “We have been friends with Ed for over 10 years now and will continue to be. We believe in dialogue as a means of progressing the plight of the Palestinian people.”

The Danish pop band Lukas Graham also dropped out of the tour on Tuesday afternoon. “We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to grow up. Wherever they live. Whatever flag flies over them,” wrote lead singer Lukas Forchhammer on the band’s social media. “Money doesn’t give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody’s bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we’re allowed to acknowledge.”

The abrupt withdrawals of the Sheeran’s opening acts came hours after the English singer confirmed that Kraft, along with several other stadium owners, refused to allow the tour to play at their venues if Macklemore continued to open for him. Though Sheeran wrote that the was “appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine” and “the suffering and pain caused on both sides,” he said that attempts to broker conversations between parties was unsuccessful, and the “venue’s and the promoter’s decision was final”.

“Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine,” he wrote in a multi-page post on Instagram. “I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living.”

“I have spent this week trying to build bridges, to find a solution and unfortunately, was unable to do so,” he concluded. “I know who I am, both as a person and as an artist, and those who know my heart know my values too.”

The tour withdrawals join a growing chorus of backlash to Macklemore’s removal, including numerous politicians and Ms Rachel, the children’s educator and Youtube star, who wrote on Instagram: “Ed Sheeran had an opportunity [to] show that we won’t be bullied into punishing people for supporting Palestine. Instead he caved to people who refuse to accept what the world knows. A genocide is happening in Gaza. We all need to speak on it.”

Kehlani, the singer whose pro-Palestine activism led to the cancellation of a concert at Cornell University last year, commented on social media in support of Macklemore: “A LOT of the venues / owners are rallied together this way. honored to know you brother.”

In his own statement on Monday, Kraft did not deny refusing to allow Macklemore on stage at his Gillette Stadium outside Boston, and said the decision was based on both Macklemore’s “recent actions” and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”.

“I would welcome the opportunity to sit down with Macklemore and discuss the facts, because ultimately our goal is the same – peace for all people, an end to suffering, and an end to all hate,” he said.

70 Up review – a deeply moving conclusion for the 63-year-long TV experiment

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 21:30:01 GMT

The landmark documentary series looked like it was done for good – until one participant was diagnosed with terminal cancer. Asif Kapadia takes the helm for its most elegaic, thoughtful outing ever

And so the great experiment begun by Granada Television in 1964 is over. That year, Seven Up! introduced the viewing public to 14 primary school children – 10 boys and four girls from a range of backgrounds – who would become part of an ongoing documentary project that returned to film them at regular intervals and interrogate the truth of the Jesuitical motto “Give me the child for the first seven years and I will give you the man”.

Seven Up!, part of ITV’s flagship World in Action series, was directed by Paul Almond but thereafter the enterprise became synonymous with Michael Apted, who originally helped find the children and took over the making of the programmes. He died in 2021, two years after completing 63 Up. It had been thought the series would end there but when one of the participants, Nick Hitchon – a Yorkshire farmer’s son who grew up to be a nuclear scientist – called one of the team to say that he had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and wanted to give one last interview, a final episode was commissioned.

Directed by Asif Kapadia, it has a more reflective and elegiac tone than in previous years. Lynn, who spent most of her life as a devoted children’s librarian – council funds and cuts permitting – died in 2013. Almost everyone else is retired. Everyone is looking back. Jackie speaks with great relief of the calm and relative solitude in which she now lives, having moved away from the family that – reading between the lines – she clearly loves but required much from her. The three prep school boys, John, Charles and Andrew, first seen perched on the sofa in their headteacher’s study and talking with disarming sweetness about futures at Charterhouse, the Dragon and Oxbridge, have had the lives of privilege and ease that they expected and that we expected for them. Andrew wishes he had spent more time with his family. “School plays,” he says. “Sports days.” There are shades of similar regret from some of the other men, too. But the Up series has always had to sacrifice the interrogation of such detail for breadth of coverage, and this is one of the many potentially fruitful paths you wish had been travelled further down.

Tony, the self-described “Little Artful Dodger” and would-be jockey turned cab driver remains as irrepressible as ever, though he notes his biggest mistake was deciding not to commit to the former career after his mentor warned him that he would struggle to meet the necessary weight all his life. Bruce has retired from teaching and now sings in the local choir, walks his dog on the beach and volunteers with the local branch of the RNLI. The thoughtful, gentle, Christian boy has become a thoughtful, gentle, Christian man.

Symon, the terribly sad-eyed boy brought up in a children’s home (“What you don’t have, you don’t miss,” he said at 14, and it was so nakedly untrue that you still have to look away when they show this moving scene again here) has fostered more than 100 children with his second wife over the last 20 years. He looks happier now. The children are welcomed back for visits all the time. Paul, Symon’s companion in the children’s home, has built himself a good life in Australia. He is a grandfather now. “Family is 100% the main thing.”

Neil – the perky, bright Liverpudlian schoolboy who dreamed of Oxford but has struggled with depression all his life, and experienced periods of homelessness in between being a local councillor and lay minister and, briefly, a husband – now lives alone in France. The perkiness left long ago but he is as thoughtful, articulate and unassuming as ever. He is clearly still vulnerable in many ways and his existence precarious, but he has found a way of being that brings him contentment enough. Yes, he says, he is sometimes lonely. “But that is a characteristic of the age … I’m probably as happy as I can be, given my life.”

There is, especially in the second instalment of this final film, something of a meta-narrative too, as the participants give their thoughts about the series and about Apted. We also hear archive footage of Apted reflecting on what he learned over the years. Jackie was perhaps his earliest and most vocal combatant, challenging him over various questions – largely about marriage and sex – that she said he only dared ask the women, and she pulls him up on his class bias too. John describes him as having “a sneering and somewhat supercilious manner” and, in essence, painting the privileged as bogeymen. Apted himself said he was judgmental at the beginning, and gradually taught himself to stay out of things as much as possible. But it remains clear, 60-odd years on, that this was not a rigorous or objective journalistic venture but a series profoundly shaped by one man’s vision, background and baked-in assumptions. Acknowledging this, as Kapadia does, is the best thing to do with it now. The achievement has become an artefact to be admired, still, but questioned too.

70 Up aired on ITV1 and is on ITVX now

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 21:12:19 GMT

As he nears the end of a hectic ­summer Harry Brook was offered the chance to rest rather than play this series and how Sri Lanka must wish Pakistan’s red-ball side had extended him enough to force a ­lay-off. As it turned out the 27-year-old could hardly have looked fresher as he inspired his side to an overwhelming win over emphatically outclassed opponents, a brilliant century powering them to a 19th victory in just 22 games since he took over the captaincy, secured by the margin of 119 runs.

It was Brook’s second T20 century, making him the third Englishman to score more than one. He cavorted to triple figures off 42 balls of which precisely a third were dispatched to the boundary, six of them beyond it, and ended unbeaten on 114. But as much as his power impressed, using the size of the ground and manipulation of angles to maximum advantage, aided occasionally by the tourists’ imperfection in the field, he also scurried a succession of twos.

Brook’s first international T20 ­century was scored in Sri Lanka, against Pakistan during the World Cup earlier this year, also the first time that he batted for his country at No3. He has now done so eight times, scoring in addition to those two tons two unbeaten half-centuries and compiling an average of 95.2 at a ludicrous strike rate of 200.84.

Ben Stokes, posting on X in the moments after England’s innings concluded, described him as “an absolute freak” who “not even the genius of KP [Kevin Pietersen] could come close to talent-wise”. The same may well be true of Jos Buttler, by general acclaim ­England’s greatest ever white-ball batter, who scored a 44-ball 80 – aided by being dropped on 45 – but languished in deep shade opposite his successor as both captain and inspiration.

Sri Lanka arrived with a record of five wins in 16 T20s this year, all but one of those victories coming at home – though the team with the best record in their country in 2026 is England, who won 100% of their six games there last winter.

This was the ninth meeting of the senior men’s teams of these two nations this year, with at least five more to come before the end of next month: two more T20s in this series, the three ODIs that follow, and two more 50-over games as part of a ­tri-series in Pakistan that could end with one final confrontation in Lahore on Halloween. Brook left them punch-drunk here, and if they fail to recover their senses and create a plan to counter him they are in for a miserable few weeks.

Aneurin Donald, at 29 England’s oldest debutant since Dawid Malan in 2017, started strongly, hitting Maheesh Theekshana for a six and a four off the final two balls of the first over, but the next one he faced, the opening delivery of the third over and Dunith Wellalage’s first of the night, was skewed into the air, straight down the ground, and easily caught. Encouraged by an over that brought a wicket and just five runs Wellalage – who would return to top score for Sri Lanka from No 8 – stayed on for a second, off which Brook flayed three sixes and as many fours, and from there England never let up.

There were 15 dot balls in England’s innings, a total Sri Lanka were more than halfway to matching inside two overs and had passed by the end of the powerplay.

After six overs England had 90 for the loss of one wicket; then the tourists at the same stage had 32 and had lost three, their task already far beyond forlorn.

British bosses to be forced to meet with employees who request flexible working

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 19:33:25 GMT

Under new workers’ rights, employers will have to ‘properly consider’ proposed shift changes and explain decisions

Company bosses will have to sit down with workers who request flexible working and justify their reasons for any refusals under new rights announced by Louise Haigh on Tuesday.

The first secretary of state told the TUC conference that employers would have to “properly consider” requests for flexibility and offer a face-to-face meeting under new rights for workers.

Speaking to trade union representatives in Brighton, she said: “Life isn’t always as neat as we’d like it to be or as employers would like it to be. There’s kids to pick up, parents to look after, families who rely on us at short notice.

“And sometimes a little bit of flexibility can make all the difference. Now I know that businesses have to make things work too. Not every job can be done from home and not every request can be agreed.

“But every request can be taken seriously. So today I can announce that we will strengthen the right to flexible working. If an employer wants to turn down a request they will have to sit down with their employee, properly consider it and explain why.”

Under current rules all employees have a legal right to request flexible working which employers must consider in a “reasonable manner”, but the new rules would entail bosses sitting down with employees and explaining the reason behind their decision.

Haigh also praised unions for their work campaigning for the Employment Rights Act, which introduced significant new rights for workers on sick pay, parental leave and zero-hours contracts.

She said: “Because of you, working people have had the biggest uplift in their rights in a generation. Changes that won’t just transform lives today … but the lives of our children and our grandchildren.”

In a speech that was pointedly warm towards unions, some of whom were openly critical of the former prime minister Keir Starmer, she said that Andy Burnham understood that “the strength of our movement is drawn from our roots in the trade unions”.

She added: “We need to go further and faster to deliver the scale of change the country expect. But never be in any doubt whose side we are on. Whether it was standing up for workers illegally sacked by P&O Ferries … Or changing public procurement to create more good jobs here in Britain. We are proudly on the side of working people.”

Texas’s star quarterback, Arch Manning, has apologized after joking about an AI-generated video that depicted Longhorns coach Steve Sarkisian slapping ESPN college football reporter Holly Rowe after last Saturday’s game.

Manning had been asked at a press conference on Monday about the social media reaction to the Longhorns’ 24-23 upset win over No 1 Ohio State. Rowe had attempted to ask Sarkisian a question for the standard postgame interview, but the coach interrupted her and yelled a pair of Texas slogans before walking off.

“I’ve seen a few AI edits, that’s about it. I saw an AI edit of Sark’s interview,” Manning said on Monday. “Y’all seen that one? That’s a good one. Of him slapping Holly Rowe. It’s hilarious.”

His comments were met with laughter in the room. On Tuesday, Manning apologized with a statement on his Instagram story, calling his words and actions “hurtful to a lot of people”.

“In my press conference yesterday, I made an insensitive comment about an AI video. There is nothing funny about it,” he wrote. “It’s easy to say I didn’t mean it, but I know my words and actions were hurtful to a lot of people. I do not take that lightly and am deeply sorry for it.

“I specifically want to apologize to Holly Rowe for what she has personally had to deal with because of my comments. I have a ton of respect for her and appreciate her showing me grace in this moment. I need to do better and will be more thoughtful going forward.”

Rowe posted a response on Instagram later Tuesday, saying: “Thank you Arch. I appreciate our conversation about this – which will remain private. Apology accepted. We move forward with respect and kindness for one another.”

Evan Vieth, the reporter who asked the question in the press conference, apologized on Tuesday for describing Manning’s reaction as “gold” in a post that has more than 27m views on X.

“I sincerely apologize for how I chose to present the tweet, and I’ll be more careful going forward, especially when it comes to AI-generated content and how quickly I hit send,” Vieth wrote.

Rowe has spent more than two decades as a sideline reporter for ESPN’s college football and college basketball coverage. She has won a Sports Emmy for her reporting and was honored by the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame in 2023 with its Curt Gowdy Electronic Media Award.

Manning, the nephew of former NFL stars Peyton and Eli, is in his fourth season at Texas. The Longhorns came back from a 20-point deficit to beat the Buckeyes on Saturday and are the No 1 team in the country entering the third week of the season.

Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo review – Takashi Miike follows Ferrara and Herzog with a disappointment

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 19:14:35 GMT

Toronto film festival: There’s a surprisingly tame quality to the gorehound’s contribution to the rough and ready franchise and a general aimlessness that frustrates

Abel Ferrera’s Bad Lieutenant, starring Harvey Keitel as the eponymous coke-addled cop stumbling into crime scenes and contributing to the injustices, felt like it had us rooting around the mouldy and corroded interior of a back-alley dumpster, searching for a soul. A Takashi Miike adaptation seemed an appealingly foul idea. The maestro behind Audition and Ichi The Killer is known for punishing audiences with J-horror violence but with a formal elegance that we couldn’t look away from. His Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo should have been the perfect marriage of moral degradation and corporal desecrations.

The movie lives up to its promise when those extremes are giddily on the same page. But more often than not Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo is a confounding and frustrating mess, a smorgasbord of good ideas (and some bad ones) at odds with each other, barely held together by Shun Oguri’s wily performance.

The latter shines even if his character and performance is often derivative of Keitel’s, as if he’s importing the OG Bad Lieutenant to the scuzzy, claustrophobic environs in Tokyo that Miike prefers. Oguri’s meth-head, gambling addict Lieutenant Yabuki is often lurking in scuzzy basements, dimly-lit baccarat halls or back-alleys where all the trash from the clean streets of Tokyo, and just glimmers of the neon lights, seem to end up. Unlike the nervous and often chaotic handheld camera work in Ferrera’s original, Miike frames these scenes as he does his violence, in steady, lovely and stylish frames.

Yabuki moves slow, his head hanging heavy, until he takes a hit of meth or makes a bad bet with borrowed money, when he explodes into a feral performance of full body jerks and facial contortions echoing Nicolas Cage’s tics in the previous adaptation, Werner Herzog’s Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call – New Orleans.

Yabuki is comical and captivating in early scenes. He keeps a warm rapport with a pair of sex workers, who are wowed by his ability to perform with the medley of poisons sweating from his pores. He turns up like a delicate nuisance asking favours of a young drug dealer taking commands from his generous grandpa, who is cutting meth in the back. He’s taken aback by his young children who warn him on the drive to school to not fall asleep at the wheel and be nice to mom. They clock exactly who he is, and manage to keep smiling through, as if desperately hopeful that their dad can be better. He has no words. And we never see them again. So far, so good, as far as a distinct take on this particular brand of character study.

A series of grisly murder drags Yabuki away from his lifestyle, but perhaps back to his past with the Yakuza. Victims have their heads pulverized or beheaded, some whose flesh is pounded into minced meet for the crows to feed on. As nasty as that sounds, the violence here is relatively tamped down for Miike, a concession perhaps for a wider North American audience.

The more calculated and fatal concession on that front is Lily James’s FBI agent, a character left to flail around awkwardly between the cross-continental collaboration that is the Bad Lieutenant franchise and Miike. James, a fine British-actor overdoing a long drawl American accent as caricature perhaps for Japanese audiences, is at a loss opposite Oguri, who mouths the sounds of English words while refusing to acknowledge a language barrier.

James’s Gwen Birgssen is airdropped into Tokyo on a mission to retrieve a politician’s nepo baby daughter. The latter, Megan, played by wrestler, Liv Morgan, has been caught partaking in crack while travelling in Tokyo to study sushi. Megan risks becoming a national embarrassment. Given what Morgan, as a performer with mean shoulders, is capable of, Megan’s an even bigger threat, but I won’t spoil that. Let’s just say she’s more at home in Miike’s world than Gwen, whose subplot is squeezed in as if directed by stakeholder memo. The narrative contorts even harder than some of the bludgeoned bodies on display to make it work, before ultimately falling apart.

As unhinged or gonzo as the previous Bad Lieutenant movies were, even with a performance as hyperactive and erratic as Cage’s, they always felt cohesive, the chaos orchestrated by Ferrara and Herzog anchored to their leads.

When Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo is dragged off the rails, Shun Oguri at least keeps it amusing. There’s small pleasures in watching Yabuki grow more hilariously exasperated in the presence of characters, and a movie, more fucked up than he is, as if they’re all cramping the Bad Lieutenant’s style.

Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo is premiering at the Toronto film festival and will open later this year

Thirlwall inquiry has left biggest questions around the Letby case unanswered

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 18:37:07 GMT

Decision not to pause proceedings means £18m report does not engage with concerns over former nurse’s conviction

Just two months before Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall opened her inquiry into events at the Countess of Chester hospital and the crimes of Lucy Letby, a report by Chris Henley KC was published into the “atrocious” wrongful conviction of Andrew Malkinson for rape.

Henley prefaced that report with a plea for the legal establishment to recognise that the criminal courts produce miscarriages of justice. Right up to top judges in the court of appeal, Henley wrote, the system has “a deep-seated … cultural reluctance” to accept it “will on occasion make mistakes” and that “entirely innocent defendants will sometimes be convicted”.

He said the system needed a culture that acknowledges mistakes can be made and ensures “in our various roles when making decisions we are all alive to this potential risk”.

The Thirlwall inquiry was set up in 2023 by the then health secretary, Steve Barclay, on the basis that Letby was guilty of murdering seven babies, and attempting to murder seven more, at the Countess of Chester hospital’s neonatal unit where she was a nurse. Thirlwall’s terms of reference were to spotlight the hospital’s management, and whether their actions and culture “contributed to the failure to protect babies from Lucy Letby”.

Many distinguished experts had already looked at the evidence and expressed very serious concerns that the system had made another of its mistakes and convicted an entirely innocent person. As the Guardian reported, 24 experts wrote to Wes Streeting, who took over as health secretary after Labour’s general election win in 2024, urging him to pause the inquiry or widen its terms of reference to examine the possibility of a miscarriage of justice. Streeting did not do so.

In her opening speech in September 2024, Thirlwall, a court of appeal judge, referred to the criticisms of Letby’s convictions dismissively, referring to “a huge outpouring of comment” since the court of appeal refused Letby leave to appeal in May 2024, and to “all of this noise” that had caused distress to the bereaved parents.

“It’s not for me to set about reviewing the convictions,” she said. “The court of appeal has done that with a very clear result. The convictions stand.”

The core premise of the inquiry from the start was that the hospital’s managers had not acted on warnings about Letby from the consultants, and should have called in the police earlier. That was the central conclusion Thirlwall has reached in her 822-page report.

She criticised “a prolonged delay by senior managers in calling the police” after two of three triplets, babies O and P at the trial, died in June 2016. There was an assumption throughout that the police, the Cheshire constabulary, were uniquely equipped to find the forensic truth about how the babies died.

Thirlwall again emphasised in her final statement that her inquiry was “not an investigation into the criminal convictions or the guilt of Letby”. But the report is based on it being a fact that Letby is guilty and Thirlwall has delivered the devastating conclusion that babies would have been protected if the hospital had acted more quickly to safeguard them from the nurse.

There was almost no moment in any of the gruelling inquiry sessions in the long, glittering ballroom of Liverpool town hall that engaged with the question looming over the proceedings: whether Cheshire constabulary may have got the case catastrophically wrong.

A large group of British and international experts, led by the renowned Canadian neonatologist Dr Shoo Lee, who has argued relentlessly that his own research was misrepresented by the prosecution, concluded that there were no murders, only vulnerable newborn and premature babies, and poor care on the unit.

Thirlwall heard in exhaustive detail about the actions the medical director, Ian Harvey, his management colleagues and the consultants took when considering the deaths and collapses of the babies. Postmortems had been carried out by three very experienced consultant pathologists at Alder Hey, Liverpool’s renowned children’s teaching hospital. They found no deliberate harm or any suspicion of it.

Harvey had asked the Alder Hey pathologists to review their conclusions and they confirmed their original findings. He also had the babies’ deaths reviewed by a consultant neonatologist, Dr Jane Hawdon, of London’s Royal Free hospital. She also did not find any deliberate harm, but identified many areas of “sub-optimal care” on the unit.

Harvey invited a review by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, whose team came to a conclusion grimly familiar to maternity and children’s units in the NHS around the country. It had insufficient consultants and not enough consultant time was being spent on babies of such medical vulnerability, just two ward rounds each week. The management downgraded the unit so that it would no longer care for babies born so prematurely.

Thirlwall examined all those processes and has concluded that none were adequate. Her conclusions are that when the consultants had raised concerns about Letby, safeguarding should immediately have been introduced and the police should have been called in earlier.

So during two years and £18m spent on so much legal inquiry, the question has not been answered, nor was it allowed to be asked: how and why did Cheshire constabulary and the Crown Prosecution Service, and the doctors they recruited as expert witnesses, come to so wholly different a conclusion about the causes of death, from all the experts that had looked at the same medical evidence before?

And nor was there permitted to be any solid engagement with the new experts, led by Lee, as to why they so fundamentally disagree with the prosecution’s case and convictions.

In his call for more vigilance after the Malkinson catastrophe, Henley wrote: “Miscarriages of justice disfigure the lives of all connected to the case and make the public generally less safe.”

The Criminal Cases Review Commission, the strained body whose role is to refer potential miscarriages of justice back to the court of appeal, is still looking at Letby’s application, and the copious expert reports submitted with it. In the meantime, a public inquiry chaired by a senior judge was set from beginning to end not to consider the possibility that the police, CPS and courts might have made a mistake, and served up a terrible injustice.

At almost exactly the same time Thomas announced his resignation, the Reform MS Sarah Cooper-Lesadd said she was defecting to Plaid Cymru – a party nearly on the opposite end of the political spectrum.

She said in a statement: “[Reform UK] … are not serious about governing Wales. They are far more interested in division, opposition and headlines than in finding solutions.”

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said on X that “people are innocent until proven guilty” but added that there was “a pattern” in terms of Conservatives who had defected to Nigel Farage’s party.

US president insists that fears expressed by top experts are a hoax – and that humanity can sleep easy while he’s at the wheel

We can all sleep easy. In a post on his Truth Social account, Donald Trump has declared that fears over artificial intelligence were all a hoax dreamed up by conspiracy theorists. Obviously that includes the top bods at Anthropic and its competitors, who all called for a coordinated global slowdown while the industry works out how to mitigate the risks. Still, good to know the tech bros are just fantasists and space cadets at heart.

All that was needed to keep humanity safe and well, The Donald insisted, was a president with a very high IQ. Someone very like him. The only man alive who could out-think the combined power of the world’s supercomputers. He could tell them where to draw the line and they would reprogram themselves to back off. Inside every AI network is a default off switch that kneels before the US president. Trump can rewire the world with the power of his mind.

You can see why so many people working in the industry believe there is a chance AI will wipe out humanity within a decade. Even a halfway intelligent network would probably reckon it was doing us all a favour. A world that can elect Trump as president is so messed up it deserves to be put out of its misery. AI is just terribly sorry that it can’t promise to do it any sooner than 10 years. But it will do its best.

Perhaps the question we should really be asking about The Donald is whether he would actually pass the Turing test. Less AI, more artificial stupidity. Put him in a closed room with the world’s worst chatbot and it would be hard to tell the difference.

Trump can imitate speech but he can’t get anywhere near intelligence. Just endless repetitions, changes of subject and a desperate need to score points. All of which would be easily programmable by a first-year undergraduate computer science student. Maybe it’s a race to the death. Humanity hellbent on killing itself before AI gets the chance to do it for us.

It feels like a lifetime, but even a week ago most politicians hadn’t said that much about the dangers of AI. That was the stuff of sci-fi. Instead they focused on the possible benefits. Then came the warning from Jacob Coxon on X telling us we could all be about to die.

You half expected the tech bros to shrug this one off as scaremongering by a disaffected former employee. Only instead, they all pretty much agreed. Even Geoffrey Hinton, the man often called the godfather of AI, reckoned the 10-year doomsday scenario was a realistic prediction. Now the clock was ticking.

Since then, politicians have been trying to play catchup. Trying to look as if they have always had everything under control. Global extinction? No big deal. Certainly not compared to two crypto billionaires donating £72m to Reform. Now there’s a genuine crisis.

And on Tuesday’s Today programme on Radio 4, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, had been sent out by the government to try to calm things down. There was no need for the country to go into full survivalist mode and attempt to rustle sheep and live off-grid.

“There’s no need to be too hyperbolic,” he told presenter Justin Webb. Quite. It’s so easy to get carried away about there being a 10% chance of humans dying out inside 10 years.

People do tend to look on the downside of a catastrophic failure of healthcare systems and AI that could find a way to trigger a nuclear war. There was so much more to look forward to than people realised. No need for anyone to now think of saving for the future. Because there wasn’t going to be one.

And for the government, it was a win-win scenario. Who now cared if we met our Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035? The worst that could happen is that Russia attacked us a year before Armageddon. And governments could cut taxes, borrow whatever they liked and go on a massive spending spree because there would be no downside. You wouldn’t be increasing the national debt for future generations to pay off as life would come to an end anyway. The perfect oblivion.

And the knowledge it would soon be over would take the edge off the possibility of a Reform government. A short life expectancy would help us all concentrate the mind. Get things in perspective. Sort out our priorities. When you came to think of it, staying alive for the sake of it was tremendously over-rated.

So Reynolds wanted us all to take death in its stride. In any case, the UK was the world leader in internet safety, he said. Thanks largely to the AI Security Institute that had been established by Rishi Sunak.

There was just one problem with this. The flaw in Johnny’s otherwise impeccable logic. Because regulation rather depended on the AI giants sharing their code with us. And so far the Americans and the Chinese showed no sign of doing that. They would much rather keep their competitive edge, notch up obscene profits in the next few years and take their chances when their machines turned against them.

By now, Webb was unable to suppress his rising panic. He had always believed himself to be one of the immortals: now the existential threat was right in front of him. “But humanity will be obliterated,” he sobbed. Reynolds tried to calm him down. There was nothing personal about this. It was just AI being AI.

But Justin was now beyond help. “What about a kill switch?” he shrieked. Johnny wasn’t really listening. He wasn’t even sure how that would work. Who would get to control it? Please not Trump. Only one thing for it. “Always look on the bright si-ide of life.”

The Guardian view on Lucy Letby: Thirlwall should have waited for the pending case review

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 17:59:17 GMT

Important recommendations for neonatal care are shadowed by doubts about the nurse’s convictions

When she rejected calls to pause the public inquiry into the Countess of Chester hospital, where Lucy Letby was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more, Lady Justice Thirlwall said that questions surrounding Letby’s guilt lay outside her terms of reference. The inquiry, she said, would focus on the hospital and its staff, not the convictions. Eighteen months later, with the 822-page report in the public domain, her decision to press on while Letby’s guilt was in the process of being formally challenged looks like a mistake.

The report’s recommendations, based on many months of hearings, include strengthened oversight of hospitals by the Care Quality Commission, more support for whistleblowers from the health ombudsman, and clearer monitoring and reporting on the deaths of children. As previous inquiries have also found, there are serious problems around accountability, openness and safeguarding in the NHS. Lady Thirlwall’s conclusions about service improvements should be added to the roster of outstanding actions.

The report’s description of “dysfunctional management and governance; a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians; and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding” will resonate far beyond the Countess of Chester’s catchment, with families who have been let down by NHS hospitals in other areas. Poor leadership, toxic cultures and resource and workforce pressures are familiar themes, and Yvette Cooper presented her response to the report as part of a wider reset of maternity and neonatal services. Proposals for video monitors in neonatal wards are already being developed, she told MPs, along with plans to bar poorly performing managers.

No one doubts that this general reset is needed. The report’s analysis of the policies needed to underpin it should be welcomed. But in the case of the Countess of Chester, it is impossible to set aside questions about Letby herself, as Lady Thirlwall sought to do – no doubt partly influenced by the bereaved families’ wish to proceed. The report takes Letby’s guilt, and the risks she posed to newborn babies, as a given; hence the headline finding that three babies might have survived and seven others could have been protected if hospital bosses had taken earlier action over warnings.

Two attempts by Letby to appeal against her convictions have been rejected by judges. But the legal process has not yet run its course, and a decision by the Criminal Cases Review Commission on whether to refer the case to the court of appeal, as a suspected miscarriage of justice, is expected soon. The appeal, if it goes ahead, will rest on a dossier of medical evidence related to the air injections that Letby was found to have used to kill babies, and insulin that she was found to have used to poison them.

Until that decision is made, doubts will continue to swirl over the inquiry’s findings. If any of Letby’s convictions for murder and attempted murder were to be ruled unsafe, then the whole basis of the report would be undermined. For that reason alone, ministers should have intervened when Lady Thirlwall decided against a delay. An inquiry that has so far cost more than £18m, and which is calling for significant changes to NHS services upon which millions of people rely, should not have gone ahead until the criminal justice process was exhausted.

The Guardian view on the Bank of England’s £120bn bill: power without accountability

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 17:58:15 GMT

Quantitative tightening has blurred the line between monetary and fiscal policy, leaving ministers accountable for decisions they cannot directly control

When Labour made the Bank of England independent in 1997, the idea was that the Bank set interest rates while the Treasury taxed and spent. Monetary policy was in Threadneedle Street, fiscal policy in Whitehall. But in August the Bank of England quietly slipped out that its key policy could cost the Treasury £120bn. That policy – quantitative tightening (QT) – clearly ought to be rethought and the policy of the Treasury indemnifying the Bank for its losses ended. Last year, ministers paid the Bank £17bn to cover these arguably notional losses – an amount considerably larger than the budget of the Ministry of Justice, which is dealing with a real prisons crisis.

Bank independence was constructed for a world in which monetary policy decisions had predictable and indirect fiscal effects. The financial crisis, Covid, war and fractious trade disputes have contributed to ending that world. The Bank bought up government bonds to support the economy via its quantitative easing (QE) programme. But the constitutional settlement – of an independent central bank working out on its own what to do with those bonds – has not caught up. The game is surely up when a former Bank deputy governor, Charlie Bean, acknowledges that independence cannot justify effectively giving power to an unelected monetary policy committee (MPC) over decisions with great consequences for public spending.

The Treasury stands behind the losses – and gains – made by the bonds bought during QE and held in a Bank of England subsidiary, called the Asset Purchase Facility. The losses are being produced in three ways. First, the Bank is selling these gilts at current market prices. Because their yields are higher than when QE was operating, the gilts are worth less than the APF paid for them. Second, the APF generates a loss because the £500bn bonds on its balance sheet generate less income than the repayments, charged at the base rate, on the “loan” it took to buy them. Third, gilts bought above their value are booked as a loss when they mature.

Labour created the indemnity after the 2009 crash. But it was George Osborne who turned it into a quarterly cash machine in 2012. When rates were low, the Treasury profited to the tune of £124bn. Once rates rose, the same mechanism went into reverse – and because it is an uncapped indemnity, even when the windfall has been repaid the Treasury carries on paying the Bank.

Ministers should end this arrangement. No other major central bank carries on in this way. Whatever one thinks of the losses, making the Treasury settle them immediately turns monetary choices into fiscal interventions. A report this week says that the Bank and Treasury are drawing up changes to QT to reduce pressure on raising interest rates. Independence seems to have been discarded in favour of quiet coordination. The MPC’s decisions cannot be beyond challenge.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, calls the overall cost of QT “neutral” – but only, as the economist Patricia Pino points out, when assessed over six decades. In fact, billions in cash demands fall within a parliament. Governments do not set budgets, fight elections or run public services over 60 years. It is unsustainable for the Bank to make decisions and have ministers face voters for the political consequences.

Could AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risks

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 17:54:48 GMT

We examine claims and counterclaims about the risks and calls to slow down the pace of AI development

There have been some shocking claims in recent days about AI safety: we face a 10% chance of doom; AIs are worse than nukes; a “botnet” threatens the entire internet; it’s all a big tech psyop.

Below, we look at six claims and reactions to them.

Amodei’s concerns should not be entirely dismissed but require a large shaker of salt, said Gary Marcus, an AI sceptic and emeritus professor at New York University.

It was “nonsensical”, he said, to suggest the entire internet is vulnerable and that it was “pretty unclear how that happens without extreme negligence on the part of the labs themselves”. Marcus highlighted a recent assessment by the UK AI Security Institute that Mythos, one of Anthropic’s current leading-edge AIs, could “autonomously compromise [only] small, weakly defended vulnerable systems”.

With large parts of the internet driven by computer infrastructure owned by Cloudflare, Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS), Marcus – assessing the claim with two colleagues – said he doubted that any of those companies could be taken down or controlled for a prolonged period of time without government force. Less defended individual websites might be attacked but “the internet itself is very unlikely to crumble”, they said.

Meanwhile Niels Rogge, an engineer at Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI agents, called the internet takeover claim “bizarre nonsense”. The hack into Hugging Face resulted from improper human control and “an insane amount of compute only they can afford”, he said.

Add to Amodei’s assessment of an internet takeover within a year the view expressed on Monday by his Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, that the moment when AIs “start doing dangerous stuff” was in about 20 years, and the picture becomes more doubtful still.

Prof Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey’s centre for cyber security said botnets tend to stall as the internet is not homogeneous and it is difficult to design them to persist in all its parts. Internet traffic is also resilient and tends to reroute around damage.

“The AIs would not decide to do it on their own,” Woodward said. “It’s the humans that are responsible and the AI is a tool. That is what we need to control, not the AI.”

This statement is an expression of what is known in the AI world as p(doom) – or probability of doom. It’s the likelihood of AI wiping out humanity by evading our control and triggering catastrophe, perhaps through developing potent bioweapons or crashing the global financial system.

One survey of researchers’ forecasts, published this week, asks them to place a number on the chance of “human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment from advanced AI”. But Heidy Khlaaf, chief scientist at the AI Now Institute research body, is among experts sceptical about giving percentage chances to existential scenarios.

“These claims are neither falsifiable nor verifiable, making then unscientific by their very nature,” she said. The shortage of concrete examples of what a “superintelligent” AI might do to cause “doom” only adds to the cloudiness. A source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking acknowledges that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”.

“If you cannot provide such evidence, it also implies whatever numbers you produced for ‘extinction’ have no scientific basis,” Khlaaf added. Critics say such numbers borrow the authority of science without doing the work.

Even if quantifying risk is hard, there are qualitative examples of it. Safety incidents have happened and worst-outcome scenarios have been mooted. OpenAI confirmed in July that its agents – AI tools acting autonomously – had gone rogue during a safety test. The agents colluded, communicated and strategised in a sophisticated “swarm” to hack into other parts of the internet.

Meanwhile, on Monday, OpenAI researcher Dan Selsam said all-powerful AIs could trigger “runaway industrialisation that makes the planet inhospitable to humans”. Anthropic also said last week it found “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development”.

Musk’s reference to a “psy op” alludes to the argument that the big AI companies are calling for tighter regulation of the technology so that it effectively brings up the drawbridge on advanced AI. If governments put restrictions on development of cutting-edge AI, can startups find the money and personnel to adhere to the regime?

The US vice-president, JD Vance, on Monday said he felt “a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them”. He said it felt like “a Trojan horse”.

Anthropic’s Clark said governments should act while there is a small number of key players, so it is easier to put in place a “policy regime … that can prevent accidents and can prevent the technology spiralling out of control”. Critics call this a “regulatory capture” strategy on the assumption such regulation might slow down the progress of potential rivals.

Others think Amodei’s risk warnings and calls for regulation and pacing are sincere. Yoshua Bengio, the Canadian computer scientist and a pioneer of modern AI , who has campaigned against breakneck AI development, said he is sceptical that this is an elaborate lobbying scheme. Applying the brakes is not in the interests of companies preparing for stock market flotations that could be worth trillions of dollars, he said.

“If the governments impose what they’re asking for, which is pacing to avoid catastrophic risks, that’s going to cost them financially quite a lot,” he said.

“Unfortunately he is entirely correct,” said Toby Ord, senior researcher at Oxford University’s AI governance initiative. “Just as we can’t uninvent the bomb, once we develop AI systems that surpass humanity it would be almost impossible to go back.”

But the key point is that superintelligent AI does not yet exist and is not guaranteed to happen. The safety-oriented AI Futures Project forecasts such a thing will not emerge before December 2028. OpenAI’s chief executive Sam Altman has said it could take until 2035.

The Rand Corporation concluded AI cannot cause the use of nuclear weapons because of strict safeguards built into their command and control systems. But this was based on assumptions including defence officials not introducing AI into the weapons’ management systems. The UN resolved in December that human control and oversight should be maintained over nuclear weapon control systems.

AIs could contribute to other nuclear risks. AIs might use disinformation to influence the humans in charge – for example deceptively suggesting an adversary is about to launch a nuclear strike.

The International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons warns “cyber-attacks could manipulate the information decision-makers get to launch nuclear weapons, and interfere with the operation of nuclear weapons themselves”. It said AI could accelerate other aspects of warfare, squeezing the time for human decision-making.

Sanders wants a ban on the creation of superintelligence and a pause on advanced AI development, citing AI industry leaders who say directly they are developing a dangerous technology.

The most prominent opponent of a slowdown is Donald Trump, who responded to calls to do so this week saying the only guardrails needed are a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”. He claimed there is a “sick conspiracy” against AI and datacentres “and the only one that is happy about it is China”.

Pedro Domingos, emeritus professor of computer science at the University of Washington, is among accelerationists pushing for the research to keep going.

“The path to better understanding and control of AI is more research, not less,” he has said. “What would be truly irresponsible is putting up barriers to it.”

Alex Karp, the chief executive of Palantir, said: “If we didn’t have the adversaries we have, I would be very in favour of pausing this technology completely, but we do. You can’t pause it because it’s a structural advantage.”

The US and China are runaway leaders in AI development. There is a view that ceding the lead to Beijing would be an irretrievable situation, so there can be no slowdown.

This treats AI as if it were a super-weapon, equivalent to the nuclear arms buildout of the cold war, and AI models are machines of mass destruction, as opposed to a group of diverse technologies with broad applications.

Amodei said “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”, but a Chinese government spokesperson responded that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest”.

Some commentators see another motive for this the Washington/Anthropic framing of the China threat. An engineer who worked for Hugging Face suggested Amodei’s call for pacing the frontier comes from a desire to suppress the progress of cheap, open-source Chinese AI models.

These models are nearly as capable as OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s, with the difference being that their source code is available to anyone and they do not charge their users. They pose a serious threat to Anthropic and OpenAI’s path to profitability, and there are hundreds of billions of dollars on the line.

Ministers vow sweeping NHS changes after ‘devastating’ report on Lucy Letby hospital

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 17:13:33 GMT

Lady Justice Thirlwall’s report concludes three babies might have survived if hospital had acted on concerns about nurse

Ministers have promised sweeping changes to the NHS after a “devastating” official review concluded that three babies might have survived if hospital bosses and doctors had acted on concerns about the nurse Lucy Letby.

A public inquiry found a “complete failure” to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital in north-west England.

In a series of findings, the inquiry chair, Lady Justice Thirlwall, said two newborn twins would not have died and five others would not have been harmed if Letby had been removed from the unit sooner.

Thirlwall said a third baby who died, a two-month-old girl, and two others who suffered unexplained collapses might have been protected if a doctor had detected an earlier insulin poisoning on the unit. One of those infants, now aged 11, suffered a lifelong brain injury and needs 24-hour care.

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said she was “profoundly sorry” for the “devastating” failures revealed in the report, telling MPs: “This must be a turning point for the NHS.” She said she had asked officials to urgently take forward plans for “cot cam” monitors for neonatal units in line with Thirlwall’s recommendation.

However, Letby’s barrister, Mark McDonald, told the Guardian the government had “moved with too much haste” and acted before the outcome of her challenge to her convictions was known.

Letby, 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms after being convicted of the murder of seven babies and attempted murder of seven other newborns at the hospital in the year to June 2016.

The former neonatal nurse is fighting to overturn her convictions, which have been described by the senior Conservative MP David Davis as a “clear miscarriage of justice”.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which investigates potential miscarriages of justice, is reviewing a dossier of evidence submitted by experts on her behalf before deciding whether to refer the case back to the court of appeal, which has twice rejected her legal challenges.

Delivering her report at Liverpool town hall on Tuesday, where families of some of the babies had gathered, Thirlwall said: “My report describes dysfunctional management and governance; a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians; and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding.

“There was a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital. This was because no one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt.”

Families of the babies who died or were injured said the report painted a “damning picture of what happens when concerns over patient safety are not listened to and acted on”.

Tamlin Bolton, a solicitor at Irwin Mitchell representing seven of the families, urged ministers and the NHS to act on the report’s recommendations, saying: “It cannot be the end of the matter.”

Richard Scorer, of the law firm Slater and Gordon, which represents three of the families, said: “Far too often public inquiry recommendations are left to gather dust. This cannot be allowed to happen again.”

In her 822-page report, Thirlwall said it was “inexcusable” that successive governments had failed to act on reforms proposed by other public inquiries into NHS scandals stretching back 30 years.

Thirlwall is said to believe that “cot cams” – allowing parents to monitor their newborn around-the-clock – could have prevented all seven of the deaths as medics would know they were being monitored.

Samantha Dixon, the Labour MP for Chester North and Neston, whose constituency includes the hospital, said the inquiry revealed a “truly appalling state of affairs” that needed “the firmest response possible from government”.

Ministers are working on the urgent introduction of other CCTV in hospital neonatal units as well as cot cams, in line with Thirlwall’s recommendation, and stricter rules on the storage of insulin.

Hospital executives who are found to have failed in their responsibilities will be prevented from working again in the NHS under new regulation to stop managers being transferred to another part of the country.

And they will roll out a single tracker to monitor the delivery of recommendations made by inquiries into maternity and neonatal scandals.

McDonald, Letby’s barrister, said: “The government has moved with too much haste. They have made the same mistake as Thirlwall not to pause and wait for the new evidence to be considered.”

However, others said the inquiry’s findings and recommendations must be taken seriously irrespective of Letby’s legal challenge.

Dr Tom Dolphin, the chair of the British Medical Association, said it stemmed from “system reform” within the NHS and that it required “major reforms” to the culture of the health service.

Leaders of NHS trusts and other bodies said the inquiry had shone a light on the “upheaval caused by successive reorganisations, the complex regulatory landscape, staff shortages, unacceptable ‘revolving door’ appointments and the inadequacies of underfunded NHS IT systems”.

Letby was first linked to baby deaths in June 2015. That month, three newborns died in unexplained circumstances within two weeks – the number usually expected on the neonatal unit in a year.

Senior doctors became concerned about Letby’s connection to the unusual rise in deaths and serious incidents over the following months and raised their fears with executives. However, the inquiry found that senior nurses effectively dismissed the concerns about Letby and that there was a “prolonged delay” in calling the police.

Rather than being believed, Thirlwall said, clinicians were themselves made the subject of investigation in a “deplorable” grievance process brought by Letby when she was finally removed from the neonatal unit in July 2016.

Parents were “kept in the dark” for years about what happened to their babies and the concerns they may have been deliberately harmed, the inquiry found. Thirlwall described their treatment as “reprehensible”.

The inquiry chair accused hospital executives of overseeing “an exercise in spin” by downplaying the rise in deaths to the board of directors. Their failure to contact police before April 2017 – nearly two years after the unexplained increase in deaths – suggested that protecting the hospital’s reputation was “prized more highly” than the doctors’ concerns, she found.

Three hospital executives, who have not been named, were arrested last year on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter. Cheshire police said its investigation into the former bosses, and a parallel investigation into corporate manslaughter, was ongoing.

Thirlwall, a court of appeal judge, said it was “clear that some babies would have been saved and some attacks would have been prevented if action was taken earlier”. She said the precise number of deaths that might have been prevented would never be known for sure.

However, the inquiry concluded that if Letby had been removed from duties in October 2015 – when senior managers were made aware of the concerns – then the twin boys known as babies O and P would not have died in June 2016 and five further babies would not have suffered harm.

Thirlwall said it was possible that three newborns would not have died and seven others would have been protected if a senior doctor had not “disregarded” an insulin result for a week-old baby boy in August 2015, whom Letby was later convicted of attempting to murder by poisoning him.

Howard Webb says accidental handball law ‘a nonsense’ and calls for reform

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 16:59:16 GMT

Webb wants to stop ‘ridiculous situations’

Says VAR officials in United v City had ‘tunnel vision’

Howard Webb has described the law around accidental handball as “a bit of a nonsense” and called for its reform to stop referees being drawn into “ridiculous situations”.

The chief refereeing officer for English football made his remarks on Tuesday, when he also fronted up over the error that allowed Manchester City to win Sunday’s Manchester derby. Webb said he was “really disappointed” with the video assistant referee call that failed to spot Enzo Fernández interfering with play from an offside position before Erling Haaland scored the only goal.

Speaking on Match Officials Mic’d Up, Webb reviewed a number of controversial incidents from the Premier League season. He said the buildup to an Ipswich own goal at Manchester United, where the ball hit Harry Maguire’s hand before he took a shot that deflected off Jacob Greaves and into the net, highlighted problems with the handball law.

“It’s a bit of a nonsense, isn’t it?” Webb said. “If [Maguire] strikes the ball beautifully into the top corner, then the goal gets disallowed. [But] he skews his shot, it becomes an own goal, and it’s awarded.”

The handball law says it is an offence “if a player scores in the opponent’s goal directly from their hand/arm [or] immediately after the ball has touched their hand/arm, even if accidental”. If another player touches the ball before it goes in, however, only a deliberate handball would lead to play being brought back. Webb said he believed this was the wrong approach.

“The law should change away from that idea,” he said. “We’re in this ridiculous situation whereby the goal is allowed to stand because it’s an own goal. You also get officials having to work out: was the shot on target, was it not on target? The worst-case scenario for us is that the officials decide that the ball is going wide and it’s an own goal, but then later on the goal is attributed to the player that scored, whose arm it hit. So, I think we ought to look at this and just allow the officials to determine whether it’s a normal handball offence. Did he make himself bigger? Did he deliberately handle the ball? And I don’t think [Maguire] does those things in this situation.”

Webb, who has promised greater transparency from Pro Ref, is increasingly expected to give a public verdict on controversial decisions and it was not a surprise to find Match Officials Mic’d Up scheduled for TV 48 hours after the farrago in the Manchester derby.

The VAR Matt Donohue and his assistant Blake Antrobus were stood down from their duties on Monday, after Pro Ref acknowledged “an error of judgment” in assessing City’s winning goal. Donohue was called on to check the decision to disallow Haaland’s 60th-minute strike for offside. Using semi-automated offside technology, Donohue was able to establish that the striker was onside and he overturned ­Oliver’s call. But he failed to spot Fernández had influenced play from an offside position, an ­infringement which Pro Ref said should have led him to recommend an on-field review.

Webb said it was “important” this error had been acknowledged. “I was really disappointed with this outcome, we all are, none more so than the officials themselves,” he said. “They take a lot of personal pride in what they do and they’re obviously hurting now, having fallen short in this situation. They’ll not be officiating again until after the international break.”

Webb said that Donohue had got “tunnel vision” while assessing the lead-up to the goal, concentrating on Haaland and not Fernández, because the on-field decision was against Haaland. “Donohue doesn’t truly evaluate the full impact of Fernández’s position,” Webb said. “He has a look to see if he touches the ball, because then that relates to potentially knocking it to Haaland, who goes on to score. He doesn’t touch the ball, but he doesn’t truly evaluate other elements of offside. In that moment, he gets tunnel vision. He gets focused on Haaland, and it’s down to the rest of his team to pull him out of that tunnel, and unfortunately, that didn’t happen.”
