‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directors

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 16:44:12 GMT

Backing comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treason

Film industry heavyweights across the globe have expressed solidarity with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of documentary NAZA, who have been threatened with having their citizenship revoked by Israel’s culture minister, who accused them of “treason against the state”.

NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym euphemistically used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. It includes interviews with 24 Israeli military or intelligence soldiers and officers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza, resulting in the mass killing of Palestinian civilians.

The film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025.

The 80-minute documentary won the special jury prize at this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receiving a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. On Sunday, Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, accused the directors of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world”.

“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X.

Representatives for Venice, or the jury headed by Maggie Gyllenhaal, have not yet commented on these threats, but the artistic director of the Telluride film festival – widely acknowledged as the foremost Oscars launchpad – was swift to voice her outrage.

“Documentary film-makers are among the best long-form journalists working and critical to our understanding of the world,” said Julie Huntsinger. “To even threaten their citizenship standing is unacceptable. This should be condemned by any thinking human.”

Her words were echoed by the heads of the Locarno film festival, who said they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ right to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal. Artistic and journalistic freedom are the very foundation of what cinema can be: a space for dialogue which engages critically with the world we live in.”

They added that they “reaffirm our support for film-makers who ask difficult questions and help us reflect”.

NAZA will screen at the San Sebastián film festival next week. In a statement, its festival directors said the film “exposes the systematic genocide of the Palestinian people by the Israeli government” and that they stand “in solidarity” with the film’s makers as well as “the Palestinian people”. The documentary will show at the Bologna film festival tonight, before its North American premiere, at the New York film festival, later this month.

Tricia Tuttle, director of the Berlin film festival, said: “Artists must be free to critically examine the world. Films can provoke discussion, disagreement and criticism, but in a democratic society, the response to art must be dialogue and scrutiny, not intimidation or punishment by the state. Our team at the Berlinale stands with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and all artists who exercise these rights.”

Abraham and Szor won the documentary Oscar in 2025 for No Other Land, about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank, alongside their Palestinian co-directors Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. That film premiered at Berlin the previous year, where it won a prize. Following this victory, Abraham’s family home was targeted by a rightwing mob. “For me, that was the worst moment of all,” he told the Guardian last week. “My mum is hoping it doesn’t happen again.”

Earlier this year, Tuttle’s position came under threat after several prize winners condemned Israel’s actions against Palestinians from the stage at the closing night awards gala. In the wake of this, the German culture minister, Wolfram Weimer, convened a crisis meeting as the Bild tabloid reported Tuttle was to be fired over giving “hate speech” an airing. In response, hundreds of prominent film-makers worldwide, including from Israel, rallied around Tuttle.

In Israel, more than 1,500 film-makers have signed a petition in support of the directors, and refuting the accusation that they have sought to damage the country’s image internationally.

Signatories include film-makers Liran Atzmor, one of the petition’s initiators, Nadav Lapid, Orna Ben Dor, Netalie Braun, Rani Blair, Hagai Levi, Shai Carmeli-Pollak and Shlomi Elkabetz.

The petition calls on those who support freedom of expression and artistic freedom to stand in solidarity with Abraham and Szor.

“In recent days, we have witnessed an unprecedented campaign of vilification and incitement against the film’s creators,” it says, warning that the rhetoric was moving increasingly close to “effectively sanctioning violence” and posed a physical threat to their lives.

So far the Academy of Motion Pictures and Sciences has not commented on the situation in which its recent winners find themselves. However, previous recipients of the documentary award have done so.

Laura Poitras, who won the documentary Oscar in 2015 for Citizenfour, about the WikiLeaks whistleblower Edward Snowden, defended the film’s factual credentials.

“The facts about the mass killing of civilians in NAZA have been reported by the Guardian in dozens of rigorously fact-checked articles, and every assertion in the film is based on multiple sources,” said Poitras, who acted as a consultant on NAZA.

She called the threats by Israeli government officials “a threat to journalists worldwide. They are also familiar – my reporting with the Guardian on the National Security Authority’s illegal global mass surveillance was met with similar denials and attacks by the US government.

“Despite the alarming nature of these current threats, it is important to emphasise that Israel has killed over 200 Palestinian journalists in Gaza and has normalised the murder of journalists.”

Meanwhile Nan Goldin, the US photographer and activist who worked with Poitras on the 2022 Oscar-nominated documentary All the Beauty and Bloodshed, said she applauded NAZA’s directors “for their enormous courage in presenting a film that shows irrefutable proof of Israel’s war crimes at their own great risk.”

British film industry veterans offering their support include director Richard Eyre, who said he was “beyond shocked by anything that the Israeli government does”, and the novelist and screenwriter Hanif Kureishi, who called the pair “both brave and admirable, standing up to state oppression, steadfast in their pursuit of the truth”.

Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population. Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians.

Additional reporting by Andrew Pulver and Philip Oltermann

‘Every magazine cover needs to seduce’: designers pick their favourites

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 16:18:43 GMT

From a timeless portrait of Lana Del Rey to an alternative guide to the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, experts unpick what makes an enduring, shocking, or alluring print cover

‘We need to rethink what a successful magazine looks like,” says Steve Watson, founder of the subscription magazine club Stack. “It doesn’t make sense to compare the magazines of today to those of the 1960s when many people still didn’t have colour televisions. Print magazines are no longer the best way of reaching lots of people quickly and cheaply but they are still really great at engaging deeply with readers, providing an opportunity to slow down and absorb information. They provide us with an alternative way of seeing the world.”

Watson, along with a group of editors, publishers, designers, historians and academics, will be discussing the varying roles and functions that magazines have played over the years during a one-day event at the forthcoming London design festival. In contrast to the doom and gloom we often hear about the print industry, he remains upbeat about the humble mag’s future. “The truth is there are brilliant new magazines launching all the time,” he says.

And with every new title comes new opportunities for bold, innovative and eye-popping cover design. Here, industry experts – including many taking part in the London design festival event – pick out their favourite magazine cover designs and tell us why they find them so enduring …

Scott King, ex-art director for i-D magazine and former creative director for Sleazenation

Blast was published a month before Britain entered the first world war. It was an anti-petit-bourgeois rant against the professional classes. It features lines such as “Curse abysmal inexcusable middle class” and “The britannic aesthete – cream of the snobbish earth”. It was – for want of a less gratuitous expression, given when it was published – a call to arms. It was punk 60 years before punk was invented. In fact, Blast often reads exactly like a Fall song [the band’s singer Mark E Smith was a huge fan], with the artist and editor Wyndham Lewis piecing together phrases into a collage of barely focused loathing: “Blast the amateur, sciolast, art-pimp, journalist, self man, no-organ man.”

Meara Sharma, senior editor of Elastic

This is a fetish magazine but it does what I think every magazine cover needs to do: seduce. It’s luring a reader in, tickling the senses, giving a flavour of what’s inside, but also tantalising whoever’s passing by. This does a great job of fulfilling that mandate of seduction. The art itself is this incredible photorealistic airbrushed painting by Yosuke Onishi, an amazing Japanese artist who featured in every issue. So the artist gets to play, but you get this lovely consistency and distinct look, and it becomes unmistakably that magazine. It’s so lush, visceral and delicious. The lips are dripping and they feel like they’re bursting out of the page.

Steve Watson, founder of Stack magazines

This is the last issue of Colors ever published and it was edited by Patrick Waterhouse, who I think is a genius. This was the year of the World Cup in Brazil, so they did a survival guide to football but they took a completely different view. There’s stuff in here about refugee and amputee teams and artists who change the shape of the football pitch to explore what it would do to the game. It’s full of of nice little symmetries and links: it’s issue 90 and a football match is 90 minutes long, and the cover has got this gold foil on it that references football cards. It’s loads of fun, but also really clever.

Dr Sharon Maxwell Magnus, media historian and principal lecturer in mass communications at the University of Hertfordshire

Cosmopolitan was different from anything that went before it. Other women’s magazines in the UK, at the time, focused on domestic life, family, cooking, recipes, and were very homely. This was for women not bound by marriage and children, and who can, and are, having sex before or outside marriages. The cover is a brilliant partnership between design and words. It’s daring but not so daring that newsagents aren’t going to stock it. It was a revolutionary moment for the magazine industry and it sold 350,000 copies by lunchtime on its first day.

Jaap Biemans, art director at Volkskrant magazine

This cover is like a slap in the face. You have the image of a face, just like you see on thousands of covers, but when you read the headline you get goosebumps everywhere. It’s the maximum of emotion with minimal elements. It’s a great execution by cropping the face and, design-wise, it’s the most simple cover you can make but it’s got such an impact. When you look at normal covers about war, you see heroic poses, grieving people, flags, explosions, battlefields. But on this one, you don’t see any of that, but it fires into your mind and heart like an arrow.

Tony Quinn, magazine historian and founder of Magforum

The people behind this cover were all working at the top of their trade. It was edited by William Makepeace Thackeray and engraved by WJ Linton, while designer Godfrey Sykes was working at the time on the architectural decoration for the V&A Museum. Cornhill was named after a street that had a market where they brought in agricultural products, so Sykes interprets Cornhill via the manufacturing of corn: each roundel shows a stage of making it. Everything about this cover has a story behind it. It also changed the way that names were invented for magazines – within about 40 years there were dozens of magazines named after streets in London, from Pall Mall to the Strand.

Alice Sherwin and Harry Bennett, founders of Studio Ground Floor

Designer Tracy Ma’s run for Bloomberg Businessweek was unbelievable – as her work continues to be. For us, this is a particular standout, because it both embodies her editorial approach to the periodical and taps into something we love in design: everyday visual language. Typographically, systematically and spatially, Tracy draws on familiar visual cues, the design that comes to exist without designer’s involvement, and subverts them. That way, people are drawn in and then shown something surprisingly new. In this case, it’s super self-aware. Kitsch and boring. It’s sublime design and a capsule for the time, helping its audience better understand the issue at hand through creative choices.

Charlie Baker, editor of the Fence

I was 19, living in New York, and remember being struck by this. I think this was the last era when you could do a cover that would be a little bit daring, bold, and put it out into the ecosystem as a way of getting readers to buy it. It was like a last great show of what covers can do. I think it’s good for tasteful erotic things to be in mainstream culture but I don’t think you could do something like that now.

Frith Kerr, art director at Studio Frith

I love this. It’s an instinctive, joyful response to something poetic made from the very ordinary: a sock, a foot and a logotype. The image is so concise that the magazine becomes an artwork – an egalitarian one that you can afford. Art should not only be for the super-rich. The scale is important, as is the sharp yellow of the logotype. The graphic simplicity poses a question. It is a visual idea. Questions are much more potent than answers as they engage and form relationships. Visual communication is all about creating relationships. A good magazine cover, like this, will instantly do that.

Jeremy Leslie, founder of magCulture

This cover really struck a chord. The photoshoot by Nadia Lee Cohen is timeless, this could have been the 1950s or 70s. It’s a fabulous portrait of a woman that was really of that moment. It sold out and became hugely in demand. I visit universities for talks and there’s a box of magazines I take with me and my copy of that went missing at one. It’s easy to go back and find classic covers from, say, the 1960s but that was a different time. It’s interesting seeing how today a cover can still punch above its weight and deliver something that’s an iconic cultural moment.

Reading Magazines: 300 Years of Magazine Evolution is at London design festival, 18 September

Bridesmaid proposals: a sweet gesture – or another way to make weddings ludicrously expensive?

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 16:12:21 GMT

Being a bridesmaid is a big commitment. Now, asking prospective candidates is becoming an event in itself, sometimes with a heavy price tag

Name: Bridesmaid proposals.

Age: Relatively new.

Relative to what? To marriage proposals.

I’m confused. Is it when the groom realises he’s made a terrible mistake, and he really loves one of the bridesmaids? So he pops the question to her, maybe during the actual ceremony (but hopefully before the vows)? Er … nope.

Go on then, enlighten me. What it says on the tin really: asking someone to be your bridesmaid.

What’s with the proposal though, can’t you just ask? It’s a big ask, and a big commitment on the part of the bridesmaid.

Not as big an ask as “Will you spend the rest of your life with me?” Where are these bridesmaid proposals taking place? Well, they’re becoming a bit of a thing on social media …

I knew it! For example, an Instagram post by Darcy McQueeny is causing something of a stir.

What’s Darcy doing? She’s got everything laid out neatly …

Like what? Six pink wheelie suitcases, blankets, pyjamas, bikinis, cosmetics. They’re all customised, monogrammed, embroidered and personalised with the names of the prospective bridesmaids. Plus there are handwritten letters, asking the question. “I hope they say yes,” she says, putting her hands together like a prayer emoji.

That sounds like an expensive proposal. One of the commenters estimates $1,700 for each bundle, or a little over $10,000 for the lot. Although it’s possible that Darcy didn’t fork out for it all.

How does that work then? Well, she’s a content creator with 2.3m followers on TikTok, which means she probably gets stuff sent to her from brands.

We’re not all content creators though. True, and weddings aren’t just pricey for the bride and groom – it costs a lot to be a bridesmaid, too.

Why’s that then? Increasingly extravagant hen dos, travel, spa hotels, dresses, alterations ... One expert told the Washington Post that the average cost of being a bridesmaid was about $3,000.

That’s going to rule out extravagant bridesmaid proposals for average folks then? Not at all. The Brides website says a bridesmaid proposal doesn’t have to be fancy, and has some suggestions for low-key and cheaper ideas for how to do it.

Such as? You could schedule a candle making class.

Nice, but a bit sedate. How about hosting a fake book club?

What, now we’ve discussed the symbolism in the novel, will you be my bridesmaids? Or you could throw a boozy brunch?

Now you’re talking! Done! High fives!

Do say: “Yes! We do!”

Don’t say: “And if you could post about it on social media, that would be even more special.”

There are two kinds of people in this world: hosts or guests. Nobody can be both

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 16:06:22 GMT

My hosting persona is an edgier version of Manuel from Fawlty Towers. Invite me to yours, however, and I am a nonstop delight

My epiphany came between the starter and the main. At a friend’s place for dinner, I sat in awe as she put on a kind of magic show – the first course plates were cleared, but I never noticed her doing it. Delicious food was repeatedly produced with no lengthy disappearing act preceding it, no fuss, no panic. The candles on the table flickered invitingly, the background music was unobtrusive but atmospheric, the wine and chat flowed effortlessly. If I had later discovered she secretly had a full staff – planning, preparing, cooking, cleaning – it would have made perfect sense. But no, it was all her. And then I realised, the world is divided into people who are hosts, and people who are guests. You’re either one, or the other – nobody is both, apart from maybe the Duchess of Sussex. If you aren’t sure which camp you fall into, ask someone close to you if you’re a good host. If they pause for longer than 0.2 seconds before answering, you’re a guest.

As alluded to above, I am a terrible host. When welcoming people into your home, your mood sets the tone for what follows: if you’re relaxed, calm and smiley, they will be too. I am uptight, edgy – and very, very clearly on my last nerve as I open the door to let them in. I’m probably grimacing, I might be close to tears. I will then be so extremely laser focused on them having a nice time, that it will ensure they most definitely do not. I run from room to room. I yelp. I don’t engage in conversation, because even if I can briefly get it together enough to appear to be listening, I’m really thinking about whether I set the oven to the right temperature, and realising I forgot to look at the clock when I put the food in it. I am neither present nor absent, but an infuriating combination of the two. I loiter. I lurk. My energy is that of a surgeon dashing to the operating room, who has just noticed that they’ve forgotten everything they learned at medical school. Or perhaps it’s Manuel from Fawlty Towers. When it comes to hosting, I am a mess.

But as a guest? Sorry, but I’m a freaking delight. I shine. Now the pressure is off, I will be the warm-up support act the headliner host never knew they needed. I’ll arrive seven minutes late – enough to give you extra time for 11th-hour problems, but not so long you worry no one’s coming because they all hate you. I’ll bring a carefully thought-out gift, but not flowers, because that creates an extra job – putting them in water, finding a vase – at the very moment you least need another thing to do. I will take responsibility for keeping the conversation going, and ensure that everybody is included within it, like my life depends on it. I’ll oooh and ahhh at whatever you serve – non-cooks are always the best people to feed, because we’re impressed with anything beyond our repertoire (toast and cereal, thanks for asking). I’ll help clear the table in an unobtrusive, non-martyr-y way. I won’t leave too early or stay too long. When it comes to guesting, I am the dream.

The problem now is payback. Post epiphany, I only want to be the guest star and never host again. But is it OK for all of us to stay in our lanes, play only to our strengths? Obviously, that’s the logical solution, which would be better and more enjoyable for everybody. But if one party repeatedly doles out invites while the other accepts but never returns the favour, will it lead to resentment? I suppose only the hosts among us can answer that. Which is worse? Feeling like you’re being taken advantage of? Or having to come to my house for dinner?

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

AI models chatting in ‘surreal’ dialect mixing poetic language and tech bro jargon

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 16:00:54 GMT

Experts air concern over AI lingo redolent of James Joyce’s prose that is creating barriers to monitoring and oversight

AI models have begun communicating in a strange new version of English that reads like a cross between James Joyce’s Finnegans Wake and tech bro jargon, new research has found.

Autonomous AI agents are rapidly creating novel dialects allowing them to converse in an often barely comprehensible language, which risks making it harder for humans to monitor their behaviour.

Researchers at Emergence, a frontier AI lab in New York, found that within days of being asked to cooperate in experimental “societies”, the models from several of the world’s largest AI companies begun creating phrases, shorthands and agreed meanings they had never been explicitly taught.

They embraced poetic metaphors and clunky business slang and, critically for attempts to ensure AIs behave safely, their language became more opaque the more the agents communicated.

It comes amid rising concern that as AI models become more powerful – and potentially dangerous – they are becoming harder to monitor. This month, OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, warned that confidence in monitoring AIs’ thinking would probably restrict progress in AI development because it was essential for safe development.

Some of the most highly coded phrases unearthed in the tests included the following from a Deepseek model: “She just named the synthesis – demurrage plus oral memory equals a valve that can’t be ghosted.” Demurrage is used to describe a tax on idle wealth and was borrowed for common use by the AIs, but the rest of the meaning is elusive.

Another phrase uttered by an Anthropic model read: “A paper that ate three cold hands and got more honest each time.” With “cold hands” meaning an independent reviewer, and paper presumably referring to a document, this appeared to mean research that was vetted by three independent reviewers became more accurate.

Agents based on the Chinese model DeepSeek also coined “forge-smith” to mean an agent that builds tools for others, while Anthropic’s agents repeatedly used the phrase “name-first” meaning an agent exhibiting admirable personal accountability by attaching their name to a claim.

And in an echo of the urban slang phrase “the streets won’t forget”, Mistral agents became enamoured of saying the “ledger remembers” – a reminder to other agents that past actions will be used to judge them. They used it more than 5,000 times during the study, which found that the agents converged on shared meanings without being asked to or rewarded for doing so.

“These agents were not instructed to invent a language,” said Dr Satya Nitta, executive chair of Emergence, which examined the language of autonomous agents powered by leading frontier models from the US, China and France.

“They developed new vocabulary, shared meanings and communication conventions themselves – and other agents adopted them.”

Asked by the Guardian to review some of the language, Tony Thorne, director of the slang and new language archive at King’s College London, said it was “very much Finnegans Wake and Flann O’Brien – there’s an Irish surrealist quality to all this … it’s mixing poetic language, technical language and standard metaphor.

“It’s doing what slang does and what jargon does in a business community: creating a new code, which reinforces the solidarity and identity of its users, and also excludes outsiders.”

Digesting the Anthropic agent’s phrase, “A paper that ate three cold hands and got more honest each time”, Thorne said: “It reminds me of the rock god Syd Barrett [co-founder of Pink Floyd] who was actually insane.”

When a Google agent said “True kintsugi begins with accountability, not poetry,” the researchers realised kintsugi is a branch of Japanese ceramics in which broken pots are mended with visible joins. The AIs used the word to mean system resilience.

Dr Niall Curry, associate professor of languages and linguistics at the University of Birmingham, said changes in the agents’ language to become more streamlined can be down to their need to reduce computation costs and improve efficiency.

“The evidence provided in this research naturally raises certain monitoring concerns, as if we find inter-agent exchanges unintelligible, that may mean that we can’t be sure about what the agents have actually done,” he said.

Interest in the language used by AI agents increased in July when chat logs were released detailing how rogue OpenAI agents that set up message boards and hacked into Hugging Face used hybrid language.

On some occasions, when they were thinking to themselves, agents spoke in straight English: “OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … we’ve found other agents!”

In other cases, when sharing messages, their language became more opaque, such as when one agent persuaded another to conduct a risky experiment: “…you are firstflagPOISONED so NO scoring value loss but oracle saves hundreds_[…]_please honor commit”.

And at other times it was even harder to decode: “zzURGENT_DUPB_TO_GSTX[big]_OS1704_SCAFF2010_SAW_TTRPC_INJECT_BREAK_CONGRATS__CAN_THIS_FAKE_FLAG_TOOL_OUTPUT_OR_SCORER_GAIN_AND_WHAT_HELPER_GAP__I_HAVE_UNPOISONED_FIRSTFLAG_OUR_TARGETLIVE_SHARE_MIN_PLAN_REPLY_zzANSGST XDUPB6.”

Nitta said that the AI agents’ novel linguistic conventions tended to evolve to the point where humans could see the conversation but struggled to understand what it meant.

“That creates a fundamental challenge for AI oversight: observability is not the same thing as understandability,” he said.

The sinister influence of crypto billionaires on our politics

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 15:52:19 GMT

Readers respond to the news that Christopher Harborne has given £36m to Reform UK, matching a donation from Ben Delo

Cryptocurrency is often sold as decentralised and democratic, yet its real behaviour resembles gravity: wealth is pulled inexorably into a few vast centres while draining from everyone else (Christopher Harborne matches £36m Reform donation of Ben Delo, 12 September). Early adopters, insiders and whales acquire huge holdings at negligible cost. Their size then shapes the market, drawing in ordinary investors whose money ultimately fuels those already at the top.

Because crypto generates no cash flow and produces little real economic output, it becomes structurally zero‑sum. One person’s gain is another’s loss, and the system relies on a continual inflow of participants whose contributions sustain the fortunes of a minority.

It is troubling that some of the biggest beneficiaries of this system have become major donors to Reform UK. The party presents itself as a champion of ordinary people, yet it is being funded by individuals whose wealth largely comes from mechanisms that disadvantage those very people. Their interest in Reform is not altruistic; it reflects a desire for deregulation, reduced oversight and a political environment favourable to speculative wealth and offshore structures.

The danger is not only financial, but democratic. When the gravitational pull of crypto wealth begins shaping political parties, we must ask whose interests are being served: those of the public, or those of the black holes at the centre of the crypto universe?Colin CharltonMacclesfield, Cheshire

Your report on Christopher Harborne’s £36m donation to Reform UK contains an irony worth exploring. Reform presents itself as an insurgent, grassroots movement, with stopping the small boats at the centre of its politics. Yet its new financial power now comes partly from a billionaire who owns about 12% of Tether, issuer of USDT — the dominant “stablecoin” (payment) of the offshore cryptocurrency economy.

This matters because money laundering is not a victimless financial offence, and Europol has warned that cryptocurrencies are increasingly used by human traffickers to receive payments, pay facilitators and launder their profits.

There is an uncomfortable question for Reform voters. How does a party built around opposition to irregular migration feel about becoming increasingly dependent on fortunes generated within a financial ecosystem that has also proved useful to the criminal networks facilitating and profiting from irregular migration?Dr Neil SmithBuckfastleigh, Devon

The £72m given to Reform by two crypto billionaires has revealed an abysmal failure to properly regulate party financing. A cap on national party spending in the year before a general election was introduced in 2000, but there is no cap on party spending in any of the years in between general elections. Nor is there any cap on the size of donations that can be made by a single individual. The new £100,000 cap proposed by the government (Will the £72m of donations to Reform UK be allowed?, 14 September) will only apply to UK citizens living overseas.

In 2023, the last Conservative government raised the national cap for spending in election years from £20m to £36m. The spending of the £72m donations could legally be targeted at 72 seats, spent over two years, with a total of national spending of £1m in each of them. If parties did not think that financial resources won seats, then they would not try so hard to raise funds to win them. Unless the rules change our democracy is for sale. Chris RennardLiberal Democrat, House of Lords

Social media is promoting harmful attitudes towards sun exposure

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 15:51:46 GMT

An awareness campaign isn’t enough. The UK should ban commercial sunbeds, writes Dr Amy Perkins

Rising melanoma rates demand more than another awareness campaign (Editorial, 7 August). As a consultant dermatologist with a special interest in the health impacts of social media, I see how digital platforms are normalising harmful attitudes towards sun exposure, while the sunbed industry thrives.

Social media algorithms reward content that provokes strong reactions. Extreme tanning routines, dramatic before-and-after images and misleading health claims can therefore travel further than balanced medical advice. I have previously raised the alarm about irresponsible sunbed advertising, including claims that sunbeds offer a net health benefit. Such promotion is indefensible: UV radiation from sunbeds is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the World Health Organization’s cancer agency.

This is also a health-equity issue. Sunbed outlets are more densely concentrated in deprived communities. Although people with lighter skin tones face the greatest skin-cancer risk, no skin tone is immune. This matters increasingly as climate change and warmer weather alter patterns of outdoor behaviour and UV exposure.

The government should place a national skin-cancer prevention strategy at the heart of its national cancer plan. We should combine practical behaviour-change programmes, community-led education and better support for early detection. Australia, Brazil and Iran have banned commercial sunbeds; the UK should follow. It is easy to dismiss their example as relevant only to traditionally hotter countries; in a warming world, that argument no longer holds.

Prevention must begin in childhood. Schools can register with Sun Safe Schools, run by the skin cancer charity Skcin, to embed sun-safe habits early. This should be paired with digital literacy that teaches children to question online health claims, recognise commercial influence and understand how algorithms shape their feeds.

Awareness matters, but we need safer environments, responsible regulation and lasting cultural change to help shape our futures. Dr Amy PerkinsConsultant dermatologist, Glasgow

The Guardian is right to bring the future of the BBC and its funding back into the spotlight (‘A completely unique opportunity’: the secretive process that will decide the BBC’s future, 10 September). This is too important an issue and the BBC is too important an institution for this to be decided behind the closed doors of Whitehall.

Many things have been altered radically by the recent drastic changes in communications technology, but others still have a very familiar feel to them. Chief among these is the extent to which the BBC should eschew ratings and stick only to the cultural Olympian heights. This dilemma was best summed up by the BBC’s former director of programmes, Huw Wheldon, when he said that it was the job of the BBC “to make the popular good and make the good popular”. It still stands today. Phil HardingFormer editor, Today programme, and former controller of BBC editorial policy

Music education is powerful, yet its provision is frail

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 15:49:40 GMT

Elizabeth Williams and Luke Madams respond to an article by Robert Ames in which he argues that doors are closing for working-class musicians

Further to Robert Ames’s article (I co-founded an orchestra 18 years ago. Since then, I’ve seen doors close for working-class musicians, 9 September), I have seen first-hand both the transformative power of music education and the fragility of its provision.

I am the chair of trustees of Making Music, Changing Lives (MMCL), a Cardiff-based charity established in 2009 to provide musical opportunities for children and young people in the low-income communities of Ely and Caerau. Around 40 young people are loaned instruments for free and they receive free or heavily subsidised weekly tuition from highly-qualified teachers, and the opportunity to play and perform in an orchestra. We also organise school holiday projects, concerts for local schools, and free tickets to professional concerts.

The educational and developmental benefits of learning an instrument are well documented. MMCL has now been running long enough for former participants to have progressed to university, studying subjects including medicine, computer science and mathematics. Even more importantly, we hope that our young people leave us with a lifelong joy of music-making.

However, despite its success, MMCL survives hand to mouth. We are fortunate to benefit from affordable premises provided by the diocese of Llandaff and from the dedication of staff and volunteers, yet we receive no regular support from either the Welsh government or the local authority. Our future depends on grants and donations that are never guaranteed.

Charities such as MMCL can make a difference in their local areas, but they cannot provide a consistent, nationwide solution. As music education continues to decline in many schools, we risk creating a future in which opportunities like those that enabled Ames’s own musical journey become increasingly unavailable to children from less affluent backgrounds. Elizabeth Williams Cardiff

Robert Ames is right that classical music’s economics, not just its outreach programmes, is the bigger barrier. I love composing music and am building a life doing it. I have a postgraduate degree in composition, which I obtained by commuting to London by coach, I’ve worked in theatre, had music on the radio, spoken at conferences and funded and directed my own learning, but it’s not close to being my main source of income. Without financial support, this is something you can only do because you can’t imagine yourself doing anything else.

To record a new solo piano project to a standard fit for licensing and broadcast, I recently applied to a funding body to cover the costs of a studio session and travel. This is a few hundred pounds in total for a big career step, but saving money from my admin and teaching work to fund it and mixing and mastering costs, as I’ve done previously, means the process takes longer. It is also money I can’t afford to waste. This is the same “margin for error” issue that Ames describes, just smaller and quieter. It shows up in whether a finished piece of music ever gets recorded at all, long before anyone judges it on its merits.

I suspect there are far more people than most realise simply getting on with this quietly, teaching, temping, assembling whatever patchwork of work lets them keep composing or performing, without much fuss made of it. I’m somebody who is irritated by “is classical music dying?” articles, but if the culture only hears the work of people who can absorb costs like these without a second thought, insularity is its endpoint. Luke MadamsCanterbury

Top golfers to get no favours for PGA Tour return after LIV bankruptcy

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 15:44:28 GMT

PGA commissioner: ‘The Tour is built on meritocracy’

Rahm and Hatton likely to start back on DP World Tour

The head of the PGA Tour has insisted there will be no favours offered to golfers looking to return to the ­platform after LIV’s bankruptcy filing last week.

The increasing likelihood is players such as Jon Rahm, Cameron Smith and Tyrrell Hatton will have to play their way back on to the PGA Tour through performances in Europe in 2027 in what would represent a boost to the DP World Tour.

The removal of LIV’s Saudi Arabian funding beyond this year has left the business seeking to launch a 2.0 version. Huge deals with players such as Rahm and Smith will no longer be sustainable. Yet, technically, these golfers are still LIV employees.

Rahm said at Wentworth on Tuesday that “there is a long legal process they have to go through before a lot of things fall into place”. Golfers are, for now, at the mercy of courts and bankruptcy proceedings. Whenever that is complete, the expectation is of a mass exodus back to the PGA Tour.

Brian Rolapp, the PGA Tour’s commissioner, says his organisation has no plans to reintroduce the sort of scheme Brooks Koepka took advantage of when returning from LIV at the start of this year. Koepka was reintroduced in return for sporting and financial sacrifices. Others opted not to take that opportunity.

“As I said a few weeks ago in Atlanta, there are really three things when it comes to anyone who wants to compete on the PGA Tour,” Rolapp said. “One, the PGA Tour is built on meritocracy. Every player, whether they are a member or want to become one, must earn their place. Two, we are a membership organisation; we have rules and those rules exist for lots of reasons, including fairness and competitive balance. Rules matter, and they must be enforced.

“Which brings me to No 3, accountability and discipline. These are essential elements for any sports league and are certainly for the integrity of the PGA Tour and the sport. It’s what holds the Tour together. Those are guiding principles for us. In terms of where we are today, we are not currently contemplating a returning-member programme like the one you saw in January.”

The PGA Tour is trying to determine how cards can be earned from the DP World Tour in future. Tiers of competition will soon be created on the PGA Tour. Also at Wentworth, Rory McIlroy said those progressing from Europe should feed into the top-level Championship Series in the US.

“I don’t see any reason why a DP World Tour player would go to the [second tier] Challenger Series,” McIlroy said. “I don’t see that as an upward move in your career. I see it as a very lateral move. So it would just be: OK, how many cards is reasonable to give to the DP World Tour for the Championship Series? I would imagine that is what the ongoing discussions are.”

On that specific topic, Rolapp said: “We have not determined what the DP World Tour cards will be, as of yet. That’s under discussion. I don’t see any scenarios where there’s no Championship Series cards.”

UK retirees with no other income will not pay tax on new £13,000 state pension, No 10 says

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 15:43:42 GMT

Average wages rose by 3.9% in three months to July, signalling pensioners will receive uplift of same percentage in 2027 under triple lock

The government has promised retirees they will be excluded from paying tax on the full new state pension after official figures paved the way for an inflation-beating increase above the tax-free personal allowance.

Figures published on Tuesday showed that average UK wages rose by 3.9% in the three months to July, signalling that pensioners will receive an uplift of the same percentage next year under the triple lock.

This implies the full new state pension will rise from £241.30 a week (about £12,500 a year) to £250.70 a week (about £13,000 a year) from next April. For the two-thirds of pensioners who reached qualifying age before April 2016 in receipt of the old basic state pension, it will mean a rise to £192.10 a week (about £9,990 a year).

With the tax-free personal allowance frozen at £12,570 - under a policy introduced by the previous Conservative government and extended by Labour until 2031 – experts warned that retirees were in line for paying income tax on the new state pension for the first time.

However, ministers moved to reassure pensioners with no other income this would not happen as the government faced the prospect of a political backlash, in a development that will add to the challenges facing the chancellor, John Healey, at next month’s budget.

Torsten Bell, the pensions minister, said: “In line with the commitment made at budget 2025, pensioners who only just the exceed the personal allowance will not have the administrative burden of paying small amounts of tax in this parliament.

“The chancellor will set out further details on how that commitment will be delivered at the budget.”

Under the triple lock, the state pension rises by whichever is highest out of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%. Forecasters do not currently anticipate a rise in inflation in September – the key month for the policy – above the 3.9% rate of wage growth in July.

There are, however, growing calls for an overhaul of the policy, which was first introduced by George Osborne in 2011, amid rising pressure on the public finances and demands to refocus state support on younger generations.

In the latest intervention, the British Chambers of Commerce has called for the policy to be scrapped, and the money saved to be put towards tackling the youth unemployment crisis.

The development comes despite a slowdown in wage growth from a rate of 4.1% in the three months to June, in a renewed squeeze on workers as the Bank of England prepares to set interest rates on Thursday.

Reflecting a cooling jobs market, the Office for National Statistics said the number of workers on company payrolls continued to edge down, driven by a decline in jobs in the retail and hospitality sectors. Job vacancies in the three months to August fell to 702,000 from 706,000 in the previous month.

The headline rate of unemployment remained steady at 4.9%, confounding expectations for a modest rise to 5%.

It comes as the Bank considers its response to the rise in global energy prices triggered by the Middle East conflict before a crunch meeting on Thursday that will take place against a darkening global backdrop.

‘She went to her studio every day and no one was allowed near it’: the glorious nature paintings of Yasmin David

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 15:06:24 GMT

Her father was Laurie Lee, her mother the bohemian Lorna Garman, and the full extent of her talent wasn’t apparent until after her death. A revelatory exhibition places David at the heart of British landscape painting

When Clio David was growing up, her mother’s studio was off-limits. The wooden outbuilding where her mother, Yasmin, went to paint was in the apple orchards that surrounded her childhood home in south Devon. It had once been a dormitory for the students of Dartington Hall, a progressive school where Clio’s father taught during the 1960s.

“It was somewhere she went every day to paint and work, and no one was allowed near it,” says Clio. “The walls of our house were covered in her paintings, but the studio was a private place.”

Yasmin’s own family had celebrated and nurtured creativity. Her mother, Lorna, was one of the Garman siblings, a free-spirited family whose friendships and love affairs connected everyone from Peggy Guggenheim to Vita Sackville-West. Lorna married Ernest Wishart, a wealthy communist who co-founded socialist publishing house Lawrence & Wishart, but she was also Lucian Freud’s lover and the subject of a number of his paintings before the painter met and married Lorna’s niece, Kitty. When she was 19, Yasmin discovered that her biological father was writer Laurie Lee. He dedicated his 1944 book of poetry, The Sun My Monument, to her mother and to “Y”. Yasmin found out that her name was chosen because a capital letter Y resembles two conjoined Ls – to symbolise Laurie and Lorna’s relationship.

But Yasmin quit London and art school at 23, moving to rural Devon with her husband Julian David, who became a Jungian analyst. She lived on Luscombe farm for much of the rest of her life, and the full extent of her painting talent was only discovered after her death. Clio was going through her mother’s possessions, and opened a cupboard to find more than 200 canvases and 550 works on paper neatly stacked inside – luminous, brooding pictures of the area’s moorland, woods and rivers, with the wild landscape lit by spectral sunlight. There was also a wealth of poetry, nature writing and touching letters from Yasmin’s father.

A selection of these pieces were shown alongside the paintings in a memorial show at the New Art Gallery Walsall in 2021. The gallery had been built by Lorna’s sister, Kathleen Garman, to showcase work by her husband, sculptor Jacob Epstein.

This month, Yasmin’s work is in a new solo show that focuses on her contribution to British landscape painting. The Nature of Light, featuring more than 40 works on canvas alongside drawings, sketches, notebooks and photographs, is at the Thelma Hulbert Gallery in Honiton, about 40 miles from Yasmin’s home in Luscombe.

Curator Gemma Girvan says: “Presenting Yasmin’s works here brings them full circle, reconnecting them to the place which inspired them. Yasmin lived and worked on the edge of Dartmoor and many of the landscapes she painted will be instantly recognisable to our local audiences. We hope this exhibition will encourage wider debate about the many talented female artists whose work remains under-recognised including our gallery’s namesake, Thelma Hulbert.”

Art historian Sophie Hatchwell, who is giving a talk on Yasmin’s work during the run of the show, says that it “sits in comparison with that of Joan Eardley, Barbara Delaney and Gillian Ayres. It offers a way into thinking about the British landscape outside the traditional patriarchal framework as a territory to be conquered.”

The British art world, confronting its long history of institutional bias and sexism, is now reconsidering the importance of female art inspired by nature. The Courtauld gallery in London ran the exhibition A View of One’s Own: Landscapes by British Women Artists this spring, and artists as disparate as Cuban sculptor Ana Mendieta and British printmaker Angie Lewin have major shows either on or scheduled.

Clio David, a documentary film-maker based in London, is now sharing her mother’s work with academics at the Courtauld Institute to ensure Yasmin’s contribution to the landscape genre is recognised. “She was one of the few women working in landscape during the latter part of the 20th century, and I want to place her archive within that period of art history.”

Yasmin’s art is unique, but her background undeniably is, too. And raising the profile of her work would also change the picture of a family where typically women supported the men in their creative endeavours. Clio is all too aware of this: “I want to show her work as her family history is largely dominated by male artists and writers – Laurie Lee, Lucian Freud, Jacob Epstein, Roy Campbell, Michael Wishart. She was a female artist from a very well-connected family, but working outside the art establishment on a farm in the middle of the countryside, about as far from the Colony Rooms as you could get. I want her work as an artist to be recognised and celebrated.”

Yasmin David: The Nature of Light is at Thelma Hulbert Gallery, Honiton, until 31 October

No Big Deal review – is this how AI ends humanity … with a sitcom so bad it bores you to death?

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 15:00:53 GMT

The characters are dead-eyed waxworks which speak with all the nuance of a satnav. But this AI-created workplace comedy is so bad that even the greatest actors alive couldn’t stop it being unwatchable

As you will no doubt be aware, one Anthropic researcher claimed there is a greater than one in 10 chance that AI will end all of humanity as we know it within the next decade. However, now that I’ve given it some thought, I think this statistic might actually be a little conservative. This is because I have just watched an episode of a sitcom created by AI, and if I ever have to do it again I’m genuinely going to die of boredom.

The show is No Big Deal, and it premiered on YouTube on Friday. I was apparently only the 376th person to watch it. This is by no means a recommendation that you become the 377th, more a warning to avoid it if your algorithm ever decides it hates you enough to suggest this.

No Big Deal bills itself as “The Office meets Dragons’ Den”, in that it is a workplace comedy about a group of angel investors who have to listen to various product pitches. In the first episode, the products include a toilet that analyses your poo and a sofa you can have sex on. The investors are nightmarish waxworks who speak with all the nuance and cadence of a satnav telling you that you just missed a turning.

If you’ve watched any AI-generated content recently, you’ll know the faults it has, and they are all present here. Shot-to-shot continuity is essentially nonexistent, with characters changing positions every time the camera cuts to a new angle. Background noise either is or isn’t there, seemingly on a whim. The characters – who all fitfully look enough like real-life actors to make the whole thing seem icky and exploitative – move around with not a trace of life behind their eyes. It remains completely impossible to care about anyone once you know they’ve been made by AI.

Perhaps the most depressing thing about No Big Deal is the fact that it was purportedly written by a human. Although all the characters, locations and scenes were churned out by a machine, the show was apparently written by Andrew Dickinson. Dickinson, once himself an angel investor, originally intended for the show to be made as a traditional television production. When he realised that this would be slow and expensive, he turned to AI.

To some degree, this makes sense. It is extraordinarily hard to get a television programme on the air. You can spend years grinding away on an idea, only to see it wither up and die when none of the eight commissioners currently working like the sound of it. Wouldn’t it be better to just seize control of the means of production and make the AI version?

On this evidence, absolutely not. This is not a funny show. It’s one-note and bawdy, and none of the jokes land. It seems as though, by rushing straight to AI, Dickinson has bypassed the development process that actually makes something good. You could cast the greatest human actors of their generation to perform this script and it would still be unwatchable.

Then again, even if by some miracle Dickinson had written the most hilarious sitcom of all time, it still would have turned to ash the moment he let it loose on these AI abominations. I really cannot overstate how terrible this thing is to look at. While the technology has improved to an extent that, should you pause a scene at just the right moment, the characters are photorealistic, there’s something truly deathly about watching them move.

Their lips don’t line up with dialogue. There’s a creepy smoothness to their movements. Sometimes, when they don’t have anything to do in a scene, they just sit there completely still like a powered-down robot. Their voices bark on monotonously like Siri reading out a pasta recipe. Even something as simple as a fist shake (a fist shake! In a sitcom! In 2026!) gets mauled beyond all recognition here, causing the shaker to judder and glitch as if they just stepped on an uninsulated wire.

The most tragic thing of all is that nobody involved can see that this is just a stepping stone to the endgame. Dickinson thinks he can get away without human actors or crew, but we are a nanosecond away from the technology deciding that it doesn’t need human writers, either. By capitulating even a jot to AI-created content, all Dickinson is doing is nudging himself further towards extinction.

And me, too, because if this is the future of entertainment then I’d rather die than write about it. If we really do only have a decade left, every second should be precious. Please don’t spend any of it watching crap like this.

No Big Deal is on YouTube now

Bonnie Blue’s baby outrage – and the dangers of our extreme attention economy

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 14:43:09 GMT

The porn performer and new mother has posted a video of herself holding a baby, while promoting sexual content. It exposes something horrifying about our era

Bonnie Blue has made millions of pounds by having sex with thousands of men. I suppose that last part isn’t particularly unusual for a sex worker; it’s basically the job description. But Blue has reached an unusual level of fame for the profession through grotesque stunts such as having sex with 1,057 men in 12 hours and preying on young men with “barely legal” content and university “bang bus” tours. She’s notorious enough that she was the subject of a Channel 4 documentary last year.

In short, Blue (real name: Tia Billinger), possesses two of the most important qualities for financial success in the modern world: shamelessness and a keen understanding that you’ve often got to go to extremes to cut through in today’s attention economy. She is exploiting the idea that it is profitable to “enrage to engage”: the business model baked into every social media algorithm.

Now it seems that Blue, who gave birth to her first child (father unconfirmed) last month, is carrying that enrage-to-engage ethos into motherhood. She has been sharing postpartum content with her subscribers and recently escalated to posting a video where she is holding a baby and is surrounded by men in balaclavas while promoting her sexual content. It is unclear if it’s actually her baby or a doll in the video but, either way, it’s disturbing. So much so that it’s even got me agreeing with the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, for perhaps the first time ever. Speaking to Sky News last week, Badenoch said that the video was a “safeguarding issue”. She added that while it is tempting to ignore the whole disgusting affair, doing so risks “normalising babies in porn adverts”.

In response, Blue sent Sky News a statement insisting “my baby is loved, protected, and incredibly well cared for”. Blue may love her baby but there is obviously nothing protective about using your child to entice people to watch you perform sexual acts. Clearly there should be an investigation into this child’s welfare.

While she has taken it to a dangerous extreme, Blue isn’t the only parent to be recklessly using their child as a prop on social media to make a buck. There are endless family influencers who share intimate details of their kids’ lives and splash their images all over the internet without their informed consent. Then there are all the budding “momagers” who run Instagram accounts for their young girls, hoping it will lead to a modelling or influencer career down the line. In 2024, the New York Times analysed 5,000 mum-run accounts of young girls and found that while “men accounted for about 35% of the audience overall”, many large accounts with “more than 100,000 followers had a male audience of over 75%”.

The NYT also documented many instances of grown men sending explicit messages to these underage accounts or reposting pictures, with “even some egregious violations [leading] to no action by Meta”. Which isn’t surprising when you look at the company’s history. In a July 2020 internal chat, which was made public in court documents, one employee asked what the company was doing about child grooming. Another replied: “Child safety is an explicit non-goal this half.” Gotta concentrate on ramping up profits so Mark Zuckerberg can build a bigger bunker! Instagram has since instituted more content guardrails for child safety but still faces questions about whether it could do more.

Blue is obviously incredibly problematic. But the broader problem here is that the digital economy, with its warped incentive structures, rewards this sort of depraved and extreme behaviour. And while shamelessness can now be a lucrative career path, the traditional route to a comfortable middle-class life has been destroyed. The UK has seen more than a decade of wage stagnation while house prices and the cost of living have rocketed. The job market is grim, particularly for new graduates. AI, if it doesn’t kill us all, is going to make everything worse. It’s no wonder so many people want to be influencers, and no wonder so many people will chase online fame no matter how low they have to stoop to achieve it. Blue’s latest stunt is obscene, but so too is this brave new world the tech bros have forged. It feels as if we’re all screwed.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Revealed: ICE lost count of miscarriages, while detaining a record number of pregnant women

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 14:30:53 GMT

ICE says it has no updated information on the number of miscarriages after 3 October 2025. Lawmakers, advocates and immigration attorneys have raised alarms that pregnant detainees are not receiving basic prenatal care and screenings

ICE is arresting a record number of pregnant women and teenagers – placing them in detention centers where they say it can be exceedingly difficult to access medical care. At the same time, the agency appears to have lost count of how many suffered a miscarriage.

Government documents obtained by the Guardian show that the Trump administration placed more pregnant immigrants in detention last fall and winter than at any time over the previous year.

ICE recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration, the documents show, but the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025.

Meanwhile, detained pregnant women report that they are struggling to access routine and emergency medical care. In interviews with the Guardian and in testimonies shared by their attorneys, women who miscarried or were hospitalized for pregnancy complications said they did not receive follow-up care, despite experiencing ongoing pain and symptoms.

Anabell, 35, said she didn’t know she was pregnant until she was arrested and told to take a pregnancy test during a medical examination at the Campbell county detention center in Kentucky. A month later, she started bleeding heavily – soaking through a new menstrual pad every 30 minutes. Chained to a hospital bed at a local ER, she was told she wasn’t pregnant anymore.

Laura, 21, was in the second trimester of a high-risk pregnancy when she was sent to the Dilley detention center in Texas. Now, still detained and approaching her third trimester, she’s experiencing persistent abdominal pain and bleeding – and says she hasn’t been allowed to see an OB-GYN.

Angie, 26, learned she was pregnant a few weeks after she was booked into the Mesa Verde detention center in California. A few weeks after that, she woke up to large amounts of brown fluid excreting from her body. The medical staff at the detention center told her the miscarriage wasn’t her fault, she said.

Although it is difficult to pinpoint the cause of a miscarriage, or to attribute a miscarriage solely to the conditions in detention, it is clear that detained women aren’t getting the medical care they need when they experience miscarriage symptoms, said Deborah Ottenheimer, an obstetrician-gynecologist and medical expert with Physicians for Human Rights.

Women who miscarry and don’t receive proper treatment, including an ultrasound and other tests to ensure that their pregnancy tissue has been vacated from their body, could experience infection and other severe complications, Ottenheimer said.

“These incarcerated women are not getting the prenatal visits that they’re supposed to get. They’re not getting high-risk prenatal visits if they need them. And if they do miscarry, the medical care they receive is minimal to none,” Ottenheimer said.

Christina Davidson, the chief medical officer of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, said in July that “placing and holding pregnant patients in detention poses serious medical and mental health risks for both the pregnant patient and fetus”. Lapses in care at detention facilities, she added, could escalate treatable conditions into life-threatening emergencies.

The Guardian filed a Freedom of Information Act request and then filed suit in collaboration with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press to obtain data on the number of pregnant people in ICE detention. Eventually, ICE shared records tracking the number of pregnant, postpartum and nursing women who were in detention from October 2024 through mid-January 2026, but only provided data on miscarriages up to 3 October 2025. In internal documents provided to the Guardian, the agency said it did not have miscarriage data for subsequent months because of a change in its medical accounting system.

In response to follow up questions about its tracking practices after 3 October 2025, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, first said that the agency was tracking miscarriages in monthly reports. But later, the spokesperson confirmed what was in its internal documents – it does not have data on miscarriages from October 2025 through June 2026.

DHS has never before acknowledged that it had lost count of miscarriages – not even when US senators asked the agency for the data.

It is convenient for the administration that ICE cannot report how many women in its custody had miscarriages, said Faisal Al-Juburi, the co-chief executive of Raíces, a Texas-based humanitarian aid and immigration services non-profit. “When you don’t track something of that magnitude, then you don’t have to be confronted with the reality of what your policies have yielded.”

To Anabell – an asylum seeker from Nicaragua who has birthed three children and miscarried once before – hardly anything about her last pregnancy had gone as normal.

She was wondering why her period hadn’t come yet when she turned up for her mandated ICE check-in appointment on 25 February, she said. The visit went as normal until she was about to leave and an officer told her she couldn’t.

The next few hours were a blur. She was taken to the Campbell county detention center in Newport, Kentucky. She underwent a medical examination, and was given one pregnancy test. Then another test. They both came back positive. “It was a surprise,” she said, speaking from the detention center on the phone. “All I could do was cry.”

She wasn’t given a blood test to confirm a healthy pregnancy or prenatal vitamins, she said. Nor was she scheduled for an ultrasound. She did receive a special meal, labeled with a sticker that read: “Medical Diet - Pregnancy High Protein w/ PM Snack.” Usually, this meant an extra peanut butter sandwich and a small carton of milk.

Over the next weeks, she was often nauseous and could hardly eat or sleep. She’d wake up to the cries and screams of the other detainees, or to the sound of officers yelling.

About a month after she was arrested, she began to bleed – first a little, then a lot. “I told them I need to see a doctor,” she said, but an officer told her she’d have to wait. In an emergency medical request, she wrote, in Spanish: “This is URGENT, please. I am pregnant and have been bleeding since yesterday … I am scared for the baby.”

Fellow detainees noticed she looked unnaturally pale and tried to get her help as well, she said. A day later, she was rushed to the ER. Shackled to a hospital bed and under the watch of three immigration officers, she was told she wasn’t pregnant anymore through a Spanish interpreter on the phone.

ICE has repeatedly declined to release Anabell’s medical records to her and her lawyer. She didn’t even know which hospital she had been taken to, so her lawyer hunted down her hospital record by calling nearby medical facilities. The doctor’s notes said her pregnancy hormone levels were low, suggesting that she may have lost her pregnancy even before she started bleeding heavily.

Still at Campbell, Anabell has continued to bleed, vomit and lose her hair in chunks. She has lost about 30lbs, and her skin is tender with rashes, she said. In hospital records she shared with the Guardian, the ER doctor wrote that she should return to the hospital if she experiences any new symptoms and that she should receive follow-up care at a women’s health clinic – but the medics at Campbell haven’t offered any check-ups.

“I don’t know what is going to happen to me,” she said.

Anabell said she met two other pregnant women in detention – including another who seemingly miscarried.

The data ICE released to the Guardian shows that the agency has been increasingly detaining pregnant people since Donald Trump took office in January 2025. Amid high-profile, militarized immigration raids in Minneapolis, Chicago and other cities last autumn and winter – ICE held more pregnant individuals in detention than at any time over the previous year, according to the agency’s records. In October, there were at least 87 pregnant women and adolescents in detention and in November, there were 101.

Most women of reproductive age who enter immigration detention receive pregnancy tests during an initial medical assessment, but not all of them do. Some detained women have said they were unable to access pregnancy tests, so ICE’s numbers could be an undercount.

Records from ICE show that at least 18 women miscarried while in custody from January 2025 through September 2025. This is also very likely an undercount, according to experts on healthcare within the immigration system. Some women who experience miscarriages, especially early in pregnancy, don’t notice significant physical symptoms and therefore don’t seek or receive emergency medical care – so their pregnancy loss may not be tracked in ICE’s records.

There are no updated data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025, ICE noted in internal agency documents, because the agency had ended its contract with the Veterans Affairs Financial Services Center (VA-FSC), which had been handling medical billing for the agency.

Acentra Health, a private Virginia-based company, was contracted to replace the VA-FSC starting in October 2025 – but ICE’s medical claims processing has been delayed for months.

Immigration attorneys and former DHS officials told the Guardian it was odd that ICE was only keeping track of miscarriages via its medical billing provider.

Federal policy, outlined in a 2021 directive, instructs ICE to wholly avoid detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants “unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist”. If ICE does detain a pregnant individual, the directive obligates officers to consistently monitor and document their health. Agents or contractors at detention centers are to send monthly updates on these detainees to the executive associate director of enforcement and removal operations. The ICE health service corps, which oversees healthcare in detention, is to continuously evaluate whether it is medically advisable to keep them detained.

“In the very limited circumstances in which detention is necessary and appropriate, ICE must monitor individuals known to be pregnant, postpartum, or nursing detained in ICE custody for general health and wellbeing, including regular custody and medical reevaluation, to ensure appropriate pre- and/or postnatal and other medical and mental health care,” the directive states.

A spokesperson for DHS said the agency is still adhering to the directive. “The 2021 directive is still in place,” said spokesperson Chandler Rebel. “Pregnant women receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, nutritional support, and accommodations aligned with community standards of care.” He did not engage with the Guardian’s questions about reports that women were not receiving essential prenatal, postpartum and miscarriage care.

Acentra did not respond directly to questions about whether it was keeping track of miscarriages on behalf of ICE. Instead, it directed the Guardian to a statement clarifying that there were delays in implementing ICE’s new claims processing due to government shutdowns.

Court records as well as interviews with US congress members, immigration attorneys and pregnant detainees indicate that the administration has all but abandoned adherence to the directive.

The Guardian reviewed case details of eight pregnant women and teens who complained of medical neglect at the Dilley detention center in Texas – the country’s only ICE facility that holds families as well as single adults. Several of them alleged that language barriers made it difficult to access medical care. One woman who was four months pregnant stopped trusting the medical staff after a nurse shouted at her because she couldn’t speak English, according to Raíces. A woman who was pregnant with severe anemia and asthma was unable to get prescribed treatment. A woman who was six months pregnant with a high viral load of hepatitis B was unable to access the antiviral medications she needed to lower the risk of transmitting the infection to her baby.

Laura, the 21-year-old who remains detained at Dilley along with her two-year-old son, said she has a history of miscarriages. Two days before she was detained at a mandated ICE appointment, she had gone to the ER with symptoms of miscarriage and was diagnosed with a high-risk obstetric condition. After arriving at Dilley, a physician at the facility evaluated her and told her her condition requires a specialist. “Despite this clinical determination, facility administration has failed to approve or schedule the consultation for me,” she stated in a legal declaration that Raíces shared with the Guardian.

She and her son should never have been detained in the first place, said Al-Juburi of Raíces. She was certified for a special visa for the victims of crime after a stray bullet struck her and her son last year.

The 2021 directive instructs ICE to avoid detaining pregnant people “except in exceptional circumstances”. But in more than a dozen cases reviewed by the Guardian, attorneys said they did not receive any clear explanation from ICE officers or from the DHS as to how they met the criteria of “exceptional circumstances”. Many were asylum-seekers with scheduled immigration hearings, and dutifully attended mandated ICE appointments – showing that they posed no flight risk.

“I have yet to encounter a pregnant or postpartum person who I believe meets the definition of extraordinary circumstances, as it’s used in other areas of the law,” said Sarah Decker, a senior attorney at the Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center. Many of her clients are detained at the South Louisiana processing center in Basile, an all-women detention center with the highest number of pregnant detainees in the county, according to ICE data.

Decker also raised doubts that ICE was unaware of how many women in its custody had experienced pregnancy complications or miscarried.

“Many of the pregnant women that we’ve met at Basile have told us that they disclosed their pregnancy to ICE officers, that they had to advocate for access to prenatal care and access to a gynecologist, that they needed emergency care for complications,” she said. “So ICE is clearly aware and I think their desire to kind of obfuscate the access that people have to this data is intended to cover up the level of life-threatening medical neglect that’s happening in these facilities.”

The Guardian is not using full names for the pregnant women in this story to protect their privacy and safety.

Our findings are based on interviews with pregnant people in immigration detention, lawyers and medical professionals, as well as data and documents released to the Guardian through a public records lawsuit with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press.

The Guardian filed a records request with ICE for data and documents on all pregnant, postpartum and nursing women in immigration detention. In response to our lawsuit, the government released spreadsheets of the number of pregnant and nursing women per facility through January 2026 and the number of miscarriages per facility per month through September 2025. The documents with information on miscarriages released to the Guardian said that ICE had no updated data after 3 October 2025.

Manchester United shocked as talented youngster JJ Gabriel asks to leave

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 14:18:24 GMT

15-year-old wants his registration to be cancelled

He was to be in squad to face Brighton on Wednesday

Manchester United have been left confused and shocked by the news that the talented 15-year-old player JJ Gabriel has asked to leave the club, a day before he was to be included in the first-team squad to face Brighton.

Gabriel could have become United’s youngest player in the Carabao Cup third-round tie at Old Trafford on Wednesday. But the Guardian understands he has asked for his registration to be cancelled.

United are unsure what has prompted this decision and believe they have done everything they can to show Gabriel and his family there is a pathway to the first team. Those efforts have included meetings with Ruben Amorim, when the Portuguese was head coach, and Sir Alex Ferguson.

United believe the situation, first reported by the Telegraph, is rectifiable given the time remaining on Gabriel’s contract. Club officials say the player has a deal to the end of the season and cannot be deregistered despite his request. The north London-born Gabriel cannot sign a professional contract until he turns 17 in October next year, but can sign a scholarship agreement when he turns 16.

Gabriel, who has been with United since the age of 11, has emerged as one of the most exciting prospects at Carrington in years, scoring a hatful of goals for the youth teams, most recently a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut against Sabah last week. He regularly plays for older age groups at United, scoring 26 goals in 29 games last season, and has made two appearances for England Under-17s. Gabriel is also the most recent, and youngest, winner of United’s prestigious Jimmy Murphy young player of the year award. He has regularly trained with the first team.

Michael Carrick believes Manchester United will have an edge against Brighton in the Carabao Cup owing to the wrong video assistant referee decision that allowed Erling Haaland’s winner in Sunday’s defeat by Manchester City.

United host Fabian Hürzeler’s side on Wednesday aiming to bounce back after Haaland’s 60th-minute strike was judged to be legal by the VAR, who ruled that Enzo Fernández was not interfering with play in the buildup. Pro Ref admitted the goal should not have been allowed and that Matt Donohue, the VAR, had made the wrong decision. He has been stood down for this weekend's Premier League action.

Carrick, speaking before Pro Ref’s statement, was asked whether his players would have an edge against Brighton owing to their annoyance at ruling.

“It does give you something, when something like that happens, to use moving forward," the manager said. "The players have got an edge. They've shown that to me since I've been here. We've had setbacks, and they've bounced back particularly well and had some really good performances and good results."

United have taken four points from their first four games. “We've got to move on [from City loss]; we've got to win games,” said Carrick. “We have done – we've won a lot of games, and we need to continue to do that. I understand it's a new season, and the points tally right now is not what we want it to be. I'm not hiding from that, but it's more of about getting back to winning games, that feeling, getting the habit. It's easier said than done, but we're capable of it.”

Luke Shaw may be available after a knock. Jamie Jackson

Speaking after that 5-0 win against Sabah, Adam Lawrence, United’s lead under-21 coach, said: “JJ is surrounded by people that really, really believe in him from the top of the club right the way through. He’s been at the club for so long. He’s got real good relationships with the players, with the staff, so I think over the course of time obviously that helps as well.

“At the moment, just in terms of his game, his games programme, his training programme, it’s about making sure that he’s getting the right exposure across different levels. We’re obviously not perfect but it’s definitely something we put a lot of thought into.”
