Opposition to Mamdani’s 9/11 remembrance was painful to witness

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 14:00:45 GMT

A petition against the mayor’s presence reeked of Islamophobia – and ran counter to the sense of togetherness that followed the attacks

Everyone who was in New York on 11 September 2001 has their 9/11 story. My husband and I were at JFK, boarding a plane to San Francisco. Our two sons were home in lower Manhattan, a block away from my 85-year-old mother. They watched the towers fall from our corner. The weather was radiantly beautiful.

For a long time, the faces of the missing were everywhere. Their eyes seemed to follow us from the makeshift shrine outside St Vincent’s hospital to the window of our local bodega. We cried at random moments. We slept badly.

No one who lived downtown could possibly be surprised by the recently released report about the toxicity of the air during those weeks and months. We inhaled it with every breath. Nothing else has ever smelled like that. I never want to smell that again.

But I also recall the powerful sense that New Yorkers were in this together. Every firehouse was a memorial. We brought flowers, awkwardly expressed our gratitude, paid our respects. Taxis with passengers in them slowed down and gave people rides. People asked strangers if they were OK when they obviously weren’t OK. It was a kind of a joke: if, weeks after the towers fell, you still remained too scared to be in a crowd or an elevator or to take the subway, it meant that the terrorists had won. But like so many jokes, it had a serious undercurrent.

I know that those days weren’t the same for everyone. South Asian and Middle Eastern kids were isolated and bullied at school, their families harassed on the street. A Sikh gas station owner was shot by a gunman who thought he was Muslim. But mostly I recall the tenderness with which people in the city treated one another.

That’s why I found it so painful to read, over the last few weeks, that more than 100,000 people had signed a petition designed to prevent the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, from attending the official 9/11 commemoration ceremony. Among the reasons offered by rightwing politicians and by the families of some victims was the claim that the mayor should be barred from participating because of “public positions, associations and responses to rhetoric”.

The flimsiness, vagueness and illogic of these charges only reveals the obvious. In the eyes of some, the reason why the mayor’s presence would dishonor the dead is not about anything he did. It’s about the fact that, like the men who flew their planes into the towers, Zohran Mamdani is Muslim.

Doesn’t it matter that Mamdani was nine years old at the time of the attack on the World Trade Center? Doesn’t it matter that he has never advocated state-sponsored terrorism? Doesn’t it matter that during the election and while in office he promised and has subsequently tried to make life more livable for every New Yorker, regardless of faith, race and ethnicity? Doesn’t it matter that the mayor of New York belongs at an event commemorating something historic that happened in his city?

To blame all Muslims for the crimes of a very small faction is like blaming every Christian for the evils of Hitler, Stalin and Ted Bundy, like blaming every Jew for the illicit activities of the mob boss Meyer Lansky, like holding writer Arundhati Roy responsible for India’s periodic anti-Muslim riots.

On September 11, Mayor Mamdani, who had spent the previous days visiting firehouses, talking with victims’ families, hearing about the persistent health problems of first responders and people who lived near Ground Zero, and releasing the long-secret air quality report, attended the solemn ceremony. There he did what he always does. He radiated human decency, grace, honesty and kindness, qualities in notably short supply among our current politicians. Rudy Giuliani had condemned Mamdani’s attendance, telling Newsmax: “All of the Muslims he supports are murderers” – but Mamdani shook his hand, a gesture of dignity, fellowship and forgiveness, virtues honored by every religion.

Any chance that the openness with which the mayor rose above his critics and greeted his opponents might serve as an inspiring example of maturity and reconciliation, any expectation that his presence might heal the wound being deepened by anti-Muslim agitators was more or less dashed (at least for me) when a disturbing video appeared on my phone. It documented a recent anti-Mamdani protest in Manhattan, which turned violent.

Given our troubled economy, given the loss of so many jobs, the sacrifice of so many lives to the opioid crisis, it’s not that hard to understand the roots of so much bitterness and frustration. But it’s dispiriting to see it so misdirected. And it’s scary that the anti-Muslim bigotry and propaganda seem destined to persist beyond this latest round of demonstrations.

The good news is that approximately three-quarters of New Yorkers supported Mamdani’s presence at the memorial ceremony. Perhaps some of them remember that day, as do I. I like to imagine they share my sense that those whose who died and those who survived would not want their experience used to fuel the vitriolic bigotry that, in one video clip, prompts a furious protester to spit on a reporter. The reporter is only trying to do his job, to film a response to a catastrophe in which we lost so many of every religion, every color, every age, so many innocent people who believed that they were simply going to work on a gorgeous but otherwise ordinary September morning.

Francine Prose is a former president of PEN American Center and a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences

When is an ebike not an ebike? When it has a powerful, illegal engine. Get this menace off our roads

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 14:00:45 GMT

As a cyclist I want the authorities to act with clarity. Lime bikes and renters can be annoying, but the true threat is those who dangerously flout the law

One of the curiosities of debates about cycling in the UK is that almost all of them centre on the place with the greatest concentration of not only bikes but also politicians and journalists: inner London. Inevitably this is just a small part of the story.

Much of the current focus is on so-called share bikes operated by companies such as Lime and Forest – nippy electric-assist machines that can be picked up and left on pavements. On Saturday, a Guardian investigation revealed that councils in the capital have so far this year seized 3,393 dangerously parked or abandoned ebikes, a number 23% higher than the total for the whole of last year.

Depending on your view, ebikes are either a gamechanging boon to short-distance urban transport or, if we heed the testimonies of those who have been menaced or injured, a dangerous and lawless scourge.

But even this misses the point. Outside the handful of urban areas where Lime and their competitors operate, the ebikes that exist are privately owned. And many of these are not, at least under the law, ebikes at all.

This can sound complex, but bear with me. To be classed as an ebike, a machine must have a powered speed limit of 15.5mph and a motor that only kicks in when you pedal, not via a throttle.

Wander around pretty much any UK town or city for long enough and you will see contraptions that very much do not meet these criteria. They might look broadly like a bike, with pedals and a chain. But they are often throttle-powered and can travel much, much faster than 15mph.

These are not ebikes. They are illegal electric motorbikes. This is a vital distinction to make before you start discussing ebikes, and whether they are, indeed, a brand new peril on our streets.

Now that we know where we are, how much, if at all, of the media scare stories about ebikes or their illegal cousins have a basis in fact? Again, it’s slightly more complex than it might seem.

If you hang around central London, it won’t take too long to see someone on a Lime bike sail serenely through a red light, sometimes weaving awkwardly through gaggles of pedestrians.

This is, of course, illegal, and for all that some cyclists try to justify such behaviour on self-preservation grounds, I’d also argue that it is selfish and intimidating. People should be able to cross the road at a green pedestrian signal without having to first scan the horizon for a beefy twentysomething called Josh on a Lime bike who is running late for his post-work five-a-side game.

But is there any need to panic? Not really. Cyclists are no different from drivers in that quite a few break the law if they think they can get away with it. One issue for cycling PR is that two-wheeled offences are often just more visible.

Government statistics show that when the traffic is flowing freely, fully three-quarters of drivers speed in 20mph zones. This is harder to spot, but the difference is that this sort of behaviour has a realistic chance of killing someone.

Very serious or fatal pedestrian casualties with legal bikes and ebikes do happen, but they are vanishingly rare, unlike incidents with motor vehicles. This is not a matter of morals, just physics – more specifically the way kinetic energy increases so rapidly as the inputs of mass and velocity change.

Some argue that riders of Lime-type bikes are disproportionately likely to flout the rules, in part because they are paying for the transport by the minute. I’m not sure that’s the case.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Either way, it’s undeniable that, overall, share ebikes – in fact all legal ebikes – are a good thing. They make cycling available to demographics that would not normally consider using a bike, especially people without anywhere safe to store their own machine. Despite the occasional annoyance of the Josh contingent, I welcome them to the bike lanes.

It is a very different case for the illegal variants. These are often heavier – some are designed to look like motorbikes – and can go at significant speed. It’s not uncommon for me to be overtaken by a silent, moped-weight gizmo doing 30mph or more. I am, it is fair to say, not a fan of this.

This is, however, not a cycling problem. It’s a law-enforcement problem. It’s therefore also a political problem, not least whether or not any ministers are willing to crack down on a food-delivery industry heavily reliant on riders using illegal bikes.

But the repeated conflation of these two issues has ramifications for cycling. In part it is a call for restrictions on cycling because of offences by those speeding on illegal machines. And because illegal bikes often have vast, poorly made batteries with a tendency to catch fire, some rail companies are pondering bans on all ebikes.

The cycling world is changing quickly. And it is perfectly OK to be annoyed with the Lime bike buffoons. But do remember – they’re not the problem here.

Peter Walker is the Guardian’s senior political correspondent

‘I’m fearless. I was in a boys’ rugby team’: Slow Horses’ Aimee-Ffion Edwards on playing a cocaine-snorting spy

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 13:48:09 GMT

She has played rugby for Wales, is putting a Welsh spin on Princess Leia and is returning to TV screens as Shirley, the explosive, traumatised MI5 agent. Why is Edwards so drawn to liars, crooks and sneaks?

There was a moment, just before Aimee-Ffion Edwards jumped off a nightclub balcony in Slow Horses, when she had to lie to herself about what she was about to do. “It was quite hard,” says the actor. “You basically tell yourself, ‘You’re not jumping.’ Obviously, you know you’re harnessed in, but you’re also going, ‘This is mad! This is mad! This is mad!’”

She laughs. “I couldn’t feel my fingers for a second. I was like, ‘Huwwaah!’” She sucks in her breath, then says: “But there were 200 people stood there watching. You’re like, ‘Well, I gotta do it.’”

In the scene that we see, though, Shirley Dander – the tough, traumatised, cocaine-snorting MI5 agent Edwards plays – does not hesitate, leaping from the balcony to land on a suspect. That collision (on a stuntman) was no soft landing either and, at 38, Edwards knew she’d feel it the next day. And yet she jumped off the balcony “five or six times” during filming. “I played rugby in a boys’ team,” she explains, “and I think I have a fearlessness that comes from that. It’s quite instinctive.”

Edwards is wearing an elegant sleeveless blouse, smart navy trousers and gold hoop earrings. She does not, as she sits there sipping a flat white in London’s Soho Hotel, look much like a rugby player. Yet, with some pride, she reveals that her childhood dream was to play rugby for Wales, where she was born and raised. “That was all I cared about. And I did! I played one match for Wales. Then I was like, ‘I’ve done that. I think I’m going to do some acting.’”

Edwards, a fluent Welsh speaker, still lives in Newport. She had a paper round there until she was 19 and grew up the middle child of five. “I have a strong sense of being part of a pack,” she says. The actor regularly commutes to London (“it’s so close – an hour and 35 minutes on a good train”) and finds it refreshing to be able to play a British spy with her authentic Welsh accent, pleased Shirley’s Welshness is not a talking point in the hit show.

“Nobody ever mentions it,” she says. “And I think that’s really important. It’s good to normalise it. We hear northern and other accents all the time, but Welsh accents have been underrepresented.” Except, she adds, in comedy roles. “Like there’s a novelty aspect to being Welsh – like it’s some sort of kooky thing. It’s really not.”

Before Slow Horses, which follows a ragtag bunch of reject MI5 agents who are presumed to be inept despite usually saving the day, Edwards had to fake a Brummie accent as the opportunistic criminal Esme Shelby in Peaky Blinders, and adopt a southern one as manipulative Elizabeth Barton, the “Holy Maid of Kent” in Wolf Hall.

But as Shirley, and especially as Richard Burton’s older sister Cis in the 2025 film Mr Burton, she has increasingly been able to lean into her Welsh identity. And now she is voicing Princess Leia in the first-ever Welsh language-dub of 1977 blockbuster Star Wars. Due to be broadcast in Wales on Christmas Day, its Han Solo will be voiced by Matthew Rhys. So is she a fan? “Oh my God, I was pinching myself. That was so surreal, being in a booth, watching the film and lip-syncing I was going, ‘I don’t know how I got here, but I’m here – and I’m here for it.’ It was amazing. And it’s brilliant the Welsh language dub is happening. I’d be excited even if I wasn’t in it.”

In season six of Slow Horses, about to launch on Apple TV, Shirley’s anger and grief about the death of her colleague Marcus, played by Kadiff Kirwan, keeps bubbling to the surface. This grief is, to some extent, genuine: “I found it really hard when Marcus died, especially coming in for season five, because it was quite a lonely experience.”

She and Kirwan were “partners in crime”, she says. “That unique relationship between Shirley and Marcus – it was purely platonic, but with a lot of love, a lot of frustration, a lot of projecting each other’s nonsense back at each other.” At the same time, his death has helped her to develop Shirley’s character emotionally. “There’s so much to play.”

As a strong, dangerous woman whose physical bravery and moral courage is undermined by her emotional cowardice, explosive temper and penchant for violence, Shirley is “liberating” to play. “I love that she’s scrappy,” says Edwards. “There’s so much negative energy in her and she doesn’t know what to do with it. She can’t communicate it properly.”

Edwards – whose first major role was as Sketch, the stalker in teen drama Skins – looks for contradictions in the women she plays, which may explain why she is so good at humanising liars, criminals and sneaks. “I’m fascinated by people’s strengths,” she says, “and the mechanisms we have to protect ourselves when we feel vulnerable.” Shirley, she says, gives off a “stench” of “Try it – come and get it” when she walks into a room. “But I understand why she is like she is. I keep trying to pick at those threads, to expose them a little bit.”

Gary Oldman, who plays the chain-smoking, whisky-drinking, rarely washing boss Jackson Lamb, is the joker of the cast. “He loves making people laugh. He’s always got an anecdote, a tale to tell. He’s very silly and funny – a fun father figure.”

In her spare time, Edwards exercises a lot, mainly swimming and running, because team sports are a problem. “The nature of this work means you can’t commit,” she says, adding that she also enjoys making furniture in her garage. If she ever gave up acting and working far from home, she’d like to get a dog and become a carpenter. “I love making things with wood.”

Social media doesn’t interest her much. “I’m here for YouTube videos about carpentry, but I don’t know why anyone would ever be interested in what I had for breakfast.” She prefers to keep her personal life private, to protect her family and those she loves. And perhaps as a result, even though strangers often smile at her like they know her, they rarely identify who she is, even in Newport. “They think we went to school together or I work in the corner shop, rather than know me off the telly.”

This suits her. No actor, she says, ever regrets someone appreciating their work. “If they do, they should quit.” But she feels lucky she gets to live “a normal life” in her home town, where no one bothers her. “I’ll tell you what my biggest achievement is: so many people messaged me one day, because I was once an answer on Pointless.”

The question on the TV quizshow was: name a famous Edwards. “Which is ironic, because nobody knew who I was.” She beams. “What a contradiction.”

Slow Horses series six launches on Apple TV tomorrow.

Raheem Sterling could face prison for reckless driving while using nitrous oxide

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 13:39:34 GMT

Ex-England footballer pleads guilty and admits to failing to provide a specimen as he appears in court

Raheem Sterling pleaded guilty to dangerous driving and could be sent to prison after driving his ­Lamborghini for more than an hour on motorways during rush hour while inhaling nitrous oxide.

The former Chelsea and Manchester City forward stood in the dock to accept three charges before ­Basingstoke magistrates court heard how he embarked on a ­prolonged period of reckless driving on the M25 and M3, inhaling nitrous oxide ­balloons, before crashing his £270,000 car. Sterling was disqualified from driving and bailed until 25 November, when his sentence will either be determined or referred to the crown court.

Sterling also admitted possession of nitrous oxide and refusing to ­provide a specimen.

The maximum term for Sterling would be two years in prison, although a sentence of 12 to 18 months is considered more likely and, with mitigation, that could be suspended.

Simon Jones, prosecuting, told the court one witness had “genuine concerns the driver might kill someone” and described Sterling’s driving as “absolutely horrendous”.

“As she moved past the vehicle she thought the airbag had been deployed, it was a large white deflated balloon,” Jones said. “She had no idea if the driver could see ahead.”

Between 7.45am and 8.52am on 28 May, police received multiple calls reporting dangerous driving – shortly after Sterling had returned to England after a loan at Feyenoord, where he had attempted to revive his career.

Dashcam footage provided to police by one witness showed Sterling’s car swerving between lanes and almost colliding with the central reservation. Witnesses reported seeing the driver inhaling balloons while driving.

After leaving the M3, the Lamborghini veered off the carriageway on the A327 near the Minley interchange in Hampshire. All four tyres blew out and there was damage to the bodywork. Body-worn footage from officers attending the scene, played in court, showed Sterling, 31, sitting in the passenger seat with two canisters on his lap before confirming he had been driving.

Jones said Sterling appeared keen to move a deflated balloon from beside him on to the back seat. His saliva was tested and no presence of cannabis or cocaine was found, but he later refused to provide a blood sample to test for other substances.

Another witness told police they had seen the Lamborghini driving erratically at 1.10am. They reported it entering a drive-through at “alarming speed”, Jones said, and saw the driver holding an inflated balloon.

After his arrest, Sterling was taken to Basingstoke investigation centre. “During the process he had disclosed to staff that he had a problem with nitrous oxide,” Jones said.

Sterling failed a series of impairment tests, including walking in a straight line without swaying and placing his fingertip on the end of his nose. He was also asked to judge 30 seconds with his eyes closed but recorded 52.

Jones said Sterling “appeared to be quiet, withdrawn and lethargic and actively fidgeting” during the tests. “His eyelids were drooping, consistent with fatigue or drug impairment. He said he was feeling very cold, despite this being in the middle of a heatwave with 33-degree temperatures.”

The former England international, who won 82 caps between 2012 and 2022 and played in five major tournaments, was taken to a medical room where he refused to provide a blood sample without providing a reasonable excuse and despite repeated and clear warnings.

At 5.13pm, Sterling was interviewed with a legal representative present. A signed, prepared statement was read out in which he said he had not slept all night and was tired and confused. He then answered “no comment” to officers’ questions.

Jason Bartfield KC for the defence did not dispute this was a top-category case, given the prolonged driving and clear serious impairment. Bartfield cautioned, however, that there would have been “short periods” of “serious impairment”, compared with consuming cannabis or alcohol.

Bartfield did not accept the car damage was serious, describing it as “relatively superficial” and “minor scratching” alongside the blown tyres. He also argued that the fact there were two canisters in Sterling’s lap when police arrived showed “this was very much not a case of trying to conceal anything from them”.

The court was not told the full mitigating circumstances, but ­Bartfield said: “Clearly there is extensive ­personal mitigation. Voluntary steps have been taken to address them. I hope this has weight with the court.”

District judge Kirsty Allman ordered a pre-sentence report and adjourned the hearing. She said she had not decided whether to retain jurisdiction or commit sentencing to the crown court. A magistrates court cannot impose a sentence of more than 12 months.

“I’m going to release you on unconditional bail,” she said. “If you don’t attend, a warrant will be issued for your arrest. I’m going to disqualify you from driving as of today. You must not drive a motor vehicle on the road as of today. I will determine the period if I sentence you, otherwise it will be for the crown court. You must not drive while disqualified – if you drive while disqualified you will be committing a prisonable offence.”

‘It makes you feel helpless’: patients and doctors cast doubt on standard treatment for endometriosis

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 13:22:50 GMT

Natalie Greenwood says surgery is no ‘magic fix’ for chronic pelvic pain – a view backed up by a new study

“It’s really frustrating to be in this cycle of continuous surgery. It makes you feel helpless,” says Natalie Greenwood, of a condition that affects her so badly she is “non-functioning most of the time because of the constant fatigue”.

Greenwood, 36, needs to have an operation every few years to limit the impact of the endometriosis that gives her chronic pelvic pain, as well as extreme tiredness and brain fog.

She says the trouble with depending on surgery is not just having an invasive procedure and then having to recover afterwards. It’s more that the benefit gained – the relief from persistent pain – is brief.

She is not alone in her lack of belief in surgery and hormonal medication being effective for chronic pelvic pain. A study has found that dual approach, which is the NHS’s usual way of treating the condition, does not improve quality of life for female patients.

Greenwood was diagnosed with endometriosis 13 years ago, after leaving university. It is a condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus – the endometrium – is found outside the uterus, most commonly in the pelvic cavity, and can cause inflammation and pain.

Greenwood, who is a languages teacher in West Yorkshire, has already had surgery three times: when she was 23, 28 and 32. In the first two operations she underwent ablation, in which the endometriosis is removed using heat or cold. The last procedure involved excision, in which the surgeon cuts out the endometriosis.

“The surgery is effective in that it can keep the pain at bay for a few more years. But I’ve never come out of it feeling better,” she said. “And in between surgeries I’ve still had to have hormone treatments, like a hormonal coil, or been put into chemical menopause. That keeps the endometriosis at bay by shutting down the hormones that cause it. But the endometriosis keeps growing. So you might feel better for a while but it’s always there in the background.”

Even after surgery, Greenwood has still needed what she calls her “pain management toolkit” – Tens machines, peppermint teabags, cooling patches, hot-water bottles and CBD oil.

Endometriosis is one of the main causes of chronic pelvic pain, a condition that affects between 6% and 27% of women worldwide. Others include vulvodynia and bladder pain syndrome.

“The surgery has never been a magic fix for me,” said Greenwood. “I don’t think it’s a magic fix for many people. You don’t just suddenly feel completely better. A life of surgery every five years is just not something you want to do. It’s not sustainable. It’s like a constant rut.”

Greenwood has a boy of five and is keen to have another child. But endometriosis has affected her fertility so much that she will soon start a course of IVF.

Whatever the outcome of that treatment, she is sure of one thing: “I won’t have surgery again. It’s not manageable to keep having surgery every five years. Whatever happens with the IVF, after it I’m going to have a hysterectomy and my ovaries removed because that might give me some relief from endometriosis.”

Dr Jasmine Hearn, a reader in health psychology at Manchester Metropolitan University who co-led the research in the new study, said: “Sadly patients are often left struggling due to current pain management strategies not sufficiently alleviating pain.

“Chronic pelvic pain is often invisible but its impact can be profound. Our findings highlight that women with pelvic pain report poorer quality of life when they’ve had surgery and hormonal medication for pelvic pain and better quality of life when psychological support is part of treatment.”

The 147 women in the study, who were aged 18 to 66, all reported that their pelvic pain had a major impact on both their physical and psychological quality of life and ability to function normally.

Surgery was found to be associated with lower physical quality of life while painkillers were associated with women having poorer physical, psychological and environmental quality of life.

In contrast, women who received psychological help as part of their treatment to help them manage their pain said their quality of life was better. The evidence for its effectiveness was so great that all those who suffer pelvic pain should be offered it, Hearn added.

Dr Lucy Whitaker, a researcher with the charity Wellbeing of Women and a clinical lecturer in obstetrics and gynaecology at the University of Edinburgh, agreed. She said the same suggestion was made in 2020 by Westminster’s all-party parliamentary group on endometriosis and by a confidential national inquiry into the condition in 2024.

Whitaker added: “Chronic pelvic pain conditions like endometriosis carry a well-documented psychological burden and integrating psychological support alongside medical management reflects a more holistic approach to a condition that has long been under-resourced.”

A spokesperson for NHS England said: “Chronic pelvic pain can have a significant impact on women’s lives and mental health. That’s why psychological professionals provide specialist pain-management support as part of wider physical health services – including for chronic pelvic pain – while women can also self-refer to NHS talking therapies for support with long-term physical health conditions.”

Polling turns politics into one big game. There are too many of them – and that does us no good

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 12:27:56 GMT

Surely that’s the lesson the Reform polling furore should teach us. Politics should be about actually helping people, not mastering the line on a graph

Solemn faces all round. We will listen. We will learn. We will hone and improve. Yes, it’s time for the latest bout of profound soul-searching in the UK polling industry following the allegations raised by the recent Channel 4 investigation that a polling firm reportedly failed to declare that three polls it published before the local elections in May were commissioned by Reform. By now these reckonings are becoming a regular occurrence in the wake of big elections: pollsters gather in a room, nibble biscuits, ritually self-flagellate, and pledge to learn all the right lessons from the electorate they’ve just catastrophically misread.

Yet for all its very public ignominies, political polling is one of those rare and precious industries that somehow manages to keep failing upwards. You might think that after botching the 2015 and 2017 general elections, the 2016 Brexit vote and the 2021 London mayoral poll, we might have learned better than to trust in the mystical magic graph. In this parallel universe Keir Starmer is now sitting on a colossal 318-seat majority, as forecast by Survation in its final MRP poll on the eve of the 2024 general election, overstating the actual result by a mere 144 parliamentary seats.

I am, of course, being slightly unfair. Most of the reputable pollsters enjoy just as many hits as misses – and are, by and large, staffed by smart and diligent people who genuinely care about their craft. Doubtless many among their number would object to any suggestion that the apparent misbehaviour of one firm – JL Partners, who were secretly filmed agreeing to carry out a poll favourable to Reform without disclosing who was commissioning it – can somehow be extrapolated to the wider profession as a whole. To which the only reasonable response is: well, let’s see how you like it.

And rest assured, I’ve read the Substacks. I’ve signed up to (the free version of) the newsletters. I’ve talked to polling experts. I’ve swished a curious finger up and down the interactive graphics. I’ve sat through interminable briefings in which a very nice man explains why he decided to carve up the voting public into 16 distinct blocs with catchy but absurd names: Flag Shaggers, Jealous Judies, Digital Wombats. And because Westminster is basically like the inside of a very small conch, these terms quickly pass into common parlance. “As you can see,” some wonk on the radio will opine, “the Tories are down eight points among the Angry Trevors, a whopping 13 with Disconsolate Flexitarians. But they are at least holding firm with Be At One Mums.”

But my problem has virtually nothing to do with methodology and almost everything to do with volume. There’s simply too much of this stuff, and people are taking it too seriously, investing too much predictive power. The British Polling Council (BPC) has swollen to 39 member organisations, many of them new and completely untested. In the first two weeks of September alone there have been 10 separate voting intention surveys issued by seven separate companies. We are all fatally beholden to the cult of Big Poll.

There are plenty of noble and legitimate defences of polls. They help to shape and test policy. They allow voters to make their choice with the fullest possible information. Perhaps they even function as a kind of check on an unfair electoral system, signposting to potential tactical switchers where their vote might profitably be spent. But even these defences highlight a paradox: this is a method of measuring and reflecting public opinion – and of subtly influencing it. Which is why so many lobbyists, PR firms and corporate interests are desperate to get involved.

Pollsters are not doing this out of some great altruistic duty to democracy. This is a business like any other, often using techniques borrowed wholesale from the market research and advertising sectors, and preying on a resource-starved, click-hungry media desperate for high-impact, low-cost content. “You aren’t going to pay for polling unless you are confident they can deliver the answer you want,” one public affairs executive told Politico last week. Or as George Gallup, one of the pioneers of modern-day polling, put it: “If it works for toothpaste, why not for politics?”

And so what started out as a small table in the newspaper every month has essentially become a biddable political actor in its own right, and there is a cosy symbiotic relationship between the people who conduct the polls, the people who pay for the polls and the people who publish the polls. This is how Reform can be treated like a government in waiting when they have eight MPs. This is how Starmer ends up as a lame duck within two years of his own landslide. In his 2018 memoir, the former FBI director James Comey admitted that his decision to reopen the investigation into Hillary Clinton’s emails may have been affected by the fact that she was well ahead of Donald Trump in the polls.

Beyond this, polls encourage us all to see politics as a kind of game within a game, a permanent rolling market ticker, in which the aim is not to improve the lives of human beings but to master the line on the graph, where winning elections is the end rather than the means. The BPC, with no fixed office and no full-time staff, was never going to fix this. In reality it is more of a trade body than a regulator, self-run and concerned less with ethics than trust and marketability.

And so JL Partners and the industry it belongs to are not the sole culprits here. In reality, the problem is the messenger: the people who consume and regurgitate politics for an audience, seduced by the idea that there is some all-seeing eye, a soup of numbers that will tell us all the answers. As someone whose very job deals in opinion, I know its fragility and malleability, the ridiculousness of treating it like a sacred stone tablet, or – I dunno – basing an entire generation of foreign and economic policy on how 635,000 people felt when they woke up on a Thursday in June 2016.

West Germany banned the death penalty in 1949 even though 77% of people were in favour of it. By 2000 that had fallen to 23%. Explanation, exemplar, persuasion, principle: these are the real tools of politics, at least a politics that seeks not to chase or triangulate public opinion but to mould and shape it. But if your entire existence is tied to a little line on a graph, then you’re never even going to try.

Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist

More than 1,000 women invested in companies at heart of Britain’s slave trade

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 11:00:41 GMT

Women used profits from trafficking of enslaved Africans to secure their families’ futures, research reveals

More than 1,000 women invested in the slave trade, challenging the conventional notion that they were passive beneficiaries and largely fought for its abolition.

Researchers found women bought, sold and brokered shares in the Royal African Company, South Sea Company, and other separate ventures, and used profits from the trafficking of enslaved Africans to secure financial independence and provide for their families.

By the time the RAC, which trafficked about 150,000 enslaved people, was dissolved in 1752, women made up about 10% of shareholders.

The Register of British Slave Traders, revealed exclusively in the Guardian, shows that women from across society played an active role in financing and sustaining the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

Investors ranged from queens and princesses to titled nobility, merchants, shopkeepers and cowherds.

The archives include letters in which women discuss profits from “African stock”, while company records show one investor, Helen Gladman, asking the RAC to transport a young African girl from Sherbro Island, off Sierra Leone, to England to serve in her household.

Researchers found women were involved “at almost every level” of the company’s activities. They acted as brokers, supplied goods including barrels and swords traded on the Atlantic African coast, managed company property and used their familial and social networks to strengthen the company’s finances and political influence.

Lila O’Leary Chambers, a lecturer at the University of Cambridge who researched women’s involvement for the register project, said: “This research really shows that this was not just a flash in the pan.

“Across the entirety of the Royal African Company and its various guises, there were women contributing financially and expecting a financial return from the slave trade.”

Women invested from the earliest years of enslavement, from Queen Elizabeth I’s backing in the 1560s to Lady Elizabeth Craven’s £1,000 loan financing a voyage to the Gambia through the Guinea Company. Some investors, unable to write their names, signed company records with a spidery “X”.

The research identifies 1,100 female investors across the histories of the RAC, the South Sea Company, and other separate ventures, though the true number is likely to have been higher. Of the 457 women whose marital status could be identified, almost half were widows and just over 42% were unmarried. Of the 7% who were married, most were aristocrats.

For many, these investments were crucial to gaining economic independence. “They were making the decision to invest, or they inherited shares and suddenly had this other asset they did not have before,” Chambers said.

Some became active traders and traded shares for friends and family, she added. “It was not a career as they would see it, but we might think: this has become your job.”

Chambers said the research directly challenged the conventional narrative that “white women come in at the point of abolition, see the suffering of enslaved people, identify with that oppression, and then work either to reform or ultimately abolish the slave trade and slavery itself”.

Work to overturn that misconception builds on decades of scholarship by historians from the Caribbean and west Africa, including Eric Williams, Elsa Goveia and Walter Rodney. More recent public-facing projects, such as the Legacies of British Slavery archive compiled by historians at University College London, have helped bring this history to wider audiences. The archive revealed that women were among those connected to the ownership of enslaved people who received compensation after slavery was abolished in a large portion of the empire in 1833, she said. Enslaved people received nothing.

“But this tells a much longer story, and that helps us see past a simple narrative that positions women historically as actually less complicated than they were.”

For Chambers, the accumulation of more than 1,000 names was itself a “gut punch”, because of the lack of similar information about enslaved African women.

“Historians and activists have really struggled to locate the names of enslaved people, to restore biographies to them, and to give a sense of their world,” Chambers said.

“The comparative opportunity to do this research for the people who invested is just really striking.”

Olivette Otele, a distinguished professor of the legacies and memory of slavery at Soas University of London, said while the lack of comparable detail about enslaved African women remained startling, “the more we know about enslavers, the better chance we have to know about enslaved women from the archives, because sometimes through diaries you can find more details”.

She added that archives alone cannot tell the full history, and future research should look at other evidence to help recover the lives and agency of enslaved women. “These women were the transmitters and the holders of their cultures wherever they were taken from,” she said. “Through food, music, and dancing, it’s about resistance and agency, and they transmitted that.”

The research also found that because female investors seemingly did not vote or hold board positions, they often relied on informal efforts to influence and shape a company.

Meeting minutes show women acting as witnesses, running the meeting house, delivering the goods exchanged for African lives, petitioning for wages, passing information and, most importantly, lending money and buying and selling shares.

Under English law, women who were single or widowed were in control of their own property and could operate as legal persons, while married women could not.

“That becomes really important for the Royal African Company as it stutters between financial crises,” Chambers said. “Women provided this important well of capital they could go to.”

In the early 18th century, the RAC secretary, John Perry, wrote to female investors, including Lady Dorothy Thomas and Mrs Stacy, urging them to exchange company debts for shares and persuade friends and relatives to do the same.

Chambers said: “That is a financial project, but it is also a political one, because he knows that they might not hold official positions, but women were very influential with their family members and with the way companies were perceived.”

The company survived long enough to attract at least 60 new female investors between 1713 and 1719, followed by another 250 women during a revival in the early 1720s.

The research also found many investors understood the violence underpinning their wealth. Some widows petitioned the courts for “head money” – bonuses owed to husbands according to the number of enslaved people they had trafficked.

“They would go and ask: he was supposed to get head money for 28 people he trafficked. Where is it? I am his widow and I need that,” Chambers said.

Chambers was also able to cross-reference some of the female investors with portraits of women with Black children who worked as their servants.

Women left RAC shares to their daughters to shore up their economic position, or used investment income to support widowed, disabled and vulnerable relatives.

In one letter, Mary Stanley committed to leaving £300 RAC stock and its proceeds to her son, Peter, with the caveat that if her daughter’s husband failed to provide her with “the necessaries of life”, Peter would use the stock to support her.

For Chambers, the research revealed a stark contradiction between white British women using their investments to protect their own families while investing in the destruction of African families.

“You cannot separate the way you think about investment from these structures of kinship, intimacy and violence,” she said. “That profit comes from denying those same kinship ties to African people, and denying their ability to make sure their own children are safe.

“That is so important to this story in particular, but also to how slavery shapes capitalism in general.”

Some investors endowed schools, churches, charities and universities that still exist today. Lettice Cornwallis, for example, funded education and charities while discussing acquiring an African boy for her household in family correspondence.

“This is an everyday conversation happening in houses,” Chambers said. “You see it in correspondence. There are these newsy, gossipy letters about someone getting married, someone being sick, or having a new recipe for a cordial, and then: by the way, how are your South Sea Company or Royal African Company shares doing?”

Female investors would have encountered African people in Britain, both free and enslaved, the research found. Dame Hester Buckworth, who bought £1,000 of RAC stock, knew Robert Negar, who was described in her husband’s will as his “Black servant”.

Another investor, Sarah Cornish, is thought to have shared a household with an African man named Paupey, whose legal status in England remains unclear.

Chambers often returns to the story of Susanna Sedgewick Phipps, who had a financial connection to the RAC throughout her life. Her grandson, James Phipps, later worked at Cape Coast Castle and married an Afro-Dutch woman, Catherina. He acknowledged their children in his will, some of whom later lived in England. One of their descendants, James Townsend, would eventually become Britain’s first elected Black MP.

Other women stood out to Chambers for the seeming mundanity of their concerns. She points to Sarah Clerke, who wrote frustrated letters to her nephew because she wanted to go to Tunbridge Wells to visit the spa and needed money from her African stock to do so.

‘The entire world belongs to Matthew Rhys, and we just live in it’: why the incredible actor broke Emmy records

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 10:30:32 GMT

The star of Widow’s Bay is that rarest of talents – someone who can do whatever he wants and make it utterly believable. No wonder he just made TV history

On Monday night, Matthew Rhys made history. He is now officially the first actor ever to win Emmy awards for lead roles in all three categories: drama, comedy and limited series. To make things even more extraordinary, he won two of those awards in a single night.

In the comedy category, Rhys won best lead for Widow’s Bay, the superlative Apple comedy horror where he stars as an indecisive mayor whose island suddenly plays host to a supernatural haunting. He also won best lead actor in a limited series or anthology for The Beast in Me, the Netflix drama about a property developer who may (or may not, no spoilers) have murdered his wife. Add this to his 2018 win for The Americans and the trifecta is complete. In other words, the entire world belongs to Matthew Rhys, and we’re all just living in it.

Obviously the remarkable thing here is the sheer range on display. In his two most recent shows, Rhys had to hit almost every single note that is available to an actor. The Beast in Me is possibly the most straightforward of these; it’s a pulpy thriller where he plays the antagonist, and he does so with relish. Widow’s Bay, on the other hand, seems like an incredibly difficult feat to pull off.

If you’ve seen it, you’ll know what I mean. Viewed through one lens, the series is an out-and-out horror, about the out-of-his-depth mayor of a small Martha’s Vineyard-esque island, whose tourist season is thrown into disarray when it becomes overrun by genuinely terrifying creatures. As such, Rhys has to nail all the familiar tropes of the genre: fear, uncertainty, heroism in the face of almost certain death.

But Widow’s Bay was also written by Katie Dippold, whose previous work has included Parks and Recreation. As such, folded into all this terror is a workplace comedy that isn’t afraid to be unashamedly goofy. If you watched the series week by week like I did, then you’ll know the exact moment Rhys won the Emmy. It happened during a reaction shot on a boat. In a moment of panic, the boat hits a giant wave and Rhys slides out of his seat. The face he pulls in that moment, even though it only lasts for a split second, is magisterial. His eyebrows shoot up to his hairline. His mouth widens as if he’s being possessed by the spirit of Wallace and Gromit. His neck goes slack. He’s surprised and resigned and perhaps a little bit giddy all at once. It is, without hyperbole, a perfect expression.

However, those of us who have been familiar with Rhys’s work for a while won’t be surprised by all this success. This is the 30th anniversary of his first screen credit, in the Welsh comedy film Bydd yn Wrol, and he has remained one of the industry’s most reliably great actors ever since. He played the lead in Peter Morgan’s ITV thriller Metropolis in 2000, and in the same year wowed audiences opposite Kathleen Turner in a stage run of The Graduate.

But it was in 2003, with his role as the antagonist in the final Columbo outing Columbo Likes the Nightlife, that things really moved up a gear. Within a few years he had secured a lead role on an American network drama, ABC’s Brothers and Sisters, which he augmented with roles in small but worthy films such as The Edge of Love (where he played Dylan Thomas) and the Welsh-Argentine drama Patagonia.

His career went up another notch with the debut of The Americans, a hard-boiled drama about two Russian agents living undercover in suburban Washington DC. The Americans was the golden age of television in microcosm: knotty, novelistic and steadfast in its refusal to spoon-feed viewers. Many of us who watched it said it was the best thing on television, and this was in no small part down to Rhys’s performance as Philip Jennings, a brutal KGB agent who slowly begins to doubt the cause. His performance was matched by Keri Russell, his onscreen wife who would become his real-life romantic partner.

The success of The Americans gave Rhys a blank cheque to do whatever he wanted, and he has taken this up in spades. In film he has worked with Steven Spielberg, and starred in Cocaine Bear. In television he has played the lead in a Perry Mason revival, and taken roles in Girls, BoJack Horseman and Family Guy. He has also presented a television show that was purely about how much he enjoys drinking wine.

This refusal to be pigeonholed is Rhys’s greatest asset. He is that rare actor – matched only perhaps by Bryan Cranston – who can do whatever he wants and be utterly credible. Matthew Rhys can do it all, and long may it continue.

Are you outraged by Sydney Sweeney – again? More fool you

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 09:49:48 GMT

Today it’s a silly sports betting ad, but I can’t see anything she’s done that’s worth this ire. She’s in her 20s: she does dumb things. Enjoy!

Would it be insanely unfashionable to defend Sydney Sweeney? You may or may not have heard that the Euphoria star has done an ad for a sports betting site. Sorry, I think we still have to call them “sports prediction markets” in the United States, which only recently popped its legalised sports betting cherry, and is behaving like a complete teenage boy about the whole thing. Anyway, among other poses, the ad features a naked Sydney holding a couple of American footballs over her breasts, which are – and I feel she would want us to acknowledge this – seriously among the very best in Hollywood. Maybe THE best. Listen, it is what it is. Life would be very boring if we couldn’t say so with a twinkle.

Forgive me. Life is, in fact, very, very boring, because yet another Sydney Sweeney-advertising-centred firestorm has been ignited by this ad. (Last year, some lunatic genuinely suggested her “good jeans” American Eagle ad was something to do with white supremacy and eugenics.) Her latest product endorsement has drawn the ire of a cascade of female athletes, who have described it variously as demeaning women’s sport, sexualised representation of athletes, and “a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, [and] every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity”.

Come on. With respect, I just don’t think it’s a kick in the face for any of those things. Not to be a crazed optimist, but the great thing about where women’s sport has got to today is that it feels a whole lot bigger and stronger and more compelling than whether Sydney Sweeney did or didn’t get her tits out for a gambling ad. I can’t help feeling it would have been cooler for women’s sport to simply not even mention the naked gambling ad at all. And, if it had to, maybe focus on the gambling bit rather than the woman advertising it. I haven’t definitively run the numbers on this, but instinct tells me that gambling wrecks a lot more lives than Sydney Sweeney.

Honestly, not everyone has to be the same and on-message, and I could not be more convinced that Sweeney adds to the gaiety of the nations. I love it that she’s out there in the culture, pissing off reflexively judgmental people who ignore so many bigger issues but have really strong views on sexy ad campaigns. And even slightly sexist ones. I truly loved it when, after one controversy or another a couple of years ago, Sydney posted a picture of herself in a sweatshirt reading: “SORRY FOR HAVING GREAT TITS AND CORRECT OPINIONS”. (Would also like to know where you buy this sweatshirt, etc.)

That she has emerged as such a frequent culture wars punching bag says so much more about the predictable, playable nature of her serial detractors than it does about her. Why can’t they just face it – Sydney’s gonna Sweeney. None of it feels like that big of a deal in the grand scheme of things.

Or rather, it does to some. After another ad campaign last year, some fashion analyst gasped to the New York Times: “It seems like she’s not embarrassed or ashamed promoting all of these different projects.” Hmm. Always great to see women implying other women should be feeling shame for hideous crimes like being a face of both Miu Miu AND Armani Beauty. The previous year, a columnist had described Sydney as “problematic yet unashamed”, which, ironically, I found somewhat problematic. Have to say, I’m a big fan of women not being made to feel shame unless whatever they’ve done is really quite bad.

Indeed, it was after a veteran female producer and film studies professor publicly dismissed her as not pretty and bad at acting that Sweeney gave a reactive interview in which she observed of Hollywood: “This entire industry, all people say is ‘women empowering other women’. None of it’s happening. All of it is fake and a front for all the other shit that they say behind everyone’s back.” Amazing. Because where’s the lie? Inevitably, it was her who got branded unsisterly for saying it.

A few months later, non-insult was added to non-injury once it emerged that Sydney was dating the considerably older former Taylor Swift foe/Justin Bieber manager Scooter Braun, who’s a sort of music industry vampire but not in a hot way. I saw someone who obviously fancied Sweeney lamenting this romance as “like a 19-year-old wonderkid signing for Al-Nassr”, which is a fun joke and about the level of seriousness with which we should treat other people’s dating choices. Don’t worry about it, guys! It’s not like you have to have sex with Scooter Braun. She’s doing it for you – relax.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Ultimately, I always feel somewhat compelled to defend Sydney’s right to do whatever stupid things she feels like in her 20s, safe – if not sound – in the knowledge that she will be forced to spend her entire 30s and probably her entire 40s atoning for every single one of them in every single interview, where every single reporter will just really want her to express shame and/or personal growth. It’s all such an endlessly dreary bore. There must be less repressed and joyless things to do with our time. While we spend far too long figuring those out, I do hope Sweeney finds a way to continue apparently not giving a shit – and that everyone else considers they might have more fun if they took a leaf out of her book from time to time.

Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist

London snubbed in favour of Nairobi for 2029 World Athletics Championships

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 09:45:31 GMT

Munich selected for 2031, president Seb Coe announces

Source in British bid ‘gutted’ at double disappointment

London’s bid for the 2029 World ­Athletics Championships has ended in failure after it lost out to Nairobi, the Kenyan capital which will now become the first African city to host the global championships.

Speaking at a press conference in Budapest the World Athletics president, Sebastian Coe, said the decision to go to Nairobi was historic and promised that it would stage a “­groundbreaking championships”.

While eyebrows will also be raised given that 318 elite Kenyan stars have been banned for violating anti-doping rules since the Athletics Integrity Unit was set up in 2017, a World Athletics spokesperson defended the decision, pointing out the Kenyan government had committed $5m (£3.7m) annually to anti-doping efforts.

“Kenya is much improved in this area, and we believe Nairobi hosting the world championships can act as a powerful catalyst in the Kenyan government’s continued fight against doping,” the spokesperson said. “It will put a spotlight on clean sport and galvanise the nation behind compliance.”

As Nairobi and Munich, which was awarded the 2031 championships, celebrated, London was left licking its wounds.

One senior source in the London team, which had been seen widely as the frontrunner for 2029, told the Guardian they were “totally gutted”.

Only over the weekend did some start to fear that their £45m bid, made up of £35m from the government and £10m from the mayor’s office, might not get over the line. London believed it had a strong case , and the sight of around 60,000 fans watching track and field every night for a week was a compelling proposition.

Jack Buckner, the chief executive of UK Athletics, said: “We are deeply disappointed. We believed we had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels.

“Although today’s announcement hasn’t gone our way, we will review and regroup. We know the world’s athletes love competing here and we’ll continue to explore further opportunities to make that happen.”

In hindsight, the lengthy public battle with West Ham to get permission to use the stadium in September 2029 – which was settled only on the eve of the bid being submitted – was not ideal. The sparse crowds on the opening days of last month’s European Athletics Championships in Birmingham perhaps did not help either.

after newsletter promotion

However, the London 2027 team believed those factors were irrelevant, and it simply came down to a thirst in World Athletics for Kenya to host the championships, and the size of Nairobi’s bid.

Lord Coe, though, stressed that there had been a range of factors at play. “Yes, of course, we see the historical, groundbreaking nature of taking the World Athletics Championships to Africa, but that alone is not the basis upon the decision,” he said. “It was made across budgets, it was made across financial government guarantees, it was made across the growth potential of the sport. It was also grounded in some really serious analysis.”

Coe also pushed back when he was reminded that going to Kenya would mean that Europe, which has the biggest fanbase for track and field, will have only staged one World ­Athletics Championships between one championship, in Budapest in 2023, between 2017 and 2031.

“Look, Europe is a heartland, and we openly accept that,” he said. “It is in large part the breadbasket of our sport. But we do also have a responsibility to make sure that an international governing federation made up of well over 200 federations has the opportunity to be able to take our championships into areas that strategically we think will actually grow the footprint of our sport.

“And Munich 2031 is a European city. What it does allow us to do in the next three editions is to have our World Athletics Championships globally based: in Africa, in obviously Europe, and of course our next ­edition in Asia in 2027 [Beijing] next year.”

How enslavement became state-backed operation supported by Conservative and Lib Dem forerunners

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 05:00:28 GMT

Tory and Whig MPs were central to funding trafficking of enslaved people and many opposed abolition of the slave trade

There is a British culture of celebrating the abolition of slavery without acknowledging that the country enslaved and trafficked millions of African people for centuries.

The newly published Register of British Slave Traders, which documents the thousands of investors in Britain’s near 250-year trafficking of more than 3 million enslaved African people, shows that it was a state-backed operation, fully supported by both major political parties at the time, the Tories and Whigs – the forerunners of today’s Conservatives and Liberal Democrats respectively.

Many Tory and Whig MPs were investors in the slave trade, the register shows, and many also owned plantations. But when the movement to abolish the slave trade and enslavement grew in the late 18th century, the Whigs generally moved towards supporting abolition, while Tory governments opposed and delayed it for decades.

The Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, said in response to the Guardian’s reporting of this history that he supported “full transparency” and it was “vital that we face up to the full truth of Britain’s history”.

The Conservative party referred the Guardian to a post on X by its leader, Kemi Badenoch, in March, in response to a UN declaration that the historic enslavement and trafficking of African people was “the gravest crime against humanity” and reparations should be discussed.

“Britain led the fight to end slavery,” Badenoch posted. “We shouldn’t be paying for a crime we helped eradicate and still fight today.”

More than 50 Tory MPs and about 50 Whig MPs are identified in the register as historic slave traders. Most invested in Britain’s state-backed Royal African Company (RAC) and its predecessors, and some were involved in the South Sea Company.

The involvement of Tories in the RAC was rooted in the foundation of the party. The original Tory faction formed during the 1679 exclusion crisis, in support of the then Duke of York being crowned King James II. Their opponents, the Whigs, sought to prevent James’s succession.

James became king and led the RAC, which trafficked more enslaved people – at least 150,000 African men, women and children – than any other organisation in the history of the transatlantic slave trade.

Many Tories who supported James also invested in the RAC.

Prof William Pettigrew, the lead historian of the register, said: “This platform of support for the Duke of York became the Tory party. Support for the duke’s slave-trading project, the Royal African Company, provided a further rallying point for these early Tories, while early Whigs were opposed to it. Disagreements about the best way to expand the nation’s slave trade were present at the birth of our political parties.”

The Whigs’ opposition was not to enslaving African people, but to the RAC’s royal monopoly. Many Whigs lobbied to expand the slave trade by opening the trafficking to independent “separate traders”.

Sir Benjamin Bathurst, one of many prominent Tories in the register, illustrates the elite status of the RAC investors. He was a friend of King James and Queen Anne, and the Tory MP for New Romney, Kent.

Bathurst was an assistant and leader of the RAC at various points between 1677 and 1700, when the company made 222 transatlantic voyages, transporting tens of thousands of African people to the colonies.

Sir Robert Clayton, a 17th-century banker who was a managing director of the RAC, was a Whig MP for London. Clayton donated money to St Thomas’ hospital – now part of Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS foundation trust – where a statue commemorates him.

Edward Colston, a dedicated RAC shareholder and assistant whose statue was toppled by campaigners in 2020, was the Tory MP for Bristol in 1710-13.

The register shows more Tory and Whig politicians invested in the RAC after the South Sea Company was formed in 1711. The company was developed by Robert Harley, the chancellor of the exchequer who became leader of the Tory party, and moved into trafficking enslaved people.

In 1713, Queen Anne secured from Spain’s King Philip V an asiento – an agreement to deliver a stipulated 4,800 enslaved African men to Spain’s American colonies every year. Anne gave the asiento to the South Sea Company, which contracted the RAC to fulfil it.

Several Tory and Whig MPs became directors of the South Sea Company, including Sir Richard Hoare, the Tory MP for London and a lord mayor. He founded the private bank Hoares, which is still owned by the family today.

The Whigs, in government for decades in the mid-18th century, supported Britain’s development into the world’s foremost enslaving nation as independent traffickers in Bristol, then Liverpool, industrialised slave trading operations.

When moral opposition finally came, it was an outcry led by enslaved and freed people, Quakers, and in parliament by the independent MP William Wilberforce. Some freed enslaved people, most famously Olaudah Equiano, wrote shocking accounts of their experiences.

The Tories, who were in government almost continuously from 1783-1833, continually delayed abolition, while the Whigs generally moved towards the abolitionists’ view. After the Quakers’ first parliamentary petition in 1783, enslavement remained enforced for 50 years before a new Whig government passed the abolition law in 1833. Party affiliations were not as clear as they are now, and there were exceptions on both sides.

Wilberforce’s motions in parliament to abolish the slave trade, beginning in 1791, were defeated.

The Tory home secretary, Henry Dundas intervened to add the word “gradually” to Wilberforce’s 1792 abolition bill, which was then blocked in the Lords.

Prof David Richardson, the founding director of the Wilberforce Institute at the University of Hull, wrote in his 2022 book that Dundas “played a leading role in killing the abolition bill”. Richardson identified several other Tory ministers, including the “deeply conservative, even reactionary” lord chancellor Edward Thurlow, whom he said were “powerful Tory opponents … to slave trade abolition”. A group of “Whig grandees” was also opposed to abolition, Richardson wrote.

It took until a Whig-led “ministry of all the talents” coalition government briefly replaced the Tories for the law abolishing the slave trade to be passed in 1807. During the 16 years of delay since 1791, the British slave trade was at its peak and trafficked 648,000 more African men, women and children across the Atlantic into enslavement.

When the next campaign was mounted in 1823 to abolish enslavement itself, the Tory government’s response was to delay it indefinitely, claiming enslaved people were not ready for freedom. The foreign secretary George Canning, later a Tory prime minister, had resolutions passed requiring “a progressive improvement in the character of the slave population” before they could be emancipated.

Tories were also at the forefront of claiming that if enslaved people were freed, compensation must be paid to the enslavers. Ultimately, the enslavers were paid £20m public money – the equivalent of £2.7bn today according to the lowest method of calculation. The 800,000 enslaved people in Britain’s colonies were paid nothing and consigned to “apprenticeships” – further years of forced unpaid labour.

In an 1824 Commons debate, Canning made “arguably the most racist speech in the history of the British parliament”, according to the historian Michael Taylor. Canning said: “In dealing with the negro, sir, we must remember that we are dealing with a being possessing the form and strength of a man, but the intellect only of a child.”

Sir Robert Peel, a founding father of the Conservative party, said he had “never objected to the extinction of slavery”, but he spoke in the Commons against immediate emancipation as late as 1833. He urged the house “to recollect the eloquent language of Mr Canning” and repeated Canning’s remarks. Peel claimed emancipation would mean “two distinct and separate races” had to be amalgamated, and the “distinction of colour” was an obstruction.

In 1834, the year after the abolition law finally passed under a Whig government, Peel issued his Tamworth manifesto which is seen as a foundational document of the Conservative party. He became the first Conservative prime minister.

Peel later celebrated emancipation and became associated with stopping the slave trade. As prime minister in 1845, he signed a convention with France that both countries would deploy expanded squadrons of ships to enforce the ban on transatlantic trafficking.

The Legacies of British Slavery archive at University College London, which is based on records of “compensation” paid after 1833, found there were about 80 Tory and Conservative MPs involved in the ownership of enslaved people in the decades before abolition, and in compensation claims. There were also more than 60 Whig and Liberal MPs. The largest total payment to any individual was almost £110,000, the equivalent of £14.6m today, to John Gladstone, the Tory MP who claimed for 2,508 men, women and children enslaved on his plantations in Guiana and Jamaica.

The largest single payment was to the Tory MP James Blair, who owned huge sugar plantations, collectively named Blairmont, in Guiana.

One of Blair’s only two speeches in parliament, in 1824, followed the landmark 1823 uprising of enslaved people in Demerara, Guyana. It was led by an enslaved man on Gladstone’s Success plantation, named Jack, who with his father, Quamina, had the surname Gladstone imposed on them. Quamina had been enslaved and trafficked as a child with his mother from modern-day Ghana and suffered terrible whippings. He was the head carpenter on the plantation and became a deacon at a chapel established by missionaries, where he learned to read and write. According to accounts of the uprising, Quamina was determined that enslaved people should be free, but urged Jack to be cautious.

The British colonial authorities suppressed the Demerara rebellion with their customary extreme violence, killing scores of participants and subjecting others to merciless floggings. More than 50 people were executed, and some were then decapitated, their heads stuck on poles as a warning. Quamina was tracked down and shot and his body put up to rot.

He is now a national hero in Guyana.

A rebellion on Blairmont had been suppressed with similar ruthlessness in 1814, a year before Blair inherited it: the heads of six men were put on poles.

In his 1824 speech, Blair told parliament enslaved people were “mildly and … humanely managed” and argued for a limit to amelioration.

“I conceive that unless a line be drawn and unless we are told where concession is to stop…” he said, “the negroes will never enjoy quiet, nor the planters that undisturbed possession of their property, to which they are by law entitled.”

When abolition finally came, Blair was paid £83,530, equivalent to £11m today, for the loss of his “property” – 1,598 enslaved men, women and children.

In response to the research, a Conservative party spokesperson said: “The Conservatives are proud of our country’s history, leading the world in abolishing slavery. Kemi Badenoch has been clear that in the modern age we must build a meritocracy that does not discriminate on ethnic grounds.”

Davey, the Lib Dem leader, said: “The transatlantic slave trade was an abominable crime against humanity and it is vital that we face up to the full truth of Britain’s history. The Liberal Democrats support full transparency, teaching the complete context of our colonial past in schools, and engaging in open, constructive dialogue with international partners.”

Eric Phillips, the Guyanese vice-chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, said: “The British Conservative party should examine its history and acknowledge it, not be caught up in this denial of only talking about abolition. The history happened, you can’t change it. Let’s accept it and discuss it, and move towards healing, ways to work together, and mutually beneficial solutions.”

I know why many east Germans vote AfD. And no, it’s not an inherited longing for dictatorship

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 04:00:27 GMT

Grievance politics has grown in the east of the country where I was born. But west Germans have hard questions to answer too

The fear that a fascist, far-right movement would rise to power again in Germany has been with me since my youth. On 6 September, the far-right, anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) won a landslide in Saxony-Anhalt, becoming the biggest party in the state parliament, with a shocking 44% of the vote, on a record turnout. If it finds a way to power it will be the first far-right party to govern a German state since the Nazi era.

The night before the vote, I sent a message to a friend, who, like myself, has an East German background. Was she as worried, scared even, about the vote as I was, I asked. I’d fallen into a loop for days, scrolling videos, reels, reports, interviews done on the ground. And I knew these AfD voters. They could have been relatives, friends of my parents, old teachers, former schoolmates. Why were they saying such incoherent stuff?

I did not grow up in Saxony-Anhalt, but in Saxony – a sibling eastern German state, not entirely the same but similar in many core aspects. When I went to high school in Leipzig in the late 1990s and early 2000s, the presence of rightwing extremists was part of my coming-of-age experience. Every Friday night, you felt the fear that neo-Nazis would be waiting outside the clubs, the bars, the tram stops, fists clenched or baseball bats in hand. Every 1 May was a flashpoint when neo-Nazis were allowed to march through the city-centre. And still, Saxony’s first prime minister after reunification, Kurt Biedenkopf – a West German Christian Democratic Union (CDU) politician and a close ally of Helmut Kohl – promised, stoically, throughout his 12 years in office: “Saxony is immune to rightwing extremism.”

By 2004, a year before I graduated, the far-right National Democratic party (NPD) had entered the Saxon state parliament for the first time, with 9.2% of the vote. In 2005, I left Saxony and moved to Berlin. One reason was the unbearable, dangerous presence of neo-Nazis and rightwing extremists. Many peers did the same, because it was clear that the blooming landscapes that Kohl, the German chancellor in charge of reunification, had confidently promised in 1990 weren’t going to materialise.

Instead, rightwing extremism has grown steadily in eastern Germany ever since. Only the names have changed – from NPD, to Pegida (the anti-migrant protest movement launched in 2014), to AfD. I am terrified, if not surprised. Because fascist structures, left unchecked, will always keep going.

But this result is also a function of the deeply troubled relationship between the former East and West Germany.

A couple of weeks ago, Magnus Brechtken, deputy director of the Institut für Zeitgeschichte in Munich – Germany’s leading institute for contemporary history – gave an interview to the FAZ newspaper. It went viral. The headline: “Many west Germans have had enough now.”

The interview was framed as a reminder to angry east Germans – meaning, specifically, those tempted to vote AfD out of spite towards the west – of some historical facts. Brechtken argued that the differences east Germans have been complaining about for 36 years are, by now, emotional rather than rational – the product, he suggested, of a lack of honest self-examination. He went further: the German west, he said, has spent the past 75 years proving it understands democracy and knows how to handle extremism, that it is better equipped to counter radical movements and prevent parties like the AfD from rising in the first place – while east Germans, he implied, have always had an inherited longing for authoritarian solutions.

You couldn’t help but wonder how much of it was history, and how much was personal opinion. But I do think Brechtken was right about one thing. This supposed east German anger, the AfD’s popularity, the result in Saxony-Anhalt and – in all likelihood – the party’s performance in two upcoming state elections on 20 September should be used as a reminder of some actual historical facts, and of follow-up questions Brechtken apparently decided not to ask.

The AfD was founded in west Germany. A large share of its leadership was born and raised in western states such as Rheinland-Pfalz and Nordrhein-Westfalen. The question shouldn’t only be what draws the east of Germany towards the AfD. It’s just as much: what draws a certain kind of west German towards building a party like this one, pushing it, and choosing the east as the place to make it grow?

I believe the west German states – which officially claimed to have carried out denazification after 1945, and prided themselves on the culture of remembrance, or “coming to terms” with the Nazi past – need to look, just as urgently as the east German states, at why this fascination with fascism keeps recurring. And why, by now, are there no working structures against the rise of right-extremist movements, parties and agendas – but somehow still a system that lets them flourish?

It’s also worth asking whether a party like the AfD went east only because east Germans are more susceptible – or because the visible inequalities there are excellent material to organise around.

In 1989, a lot of east Germans had hoped for something between socialism and capitalism. Reunification wasn’t necessarily the preferred option. What followed felt, to many, badly mishandled – too fast, laws and decisions imposed rather than negotiated. And then there was the Treuhand – the agency put in charge of privatising the former GDR’s entire state-owned economy. In the process of reunification, 94% of East German companies were taken over by West German or international investors. Six per cent stayed with the people of East Germany. Six per cent. Approximately two million jobs were eliminated in the east.

In the autumn and winter of 1990-91, people took to the streets again – not against their own government’s repression this time, but against the perceived occupier: West Germany. They demanded new elections, a renegotiation of the agreements that had left millions empty-handed and jobless, as unemployment in the east skyrocketed. Detlev Karsten Rohwedder, head of the Treuhand and the key figure in overhauling the former East Germany, was asked in an interview back then by a TV host: “If it doesn’t get better, aren’t you afraid there might be another revolution in East Germany?”

In those years, the former East Germany was treated like a child that had to follow the laws and orders of its wiser western counterpart – a parent. Now, that child is all grown. But it remembers the experience – and quite possibly holds on to it too tightly. Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s man in Saxony-Anhalt, was born the same year as reunification.
