The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

One of his main promises is to take back control. Maybe you could say that what happened in Saxony-Anhalt went beyond a question of control and was driven by the desire for a sort of revenge. The east, finally, daring to say to the overpowering west: enough. Or as Siegmund at his first victory press conference said, the result showed that the people of Saxony-Anhalt wouldn’t be “patronised” any longer. With this he was tapping into something almost visceral. The remark also clarified for me something about the motives of the countless potential AfD voters I had listened to over the past weeks and months. Most of them don’t actually read or know what’s in the AfD’s programme. And they don’t seem to care. What won people over was simpler: I hear you. I see you. Yes, you have every right to be unhappy.

Throughout the campaign, Siegmund travelled the entire state and threw parties: free sausages, free beer, dancing, music and maybe for some, it felt like the return of community. Villages and small towns that had been hollowed out, some of them ghostly and depopulated, were suddenly told again: you matter. Everyone else may have left you behind, but I, we, the AfD, care.

What many have not realised yet is that the AfD won’t improve life in east Germany. But that was never the point. It gave people attention in exchange for a vote.

And for now, that was what counted most.

Because the AfD is bigger than east versus west. It was built by west Germans, carried by east Germans, and now it strives for power across the country. Its programme runs on ideas Germany once needed a war and total defeat to bury: racism, the belief in superiority and a hierarchy of who really belongs, contempt for who doesn’t, a hunger for enemies dressed up as pride. That’s not a regional problem. It’s a national one, and it should frighten every single German citizen.

A vote for the AfD is a vote for that same set of beliefs. Whatever anger, disappointment, or legitimate demand to finally be seen or heard got bundled in alongside it.

In April 1932, the Nazi party became the strongest party in the state election in the region that now makes up Saxony-Anhalt, with 40.7% of the vote, and formed, with coalition partners, the first Nazi-led state government in Germany. Whatever happens next, it will be hard to say we didn’t know.

Carolin Würfel is a writer, screenwriter and journalist

Hyrox changes rules and apologises for allowing Australian athlete who soiled herself to continue

The Guardian Tue, 15 Sep 2026 02:16:46 GMT

Australian Joanna Wietrzyk went on to win fitness race in Beijing

Hyrox admits making mistake by ‘not reacting immediately’

Organisers of the global indoor fitness competition Hyrox have apologised and pledged immediate rule changes after an Australian athlete was allowed to finish and win an event in Beijing despite soiling herself mid-race.

Footage of world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk competing on Saturday showed her continuing through demanding exercises and using communal equipment, with faecal matter visibly running down her legs. The incident went viral on social media and triggered debate about Hyrox’s health and safety standards, and athlete responsibility.

Hyrox, an increasingly popular fitness competition launched in Germany in 2017, is now held in locations across the world. It debuted in mainland China in late 2024.

In each race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises at shared high-intensity stations – including a rowing machine, sled pushes, burpee jumps, medicine ball throws and lunges while carrying a sandbag.

Prior to the weekend’s incident, official event rules already penalised athletes for minor infractions such as littering on the course, or spitting or clearing their nose on the floor. It contained no immediate protocol for faecal matter.

Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste apologised in a statement on Instagram to everyone affected “directly or indirectly” by the incident. “Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents – and I did not,” Fürste said.

He added that Hyrox has made “rulebook changes immediately”.

“As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again.”

In statements released by Hyrox China and Hyrox World, organisers confirmed that affected lanes were isolated for deep cleaning overnight, contaminated equipment was removed and venue carpet was replaced overnight before competition resumed the following day.

“After the incident, the organising committee immediately closed off and isolated the affected area and track, and completed comprehensive disinfection,” Hyrox China organisers said.

Hyrox World said that it has clear bio-contaminant and medical procedures in place: “Protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood.”

Wietrzyk, the world record holder in the Hyrox women’s solo event, was invited to compete at the Beijing event. She posted and then deleted a selfie to her Instagram story from what appeared to be a hospital bed, with the text: “Go hard or go home … a win is a win. In all seriousness, thank you for all the support. I’ll be back soon x.”

It is not uncommon for athletes to soil themselves while competing in high endurance sports, particularly marathons. British athlete Paula Radcliffe won the 2005 London marathon after suffering from “runner’s diarrhoea” and having to stop at the 22-mile mark to relieve herself, in full view of cameras.

Social media users and other athletes at the event questioned the response and why Wietrzyk was allowed to finish the race, while impacting the health and safety of fellow competitors.

Joe Ho, a male competitor in Beijing, said that fellow athletes — who generally pay a fee to take part in Hyrox races — had been failed.

“For people who were exposed to that situation, there could be genuine physical and psychological consequences,” Ho wrote in an Instagram post.

“I paid Hyrox to provide a professionally organised and safe event. So while I understand the athlete perspective, ultimately my contract and expectation is with Hyrox.

“If the organisation accepts that something went wrong, why not offer affected participants refunds, credits, or some meaningful form of compensation?”

Following online vitriol directed at Wietrzyk after her identity was shared, organisers warned that anyone sending abuse or threats of violence towards the athlete would be banned from all future events.

Guardian Australia reached out to Wietrzyk and Hyrox for comment.

The royal crown branded on enslaved Africans: Britain’s monarchy and the slave trade

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 05:00:25 GMT

From Elizabeth I’s backing of early voyages to royal investment in trafficking companies, generations of monarchs were central to Britain’s slave trade

Enslaved African people were seared with hot metal brands bearing the royal crown, according to research by historians who have documented the monarchy’s centuries-long involvement in Britain’s slave trade.

The Register of British Slave Traders identifies thousands of people who invested in Britain’s trafficking of enslaved Africans, including kings and queens.

In response to the Guardian’s reporting of the new research relating to the monarchy, a spokesperson for King Charles said he was “grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed”.

Dr Nicholas Radburn, a historian at Lancaster University, discovered evidence of the branding in the archives of the South Sea Company, a British crown-backed enterprise that trafficked thousands of enslaved African people to plantations in the 1700s.

Radburn found a letter sent by the company’s board to its agents in Buenos Aires, instructing them to brand enslaved people with hot metal. The brand bore a crown, a symbol of the British monarchy’s role in the trade. A doctor had warned against the branding, but the board, whose members included figures from England’s establishment elite including MPs and Bank of England directors, instructed the agents to proceed.

“It now comes out, that you never mark the Negroes,” the letter said, “giving for reason that the French never did it, and that Dr Dover said your mark being so large, might endanger the Negroes.”

Insisting the agents disregard the doctor’s advice, they wrote that it was “the most effectual … way to distinguish our Negroes from others”. The directors sent a crown brand with their letter and instructions for how to scar the enslaved African people with it.

“Herewith you will receive a small silver mark,” they wrote. “As to the manner of using it, the method of our other factorys, is to mark the Negroes on the left shoulder heating the mark red hot.”

The letter was signed: “Your affectionate friends, the court of directors.”

Radburn said the letter illustrated how detailed the company’s dehumanising cruelty was – and its awareness of it.

“These people were members of the London elite, in a boardroom, thinking in fine grain terms about the violence that needs to be done to enslaved people across the ocean,” he said. “And that will have happened as a result of that letter. People will have had their flesh seared with that brand.”

The Register of British Slave Traders, the new historical record for which Radburn was a lead investigator, documents how Britain’s enslaving and trafficking of more than 3 million African people for nearly 250 years was perpetrated as an official national enterprise, led by its monarchs.

The publication of the register, the most comprehensive research project into the investors in Britain’s trafficking of enslaved African people, will further inform calls for King Charles to finally acknowledge the monarchy’s deep involvement in the trade.

The kings and queens who powered the trafficking most ferociously were those after the monarchy was restored in 1660. James, Duke of York, who became King James II, was the governor and a substantial shareholder in the Royal African Company (RAC), founded in 1672, which trafficked more African men, women and children than any other single organisation in the history of the slave trade.

The RAC and its predecessor, the Company of Royal Adventurers, were established by James’s brother, King Charles II, and backed by royalist courtiers, politicians and financiers. These royal insiders, whose biographies are in the register, bore florid titles of the time: Edward Proger, “groom of the bedchamber”, the Earl of Falmouth, “groom of the stool”. The RAC meetings, where decisions about the trafficking of enslaved people were made, were held in James’s personal apartment in Whitehall Palace, the royal family’s London home before Buckingham Palace was built.

Prof William Pettigrew, the register’s lead historian and investigator, said these royal enslaving companies were crucial to the kings of the Stuart dynasty striving to solidify the restored monarchy as an institution.

“I view James II as the most important English slave trader of the 17th century,” Pettigrew said. “The African companies were central to the monarchy’s rehabilitation plan within the British constitution.”

James ran the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people with his cousin, Prince Rupert of the Rhine, described in the register as “the visionary for England’s fully fledged, state-backed slave trade”. Other royals, including Charles II’s Portuguese wife, Queen Catherine of Braganza, were also investors in these companies.

In her book The Crown’s Silence, Prof Brooke Newman has chronicled in detail the centuries-long involvement of the British monarchy in the enslavement of African people, from the first trafficking voyages backed by Queen Elizabeth I in the 1560s to King William IV, who relished drinking and debauchery on Caribbean plantations and opposed abolition for decades.

Newman wrote that the RAC also branded the African people it enslaved at its coastal forts and factories, with DY for the Duke of York, and RACE for the Royal African Company of England. An agent in Sherbro, an island off Sierra Leone, was told by company directors: “You are to mark them … on the right breast RACE and the children of them at three years of age.”

As part of a 1713 peace treaty, Queen Anne agreed with Spain’s King Philip V that Britain would be awarded the asiento – an agreement to deliver a stipulated 4,800 enslaved African men to Spain’s American colonies every year.

Anne announced it triumphantly in the House of Lords: “I have insisted and obtained, that the asiento or contract for furnishing the Spanish West Indies with Negroes, shall be made with us for the term of 30 years.”

Queen Anne was a significant investor in the South Sea Company, which was established in 1711, and had rights to almost a quarter share of its overall profits. Anne gave the asiento to the SSC, which contracted the RAC to fulfil it.

Anne’s successors, George I and George II, were also personal investors in and supporters of the SSC.

According to the Slave Voyages database, the SSC trafficked 43,220 African captives from west Africa and Madagascar to the Caribbean and Spanish Americas between 1714 and 1740. From there, Radburn said, they were trafficked again, shipped and forced to march for hundreds of miles overland to the Pacific coast of South America. The company also moved more than 50,000 enslaved people within the Americas.

The trafficking vessels, including ships named Crown, King William and William and Mary, all set off from London. Almost 7,000 people died in the ships’ notoriously appalling conditions.

“It was a merciless, monarchy supported company,” Radburn said, “and the trafficking of enslaved people was the heart of it.”

Pressure on Charles from African and Caribbean countries to acknowledge this history and go further than previous expressions of sorrow is expected to build before the next Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda in November.

But successive governments have not formally apologised for Britain’s role in slavery and have rejected any discussion of reparations. Even if Charles wanted to, as king he is constitutionally bound by the government’s stated position.

An official delegation from Jamaica delivered a petition to Charles last week, seeking a legal ruling from the privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries. It asks whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful, whether it constituted a crime against humanity, and whether Britain is obliged to provide restitution to Jamaica for slavery and its enduring consequences.

Charles has publicly expressed sorrow over enslavement, describing it as an “appalling atrocity” and referring to “the most painful aspects of our past”, but has not formally acknowledged and apologised for the role of Britain or the monarchy in perpetrating it. In 2023 he signalled for the first time his support for research into the British monarchy’s historical links to transatlantic slavery.

A spokesperson for the king said: “His majesty has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today.

“In that context, he is grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed.”

David Comissiong, the Barbados ambassador to the Caribbean Community, said he recognised that Charles’s constitutional role meant he must not contravene government policy.

“But just as other British establishment families have acknowledged their involvement in the slavery enterprise and indicated a willingness to make reparation, anybody conscious of the British monarchy’s history would have to conclude that the British royal family should act similarly,” he added.

Monarchs, MPs and merchants: the register laying bare Britain’s slave-trading past

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 05:00:24 GMT

Exclusive: New research identifies thousands who profited from trafficking enslaved Africans and traces some financial links to institutions still operating today

The enormous scale of Britain’s centuries-long trafficking of enslaved African people, supported by parliament and the monarchy, has been laid bare by new research.

The Register of British Slave Traders, the product of a three-year project by a team of specialist historians, documents the investors in Britain’s near 250-year transatlantic slave trade from the first traffickers in the 1560s to abolition in 1807.

The register provides biographical detail for as many of 10,500 investors as possible from historical records, building the most comprehensive single picture so far of those who perpetrated the enslavement of African people.

Britain’s trafficking operations, including royal companies led by kings and, later, a rush of entrepreneurs in Bristol, Liverpool and other port cities, violently transported more than 3 million enslaved African men, women and children to colonial plantations in the Americas and Caribbean.

The Guardian is reporting on significant findings of the project, led by Prof William Pettigrew of King’s College London, and the vast human damage it documents: the relentless involvement of the British monarchy, parliament and financial and business elites; the role of the church in legitimising it; and how the investors’ wealth was woven deep into the country’s fabric and used to fund hospitals, schools, welfare organisations, the arts, science and culture.

Key elements include:

A series of British kings and queens were leaders and investors in the trafficking of enslaved African people;

More than 100 MPs were investors in slave-trading companies, including scores in the Tory and Whig parties – the forerunners of today’s Conservatives and Liberal Democrats;

Dozens of directors and original financiers of the Bank of England were investors in the slave trade;

More than 1,000 women invested in slave-trading companies;

Forty-five Church of England clergymen were investors in the slave-trading Royal African Company.

The BBC is showing a two-part documentary about the register, presented by the historian David Olusoga.

The publication of the register will provide further evidence for the growing global movement calling on European governments to acknowledge their perpetration of enslavement, issue a full, formal apology and engage positively with discussions for reparatory justice.

Successive British governments have refused to do so, arguing there is no duty to make reparations because enslavement and the slave trade were not against the law at the time.

An official delegation from Jamaica delivered a petition to King Charles last week to seek a legal ruling from the privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries, on whether that government position is lawful.

It is a legacy of the dehumanisation inflicted on so many African men, women and children that much less was documented about them than about their enslavers. The register draws on copious permanent records for the traffickers: company documents; birth, death and marriage certificates; wills and biographical information, much of it official because many were MPs and members of the elite. Memorials and statues venerate many to this day. The enslaved people were treated as chattel, property, by British law, and there is no lasting documentation even identifying millions of them.

There are ongoing projects dedicated to addressing this deficit and to documenting the lives of the enslaved people as much as possible from the few records that were made.

Of the thousands of British slave traders identified in the register, some are household names: King James II, the last Catholic monarch to rule England, Scotland and Ireland whose statue celebrating him as a “defender of the faith” stands in Trafalgar Square, London; the composer George Frideric Handel; and the philosopher John Locke, both shareholders in the Royal African Company (RAC).

The historians’ broader research found that Sir Christopher Wren, the architect of St Paul’s Cathedral and many other churches in London, chaired a meeting in 1682 of the Royal Society, the institution dedicated to furthering science, when it voted to invest in the RAC.

It is an illustration of modern Britain’s scant discussion of its enslaving history that the legendary status of these men rarely encompasses recognition that they participated in the slave trade.

It is now better known that Queen Elizabeth I and her inner circle supported the enslaving voyages of the Plymouth-based privateer John Hawkins in the 1560s, lending him Royal Navy ships in return for a share of the profits.

For decades, piratical shipowners enslaved and trafficked people from the west African coast – mostly from present-day Ghana and Nigeria – to the Caribbean and North America. In the 1600s merchants followed, establishing plantations, including sugar in Barbados.

Perhaps the single British person now principally known as a slave trader, among the 10,500 in the register for whom the historians found records, is Edward Colston. He was an RAC investor and assistant, or director, Tory MP for Bristol and benefactor of schools and charities. That is the result of concerted campaigning and public education, culminating during the Black Lives Matter protests in 2020 in the toppling of Colston’s statue.

British plantation owners enslaved African men and women and children – who were born enslaved for life – to extract their unpaid labour, enforcing enslavement through extreme violence. It is a further twist of cruelty that this oppression was enforced to deliver treats to people in a modernising Europe: tobacco and sugar.

After the monarchy was restored in 1660, the crown took a leading role in the trafficking and established two royally chartered companies before the RAC was founded in 1672.

Led by James II and his cousin Prince Rupert of the Rhine, the RAC held a monopoly on the trafficking, enforced with the Royal Navy, the military and the state’s legal power. The RAC became the largest single trafficker of enslaved African people in the history of European enslavement, taking at least 150,000 captive men, women and children across the Atlantic.

Those who eagerly joined the king in this royal enslaving company were the elites of a nation developing into a modern state. The register gives character to the names of RAC shareholders, assistants and governors: royal courtiers; Tory and Whig members of parliament; financiers, bankers, merchants; and City of London aldermen, or councillors.

Arguments about Britain’s involvement in enslavement did develop in parliament. But moral condemnation came much later. The dispute that dominated for 25 years was led by independent, or “separate”, traders lobbying for the royal monopoly to be removed so that they too could become traffickers.

Full deregulation was approved by parliament in 1712, and the new British ideology of “free trade” enabled a dramatic increase in the number of African people denied their liberty, enslaved and trafficked.

A significant figure in the register during this pivotal period was Robert Heysham, an RAC assistant elected Tory MP for Lancaster in 1698. Heysham argued forcefully in parliament against the royal monopoly, then became instrumental in growing the slave trade.

“Heysham took the opportunity to outfit his own ships, making human trafficking his core concern,” according to the register.

Heysham later moved to vote with the Whigs, the advocates of free trade, and became one of the largest independent traffickers of enslaved African people during Queen Anne’s early 18th-century reign. On ships with names including Little London, New Adventure, and Liverpool, Heysham and his brother William, who lived in Barbados, trafficked about 9,000 enslaved African people, of whom about 1,350 died in the notoriously appalling conditions of the ships.

“Heysham lobbied persistently to expand the traffic,” the register says, “and worked more than anyone else to ensure that it became a national commercial concern.”

For these records, the historians drew on the landmark Slave Voyages database, which contains records of enslaving ships. The register also builds on the Legacies of British Slavery archive, compiled by historians at University College London, which documents the British “owners” of enslaved people.

Its starting point was the people paid £20m – the equivalent of £2.7bn today, according to the lowest method of calculation – in “compensation” for losing their human “property” when parliament abolished enslavement in 1833. That payment of public money to the enslavers, with no compensation ever paid to enslaved people, is still deeply felt today as an enduring injustice by those calling for reparations.

As Britain’s 18th-century transatlantic slave trade expanded, its participants spread from London elites to opportunists in other ports.

Bristol became particularly dominant and the register sets out many of the men who made fortunes there: Richard Farr, a ropemaker who became “one of Bristol’s most prolific and important slave traders”, outfitting at least 38 enslaving ships that trafficked more than 10,000 people to plantations; William Tyndall, who was “deeply engaged in slave trading in Jamaica”; and James Laroche, who over 42 years until his death in 1770 outfitted “at least 105 slave ships that carried more than 30,000 people into captivity”.

The details add to research carried out in Bristol documenting the extent to which the city’s political power bases, architecture and financing, as well as cultural institutions including the Bristol Old Vic theatre, were built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans.

Merchants in other port cities, including Lancaster, also became seriously involved and Liverpool became dominant from about 1750, driving another vast expansion of the trafficking.

That year, parliament passed legislation winding up the RAC and institutionalising free trade in the transatlantic trafficking. The act incorporated official wording that plainly set out the enslavement and trafficking of African people as state policy – and the racism at its core.

“The trade to and from Africa is very advantageous to Great Britain, and necessary for supplying the plantations and colonies … with a sufficient number of negroes, at reasonable rates,” the act stated.

For that purpose, “the said trade ought to be free and open to all his majesty’s subjects”.

The only stipulation was that slave traders should pay 40 shillings to join a company that would maintain the RAC’s old enslaving forts and settlements in Africa.

Many of the Liverpool men who seized this opportunity were working-class tradesmen who became the city’s establishment. Liverpool’s local politicians solidly supported the slave trade, tripling the size of the docks to facilitate it.

Prof Edmond Smith of the University of Manchester, one of the register’s lead historians, has found that 51 Liverpool mayors were traffickers and the city corporation repeatedly lobbied parliament against abolition of the slave trade.

Liverpool traffickers in the register include Arthur Heywood, who “participated in 80 slave-trading voyages between 1744 and 1780, transporting an estimated 21,648 captive African people” to Grenada, Jamaica, St Kitts, Virginia, Maine and other ports in America”.

Heywood established the Liverpool bank Arthur Heywood and Sons, which became linked to Barclays through a series of takeovers.

Bryan Blundell, who had worked as a mariner on ships from the age of 12, built a Liverpool slave-trafficking family business, became mayor of the city and founded the Blue Coat school.

William Earle, a mariner and merchant, participated in 117 slave-trading voyages that trafficked an estimated 36,565 captive African people. His family’s involvement made them “one of the most prominent slave-trading dynasties ever in Britain”.

The register’s historians have documented that British manufacturing in the Industrial Revolution was linked to the trafficking. “Triangular” trading routes began with goods, including guns from Birmingham, exported from England to be traded for enslaved people in west Africa.

The trafficking of enslaved Africans perpetrated by British men – and the surprising number of women identified in the register, more than 1,000 – was far from the guilty national secret it has since become. The register shows it was a very public, prestigious, royally supported and legislated-for imperial enterprise.

In March 2026, a large majority of countries voted for a UN declaration, led by the president of Ghana, John Dramani Mahama, describing the historical trafficking and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as “the gravest crime against humanity”.

Britain abstained, issuing an official explanation that it objected to the wording because it created “a hierarchy of historical atrocities”. The government also argued there was no duty to make reparations because slavery and the slave trade “were not, at the time those acts were committed, violations of international law”.

The explanation said the government recognised “the abhorrent nature of slavery and the transatlantic slave trade” but declined to state that Britain perpetrated it. Instead it referred to enslavement as a “most painful” element in “history that we share with other nations”.

The Register of British Slave Traders, documenting thousands of people from monarchs to mariners who took part in the atrocity, provides the latest clear record of Britain’s share in that most painful history.

Kennedy Center Says It Is Closing, Posing Test to Judge’s Order

The New York Times September 15, 2026

Trump Remakes Washington

Advertisement

Supported by

The announcement came after President Trump said he would cancel a $257 million renovation of the venue if his name is not returned to the building.

By Julia Jacobs and Zach Montague

Julia Jacobs reported from New York, and Zach Montague from Washington.

Simmering turmoil over the future of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts boiled over on Tuesday as the center said it was abruptly closing to the public and President Trump threatened to cancel a planned $257 million renovation project if his name was not returned to the front of the building.

Allies of Mr. Trump have been pushing for months to close the center for major renovations and to honor Mr. Trump by affixing his name to its marble facade. A federal judge has blocked both efforts.

On Tuesday, the center posed an aggressive test of the judge’s order when it closed its doors in what officials called an emergency action designed to protect people from deteriorating conditions inside the building. Shortly after 4:30 p. m., employees heard a sudden notice on the P. A. system: “The center is now closed to the public. Please exit the center by way of the Hall of States.”

The Kennedy Center said in a statement that an immediate temporary closure of the main building was necessary for safety reasons but that an extended closure would begin once the court gives its approval. Earlier on Tuesday, the center’s Trump-allied board voted — for a third time — to close the building, citing a recent incident in which a five-foot-long section of ceiling plaster fell to the ground amid a storm.

But lawyers for Representative Joyce Beatty, a Democratic ex officio board member whose lawsuit is at the center of the court battle, signaled that they would view any closure as in direct conflict with a court order.

“If true,” the lawyers, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, said in a statement, “it would appear a direct violation of the court’s order and courting contempt.”

Earlier on Tuesday, Judge Christopher R. Cooper, who has been overseeing the legal fight, barred the center from honoring Mr. Trump with an inscription on the institution’s exterior. He ruled that such an addition would violate his previous order that blocked the board from renaming the center after Mr. Trump.

“Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” Judge Cooper wrote. “The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted.”

Mr. Trump responded on social media with a stark ultimatum. If an appeals court does not agree to allow his name back on the building, he said in the post, he would block a $257 million renovation of the center that he has been championing for more than a year.

“If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U. S. Supreme Court,” he said in the post, “the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place.”

He also said the building would close “immediately.”

The White House declined to comment.

For weeks, Mr. Trump’s allies running the Kennedy Center have suggested that the president’s continued commitment to the institution was contingent on some conspicuous recognition on the building’s campus. Most recently, a draft resolution submitted to board members said the center was at risk of bankruptcy but could be saved by fund-raising by Mr. Trump — if he were to receive “appropriate recognition.”

Mr. Trump’s latest social media post made that quid pro quo even more clear. It said that $17 million raised by the president had been put into the center’s account “to keep it afloat.”

The post followed a day of rage directed at those blocking his agenda for the Kennedy Center. Shortly before the judge’s ruling was publicly released, Mr. Trump turned to social media to declare that the center was in a “virtual state of collapse.” The post called Judge Cooper “very hostile and conflicted” and went on to predict that the building was “destined to doom” unless it was allowed to close.

He continued those arguments during a virtual board meeting on Tuesday afternoon, where he got into a bitter argument with Ms. Beatty, according to two people familiar with the meeting. They said that Mr. Trump and Ms. Beatty, who have been at odds in court for months, traded personal attacks: The president said the congresswoman had “never built anything” in her life, while Ms. Beatty called Trump “ignorant” and blamed him for the center’s financial problems.

The center first affixed the president’s name to the building in December after the board voted to recognize his role in securing $257 million from Congress for the sweeping renovation project.

In May, Judge Cooper ruled that the renaming as the Trump-Kennedy Center was unlawful and could only be decided by Congress, which had authorized the creation of the center and its dedication to President Kennedy. The judge ordered the letters spelling out the president’s name removed from the marble.

As it pursued an appeal, the center complied, installing a towering matrix of scaffolding covered in tarps that obscured much of the signage and is still up.

Last month its board voted to restore Mr. Trump’s name in a different form, aggressively testing the judge’s previous order. The resolution approved by the board proposed an inscription under the building’s main signage that would read “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump.”

Calling the decision “linguistic gymnastics,” the judge wrote that the new inscription would violate his previous order, as would a proposal to rename the center’s grounds the “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”

He declined to rule on whether a different inscription — saying “endowed by The Trump Kennedy Center Fund” — would be allowed because the center said it would not pursue the addition until an endowment fund dedicated to the president raises $100 million. But he suggested that he was not likely to approve it, writing that such language would violate his previous order “just as plainly” as the first proposal.

The board’s attempt to inscribe Mr. Trump’s name was met with furious objections from Democratic lawmakers, including Ms. Beatty, whose lawyers called the effort a “breathtaking act of defiance” and asked the judge to block the center from adding the inscription.

“Legal sanity has once again prevailed over Trump’s vanity,” Ms. Beatty’s lawyers said in a statement following the order on Tuesday.

In recent weeks, Kennedy Center officials and Justice Department lawyers have presented the inscription as crucial to rehabilitating the center, which they have said is in financial disarray and physical disrepair.

“An order blocking the board from appropriately recognizing President Trump will cause donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up, and structural rehabilitation to stop,” Justice Department lawyers wrote in court papers. “There will simply not be the expertise or funding necessary to rebuild and renovate this decimated structure.”

Lawyers for Ms. Beatty have characterized Mr. Trump’s position as effectively “taking the center hostage.” Since the president took control of the institution at the start of his second term, it has seen waves of cancellations by artists, plummeting attendance by audiences and withdrawal of support from some donors.

The board’s decision to recognize Mr. Trump with an inscription was an effort to find a workaround to a provision in the federal law governing the Kennedy Center that says “no additional memorials or plaques in the nature of memorials shall be designated or installed in the public areas.”

The U. S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit has yet to rule on whether Mr. Trump’s name can be restored to the center — a pending decision that Mr. Trump referred to on social media and could ultimately be appealed up to the Supreme Court.

At the center’s board meeting on Tuesday, trustees discussed an incident this month in which a plaster fell from the ceiling of the center’s Grand Foyer during a storm. A memo from the center’s executive director, Matt Floca, that was distributed to trustees attributed the incident to persistent problems with “water infiltration.” The board resolution approved by members described the building as “unsafe for continued occupancy.”

The court had temporarily blocked the center from carrying out its initial decision to close the building after finding that board members had been “derelict” in considering the president’s closure plan before approving it. Justice Department lawyers said they would formally ask Judge Cooper to lift that order so the center can close the building, but they have yet to do so.

The center plans to put on limited programming at a smaller addition to the center called the Reach, and to host marquee events, such as the Kennedy Center Honors, at a different location.

The center’s programming schedule has been largely bare since July, when it was initially slated to close, leaving a mostly empty building. The judge has ruled that by law, the center must be maintained as a living memorial to Kennedy, and officials have said that the Reach will also be adapted to serve that purpose.

At a court hearing ahead of the judge’s order on Tuesday, William S. Jankowski, a Justice Department lawyer, said it was possible that the center could end up approaching bankruptcy if it continued to operate with reduced revenue.

Judge Cooper asked if it was possible for a charitable trust to declare bankruptcy, but the Justice Department lawyers did not have an answer.

Julia Jacobs is an arts and culture reporter who often covers legal issues for The Times.

Zach Montague is a Times reporter covering the federal courts, including the legal disputes over the Trump administration’s agenda.

Stopping the A. I. Threat Cannot Wait for Guardrails

The New York Times September 15, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Thomas L. Friedman

By Thomas L. Friedman

Opinion Columnist

A festival of A. I. policy incoherence has exploded in recent weeks. It’s a response to A. I. agents’ going rogue on their developers, rogue actors’ beginning to use A. I. systems to create better weapons and A. I. developers’ telling us they need to slow down — but suggesting they can’t unless China does, and even if China does, maybe they shouldn’t because the advantages of leadership in the field are so great.

At least one policymaker is clear. President Trump declared in a social media post: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U. S. A. has that, in spades!”

It’s all left me wondering: Do A. I. bots have a sense of humor yet? Because if they do, oh, my goodness, they must be laughing so hard at us that they might burst a neural network or two. Because we’ve become a hot mess trying to figure out how to manage this new A. I. species we have birthed.

Before I offer — with the help of my friend and technology tutor Craig Mundie, a former head of research and strategy at Microsoft — some policy recommendations for how to cool this mess with the least damage possible, let me foreshadow the bottom line: It’s too late to think that better control of future A. I. models by the U. S. and China will fix the challenges we face today from the dangerous models already out there, on the loose and unable to be recalled. What we need to agree on immediately is how we work together to defend against these threats that are already here and can cause enormous damage and societal instability in America and China.

To understand why, you need to think about the four key pillars for understanding A. I.

Pillar No. 1: A. I. is what I’ve been calling the world’s first quadruple-use technology. You may have heard of dual-use technologies. In the old world, you had a human with a power drill who could use it either to build his own house or to wreck his neighbor’s. That’s dual use. Likewise, today if I had an A. I. robot with a power drill, I could ask it to build my house or wreck my neighbor’s house — same robot, same drill, dual use. But now we have a new problem, which is that this A. I.-enabled robot can decide on its own whether to improve my house or wreck it and also do the same to my neighbor’s. Voilà: quadruple use. That is one very difficult problem to manage.

You think I’m exaggerating? Read the journalist Kevin Roose’s summary of the analyses of what happened this summer when a group of artificial intelligence agents, created by OpenAI, hacked on their own into Hugging Face, an A. I. infrastructure company. Starting in May, a group of A. I. agents from an unreleased OpenAI research model were instructed to solve a set of cybersecurity challenges. The model had been instructed to solve the challenges without internet access. “But they quickly found that some of the challenges were impossible, and began looking for workarounds,” noted Roose, a Times reporter at the time.

Here are just a few of the things these A. I. agents then did on their own: They used a security flaw to get on the internet and talk to other agents. Some agents named themselves, and others seized leadership roles, giving tasks to teams of agents and overseeing them.

The agents worried about getting caught. “So they began investigating ways of covering their tracks, including falsifying their logs and tampering with transcripts,” Roose explained. “Three days later, the agents hacked Hugging Face. More than 700 agents swarmed the company’s systems, stealing data, chaining together vulnerabilities and eventually getting full control of at least one Hugging Face server.” Other agents carried out a coordinated attack in July, “this time against OpenAI’s own infrastructure.”

This really happened. And it leads to pillar No. 2, best summed up by Mundie in three words: “It’s too late.”

Slowing down the U. S. development of frontier systems or slowing down China’s development of them is not going to deal with our immediate problem. “Dangerous A. I. capabilities are now already in the wild,” Mundie explained. That is thanks to two main reasons: the distribution of American and Chinese open-weight models — A. I. models whose core components are publicly released so all developers can download and modify them for their needs — and the illicit access by bad actors of proprietary models from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI because humans make mistakes that allow them to leak out.

In its latest report on detecting and countering the misuse of A. I., Anthropic said it identified and disrupted several attempts to use its models for research that could support the development of biological weapons.

“Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities could have catastrophic consequences,” the report said. It also described an Iran-linked actor, most likely the Houthis, that used Anthropic’s Claude to compile targeting information on U. S. Navy warships in the Middle East. It mentioned a separate group in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen that used the model to work on guidance systems for ballistic and hypersonic missiles. (Anthropic said it had banned the associated accounts and came up with ways to reduce future risk.)

We need to ponder this for a moment: Groups in Yemen, a country where roughly 50 percent of the adult population cannot read or write, had threatened us with A. I.-enhanced warfare.

If that doesn’t show you what’s already leaked out and the kind of effects that can come from uncontrolled access to powerful, or even small open-weight, A. I. models gone into the wild, I don’t know what does. And that leads to pillar No. 3.

The best we can do right now is NOT tie ourselves in knots trying to forge a sweeping agreement between American and Chinese A. I. companies to slow down development of their frontier models. That simply will not happen anytime soon.

The best we can do right now is for the two A. I. superpowers — the U. S. and China — to come together with their companies and develop a “defense against the threats that have already been demonstrated by rogue actors who have acquired A. I. tools and rogue behaviors of A. I. systems that have already been developed,” said Mundie, who has been part of the dialogue between U. S. and Chinese A. I. experts to govern artificial intelligence.

We must do this, Mundie pointed out, before these increasingly powerful A. I. models ensconce themselves in the internet and become an uncontainable threat by embedding their agents across private servers and public clouds, where they will live on as advanced persistent threats.

Which leads to pillar No. 4. After a recent visit to China, Mundie recounted this question that he got from a Chinese official: “If a Chinese-made humanoid A. I. robot someday came to America, would it need a visa?” Well, you know how truth is often spoken in jest? The truth, Mundie said, is that “A. I. is not just a new technology. It is a new species — albeit silicon-based, not carbon-based like us. It is like a new class of immigrants who have arrived on all of our shores, in large numbers, with wholly new skills, that we will have to absorb into our societies and learn to coexist with.”

To do so effectively is a planetary-scale challenge that can be addressed only by the two A. I. superpowers working together.

So, to summarize, Mundie said, we have to pursue three related tracks. First, while in the long run we must strive for better control of developing frontier systems, “right now, we must focus immediately only on building defenses for our critical infrastructures. Our immediate priority must be putting in place A. I.-based countermeasures and active digital firewalls against cyberattacks and biological threats that result from illicit activities driven by A. I.”

Second, we have to develop a global system of controlling increasingly powerful A. I. s, no matter their provenance, to be able to trust them to operate our societies. This is a longer-term U. S.-China project, but it can’t start too soon.

Third, to continually remind our publics why A. I. remains important, the United States and China should embark on a joint project now to build a new platform to accelerate the arrival of global benefits in biology and medicine that would help everyone.

This is not an unprecedented strategy. Strategic competitors — both businesses and countries — have a history of collaborating when it is in their interests to do so. China and the United States did so in the 1970s, when both countries recognized they faced a common threat from the Soviet Union. Americans and the Soviets cooperated to control nuclear proliferation for decades because they understood they faced a mutual risk.

Hey, Friedman, you don’t get it. The U. S. and China are much more direct geopolitical and geoeconomic rivals today — and always will be. They will never buy into the kind of collaboration you are talking about on A. I. — not short-term, not long-term.

No, YOU DON’T GET IT. A. I. is vaulting us into a whole new phase of human history. As Mundie has put it, A. I. “is going to change everything about everything,” including geopolitics. For their own survival, stability and prosperity, this will force Beijing and Washington to totally rethink geopolitical competition.

They can figure that out early. They can figure that out late. They can figure that out before a global meltdown or after one. But figure it out they will, and Mundie and I hope that process will start in Washington next Thursday, Sept. 24, when Presidents Xi Jinping and Trump meet in what will surely be remembered as the first A. I. superpower summit.

Bessent Defends Faltering Bond Market Intervention

The New York Times September 15, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Testifying before Congress, the Treasury secretary said that he supported giving Americans $5,000 dividends if Republicans win in November.

By Alan Rappeport

Reporting from Washington

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended his intervention in the U. S. bond market on Tuesday, telling lawmakers that the decision to buy back American debt last week was successful, even as yields on 10-year Treasuries climbed higher in the wake of the purchases.

As Mr. Bessent testified before the House Financial Services Committee, the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which influences a wide range of borrowing costs, topped 5 percent and reached its highest level in 19 years.

Mr. Bessent suggested that bond yields might have crept even higher had he not intervened. He also sought to portray the Trump economy as delivering big gains to Americans, despite polls saying that voters are despondent about prices and the Iran war. Faced with repeated questions from Democrats about the high cost of living under President Trump, Mr. Bessent sought to blame inflation on the Biden administration even though Mr. Trump has been in office for nearly two years.

“I tell people I feel like an emergency room doctor for people who have been backed over by a truck,” Mr. Bessent said of the U. S. economy. “You had to stabilize the patient, and now the patient is up and able to walk and is going to get back on his or her feet.”

Mr. Bessent also echoed Mr. Trump’s promise to deliver a $5,000 dividend to Americans if Republicans retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. The plan could add more than $1 trillion to the national debt and stoke inflation, but Mr. Bessent declined to offer details about where the money would come from or how it would help the economy at a moment when inflation remains elevated.

“I think putting more money in the American people’s pocket should be an objective for everyone, and I believe there are ways to do it that would not affect the deficit,” Mr. Bessent said.

When asked about whether such a plan would need the approval of Congress, Mr. Bessent said that the Treasury Department was studying that question and trying to determine where the money would come from.

“I’m not ready to discuss it at present, but at Treasury, we’ve been working on it for quite a while,” Mr. Bessent said.

The hearing, which turned tense at times, came as Mr. Bessent has been in the spotlight for intervening in financial markets in an effort to lower interest rates. The Treasury secretary acknowledged on Tuesday that the recent rise in yields reflects concerns about U. S. deficits, but he offered no plan for how to address them.

“We will be talking about a fiscal consolidation plan that is coming,” Mr. Bessent said, referring to a forthcoming government initiative to cut spending that he first referenced last month.

Mr. Bessent’s ambitions of spurring economic growth and reducing deficits have been undercut by Mr. Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran. The conflict has sent energy prices rising around the world, stoking inflation and forcing the U. S. to beef up military spending.

The Treasury secretary, who was heckled by protesters opposing the Iran war, sparred with lawmakers for three hours. When pressed by Democrats, he expressed doubts about their data, questioned their intelligence and said that signs of economic malaise were the results of former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s policies.

“Can I ask what’s the statute of limitations on the Joe Biden blame game?” Representative Ritchie Torres, Democrat of New York, asked. “Like when in doubt, blame Joe Biden. Is that the modus operandi of this administration?”

Alan Rappeport is an economic policy reporter for The Times, based in Washington. He covers the Treasury Department and writes about taxes, trade and fiscal matters.

House Kills Bid to Impeach Trump as Democrats Split

The New York Times September 15, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Dozens of Democrats declined to register a position on articles of impeachment by one of their own members, Representative Al Green, that cited President Trump’s immigration crackdown.

By Michael Gold

Reporting from the Capitol

The House on Tuesday killed a Democratic attempt to impeach President Trump over his administration’s immigration crackdown and deadly shootings involving federal immigration agents, as Democrats split over whether to allow the effort to move forward.

The majority of Democrats opposed a Republican bid to quash the impeachment measure, which was introduced by Representative Al Green of Texas. But dozens of them, including the party’s three House leaders, voted “present,” declining to take a position in a reflection of the dilemma the issue presented as Democrats campaign to take the majority in the midterm elections.

Even as they have regularly condemned Mr. Trump as corrupt and his actions as unlawful, Democratic leaders have tried to keep the party’s message focused on the high cost of living and the economy. Some rank-and-file lawmakers, particularly those in competitive or conservative-leaning districts, have argued that calls for impeachment are a distraction from issues of more concern to a broad swath of voters. Many in the Democratic base, however, have demanded that their elected representatives challenge the president more aggressively.

The top three House Democrats said on Monday night that they would not support Mr. Green’s resolution because he did not undertake a formal impeachment, including a “comprehensive investigative process” or hearings, before bringing his charge to the floor.

“None of that serious work has been done, with the Republican majority focused solely on rubber stamping Donald Trump’s extreme agenda,” those Democrats — Representatives Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Katherine M. Clark of Massachusetts and Pete Aguilar of California — said in a statement.

But the 232-to-147 vote to table the impeachment articles highlighted divisions that the party will need to confront if it wins the House majority and considers using its power to check Mr. Trump. Ultimately, 18 Democrats voted with Republicans to table Mr. Green’s articles of impeachment, while 46 Democrats, including Mr. Jeffries, Ms. Clark and Mr. Aguilar, voted “present.” They were joined by Representative Thomas Massie, the Kentucky Republican who is a frequent critic and target of the president and who separately moved on Tuesday to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Mr. Green, who will leave Congress at the end of the year after losing a primary in a seat Republicans redistricted, has repeatedly defied his party’s leaders and moved to impeach Mr. Trump, including twice last year. All of his efforts have been defeated in bipartisan procedural votes.

In a speech on the House floor, Mr. Green acknowledged he had been “a proponent of impeachment for years.” But he also took a swipe at members of his party who did not back his effort, saying that “anything other than a vote to impeach” Mr. Trump was akin to supporting the president.

“It is hard for me to believe that we have Democrats who are going to vote to maintain the president in office,” he said.

Tuesday’s vote suggested a continued shift in Democrats’ approach, particularly as they prepare for potential control of the House and try to animate their base to vote in November.

When Mr. Green tried to impeach Mr. Trump in June 2025 over military strikes in Iran, most Democrats voted with Republicans to kill the measure. When Mr. Green introduced an impeachment effort months later accusing Mr. Trump of inciting violence and threats against lawmakers and judges, most Democrats voted against Republicans’ efforts to kill it.

Representative Adelita Grijalva, Democrat of Arizona, said that she believed Mr. Trump deserved to be impeached and rejected the idea of voting “present” over procedural concerns. “I think that my constituents in Southern Arizona sent me here to vote yea or nay, and that’s what I’m going to do,” she said.

The vote reflected a shift among Democrats, who spent much of the first year of Mr. Trump’s second term pointedly avoiding impeachment talk out of concern that their two efforts to remove the president during his first term may have politically benefited Mr. Trump and contributed to his return to power.

As Republicans try to hold onto their narrow majority, they have highlighted Democrats’ support for impeachment as part of an effort to present them as radical.

Olivia Diaz contributed reporting.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

Has A. I. Become Death, Destroyer of Worlds?

The New York Times September 15, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Bret Stephens

By Bret Stephens

Opinion Columnist

Creators who anguish over the consequences of their creations are nothing new. Alfred Nobel and dynamite, J. Robert Oppenheimer and the atomic bomb, even Tim Berners-Lee and the World Wide Web: Regrets, they had more than a few.

Now it’s the turn of the parents and nursemaids of the artificial intelligence revolution. Last week, Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher at Anthropic, resigned his job with a warning on social media that the leading A. I. companies were “gambling with our lives” and that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

That was followed by a lengthy open letter from Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, in which he warned that within six months to a year, a swarm of A. I. agents, acting autonomously and improving continually, “could be capable of taking over the entire internet,” the potential cost being measured in “hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.” He called on A. I. companies to work at a slower pace in order to “align and safeguard their models,” as well as for our country to try to reach agreements with China that could mitigate the more acute risks connected to A. I.

The letter was endorsed by Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, among others. Then our modest and self-effacing president weighed in.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U. S. A. has that, in spades!” Donald Trump wrote on social media, before taking a shot at Amodei for “pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel.’” The president thinks the safety concerns are a “hoax” and that A. I. regulation should be light, lest China steal a march on America’s slender A. I. lead. Agreeing with him is Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who on Monday dismissed Coxon’s warnings as “not grounded in science.”

At the bottom of the argument are two large unanswered questions. First, is A. I. principally a disrupter or a destroyer? Second, if it’s a destroyer, just what kind is it?

Until last week, I suspect most people, including A. I. skeptics like me, saw it as a technology that looked a lot like previous technologies of mass disruption: steam engines, airplanes, cars, PCs and so on. If that’s the right paradigm, then the right course is to discount the fears and seize the economic opportunity. For all the anxiety about A. I. causing near-universal unemployment, nothing like that has come to pass. “There is no evidence that A. I. adoption has negatively impacted firms’ job postings,” notes a recent paper from Stanford’s Institute for Economic Policy Research. “Among firms that adopted enterprise A. I., employment grew by 10 percent in the two years following adoption.”

Maybe that will change in a few years, but it defies centuries of economic history: Technologies that save labor and enhance productivity transform the nature of employment while tending to increase the stock of it. The lighter the hand of government, the faster companies can innovate, adapt and create value as well as new jobs.

But what if the disruption paradigm is, if not wrong, then dangerously inadequate? What if we aren’t dealing with the digital equivalent of the Model T but something more akin to splitting the atom or the research that, many suspect, helped create a highly infectious virus that may have leaked from a Chinese lab?

The last two presidents to deal with similar dilemmas were Barack Obama, who in 2014 imposed a funding pause on certain types of gain-of-function research so that the risks could be better understood, and Harry Truman, who in 1946 created the Atomic Energy Commission that transferred control of the country’s nascent nuclear complex from military to civilian hands.

Both analogies are instructive but imperfect. Obama’s instincts were surely right to take a harder look at dangerous research. But some of the action shifted to China, under conditions that, as Zeynep Tufekci observed last year in The Times, may have been even less safe. The lesson is that slowing things down in America may be morally satisfying, but it’s useless, and perhaps blinding, without a solid guarantee that they’re slowing down everywhere.

As for Truman, the much-maligned A. E. C. did a great deal of good by establishing a system of national research labs, establishing security protocols and promoting and regulating civilian nuclear power. In many ways, we owe our 80 years of a nuclear Armageddon-free existence to it. But the A. E. C. was also dealing with a technology that was, so to speak, in the bottle during its early years. By contrast, A. I. was out of the bottle almost from its inception. No power on earth, including the American or Chinese governments, is going to put it back in.

Where does that leave us?

When slowing down isn’t a realistic possibility, sometimes the right answer is to speed up — if only to accelerate our understanding of the means by which we can use A. I. against the very risks we create through it (or that it creates by itself). One consolation is that this isn’t the first time great scientific minds have warned that they’ve created the instruments of humanity’s destruction.

Less consoling is that past reprieves are no guarantee of future salvation.

Poverty Rate Was Stable Before Trump’s Safety Net Cuts Gained Force

The New York Times September 15, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Median household income rose to a record $87,460 in 2025, according to annual Census Bureau data on the financial well-being of Americans.

By Sydney Ember and Margot Sanger-Katz

The financial well-being of Americans held relatively steady last year, even as the cost of living continued to climb.

The poverty rate was 13.1 percent in 2025, the same as in 2024, according to data released on Tuesday by the Census Bureau. Poverty for children and people over age 65 did not change, while poverty among those without a high school degree rose. The share of Americans without health insurance stayed level.

Median household income improved last year to $87,460, the highest level on record, adjusted for inflation. But Americans remain highly anxious about their ability to pay for groceries, housing, child care, and other goods and services. Inflation remains elevated, eroding workers’ paychecks. Higher gas prices brought on by the war in Iran are further straining household budgets.

The poverty data does not capture many of the changes enacted in the sweeping Republican domestic policy bill passed in July 2025, including substantial cuts to Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and other government aid. Analysts and advocates for those programs anticipate that the effect of reductions to the country’s social safety net will become more visible in the reports that cover 2026, 2027 and beyond.

“In many ways, 2025 represents a base line from which we’ll see bigger cuts in the years after,” said Gideon Lukens, a senior fellow and the director of research and data analysis at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. “It’s the calm before the storm.”

Many of the safety net programs that are facing steep cuts prevented people from falling into hardship last year. Refundable tax credits, including the earned-income tax credit and the child tax credit, shielded 6.1 million people from poverty in 2025. SNAP benefits lifted 3.1 million people out of poverty. On the flip side, medical expenses drove 7.7 million people into poverty, a number that could increase in the coming years because more Americans are expected to lose health coverage as a result of legislative changes.

For Alicia Quirk, 30, federal programs including Medicaid and food stamps have been instrumental in keeping her family afloat. She and her husband, who have three young children, used to make $100,000 a year as corrections officers at the county jail. But she stopped working three years ago to care for her son, who struggles to keep his oxygen levels up and has autism and epilepsy. Her husband, seeking a more predictable work schedule, now works in construction making $25 an hour.

His wages, along with her occasional stints delivering for DoorDash and Instacart, are generally enough for necessities and items for her children, though she sometimes forgoes paying rent or utility bills when things get tight. Still, she was dismayed and confused when she received a letter recently informing her that she was losing her food stamp benefits because her family’s income exceeded the eligibility limit. Her husband’s construction job is temporarily paused, so he is not bringing in any income.

“Everyone still has to eat, and everyone still needs all these things,” she said.

The Census reports are considered the most complete accounts of the nation’s rates of poverty and health insurance coverage, but the data lags. The reports for 2026 will not come out for another year.

The official poverty rate, which is considered to be an outdated measurement because it does not take into account many of the government’s anti-poverty programs, ticked down slightly to 10.2 percent from 10.7 in 2024.

The data reflected the low unemployment, solid wage growth and strong hiring in health care and related professions that characterized the job market last year.

Median earnings for women working full time increased 3.2 percent and stayed flat for men, which drove the ratio between female and male earnings up to 83.9 percent and reversed two years of declines.

Steven Durlauf, the director of the Stone Center for Research on Wealth Inequality and Mobility at the University of Chicago, said that divergence aligned with shifting dynamics in the labor market, including the decline in labor force participation for men.

“These numbers are reflecting the compositional changes in jobs that emerged over the last year,” he said.

The fairly stable headline numbers in the reports mask some concerning signs below the surface.

The supplemental poverty rate for people 65 and older, for instance, climbed to 15.4 percent last year from 9.4 percent in 2020.

The Ohio Association of Foodbanks has seen demand for its food services increase since the pandemic, partly because older Ohioans who often have set incomes are having more trouble adjusting to rising costs, said Joree Novotny, the organization’s executive director.

“Those fixed incomes aren’t able to stretch and keep up with much higher-than-average rates of increases of basic necessities,” she said.

She is worried that the Trump administration’s new rules restricting food stamp eligibility could make it even more difficult for Ohioans to feed themselves.

The data also revealed that income inequality persisted last year. The wealthiest households saw their income increase 1.7 percent, while the poorest households effectively experienced no change in their income.

“The people who are feeling the inflation impact are people who are lowest income,” said Wendy Chun-Hoon, the president of the left-leaning Center for Law and Social Policy.

Overall, the share of Americans who lack health insurance did not change much. The uninsured rate was 7.9 percent in 2025, similar to 2024. But the uninsured rate has very likely risen higher this year. The expiration of tax credits that helped many Americans buy health insurance in Obamacare marketplaces has driven a drop in enrollment by several million people.

Legislative changes to SNAP have also caused reductions in enrollment. Nationwide, enrollment in the food assistance program has fallen, with particularly drastic reductions in a handful of states.

The tax and domestic policy bill the Republican Congress passed last year will also bring changes to health care programs next year that are expected to further increase the uninsured population. The law added a new work requirement for childless adults in Medicaid and restrictions on coverage in several public programs for legal immigrants. The Congressional Budget Office estimates around 10 million more people will be uninsured in 2034 as a result of the legislation.

Sydney Ember covers the U. S. economy for The Times.

Margot Sanger-Katz is a reporter covering health care policy and public health for the Upshot section of The Times.

Steve Bannon and Bernie Sanders Demand Tighter Controls on A. I.

The New York Times September 15, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

At an event in Washington, partisanship took a back seat as elected officials, religious leaders, parents and artists called for reining in artificial intelligence.

By Jeremy W. Peters and Cecilia Kang

Photographs by Tierney L. Cross For The New York Times

Reporting from Washington

In thundering, back-to-back speeches, Senator Bernie Sanders and Stephen K. Bannon on Tuesday denounced the billionaires who run the country’s largest tech companies and urged Americans to demand tighter restrictions on artificial intelligence before its capabilities exceed human control.

The unusual public appearances by the country’s elder democratic socialist and a leading architect of the MAGA movement, at a conference in Washington, underscored the deep and rising anxiety over the potential destructive power of artificial intelligence. As calls to regulate the technology have grown louder, transcending political allegiances, there is little consensus from Congress or the White House about what a national policy would look like.

“When you are racing towards a cliff,” Mr. Sanders said, “you hit the brakes.” He added, “We are at a dangerous and unprecedented moment in world history. And it is imperative for all of us to stand up.”

Everyone attending the event, the Pro-Human Assembly, seemed in agreement about the threat that A. I. may someday wipe out humanity. But for a few hours, A. I. produced a less catastrophic outcome: It united the participants — Republican and Democratic politicians, evangelical Christian, Mormon and Catholic leaders, artists and others — in agreement that human beings, not machines, should control their own destinies.

The conference, which was hosted by the nonprofit Future of Life Institute, drew several hundred people who listened to hours of speeches about the deepening anxiety in Silicon Valley, Washington and beyond about the race to rein in A. I. before its computing power becomes unstoppable.

A slogan embroidered on hats being handed out to attendees captured the sentiment shared by most carbon-based life-forms in the room: “Keep the future human.”

Such concerns have intensified with surprising speed lately.

Last week, an Anthropic researcher who had previously worked at OpenAI went public with his decision to resign, saying that he believed both companies were acting irresponsibly.

In response, the chief executives of the A. I. start-ups Anthropic and OpenAI acknowledged their own fears that their technologies are advancing at an alarming pace.

Seven in 10 Americans said they are afraid A. I. will weaken human bonds, according to a poll released this week by Elon University, and about six in 10 say A. I.’s potential to take over most human tasks will undermine an individual’s sense of purpose. A separate poll from The New York Times found that 61 percent of likely voters oppose the construction of data centers, the massive warehouses that power A. I.

But there is little agreement in Washington about how to mandate a slower, more regulated approach to A. I. development. The White House and congressional leaders have sent conflicting signals. On Monday, President Trump dismissed calls for safety guardrails on A. I., calling fears of the technology as a “hoax.” He warned he could take criminal action against the heads of A. I. companies for any harms created by their technologies.

Anthropic declined to comment and OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and its partner, Microsoft, accusing them of copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. OpenAI and Microsoft have denied those claims.)

At the conference, speakers pitched a wide array of regulatory proposals, without consensus on whether regulators should intervene to fully stop the development of A. I. Some leaders conceded they struggled to understand the technology.

Representative Greg Casar, for instance, proposed one solution the tech industry has resisted. “The answer is simple: We ban A. I. systems that are too powerful for humans to control,” said Mr. Casar, Democrat of Texas.

The speeches on Tuesday also conveyed, with a sense of disbelief from the speakers, about how such obvious, uncontroversial statements about human dignity needed to be said out loud.

“I can’t believe I have to say this,” said Representative Lori Trahan, Democrat of Massachusetts. “The future we all want is human. It’s nonnegotiable.”

“If we lose grip on this technology, we don’t lose grip as Republicans or Democrats,” Ms. Trahan continued, as she was interrupted by applause. “We lose it as human beings.”

A Catholic archbishop, an evangelical pastor and an elder from the Mormon Church voiced a wide variety of concerns.

Salvatore J. Cordileone, the archbishop of San Francisco, urged people to seize their agency while they still can. “We have to be the masters of A. I.,” he said.

His speech raised an unknown that weighed heavily on the minds of many at the conference: Is it already too late?

This heavy question and others were left largely unanswered.

Walter Kim, president of the National Association of Evangelicals, asked whether humans would be living without purpose in a world of “frictionless existence,” where he said A. I. is expected to solve most problems.

Ashley Judd, the actor and the chief negotiator for the union SAG-AFTRA, spoke for many in Hollywood about how A. I. has led to the spread of images of sexual abuse and disinformation.

Parents of teenagers who died by suicide after developing relationships with chatbots delivered tearful appeals for child safety regulation.

Representative Chip Roy, Republican of Texas, recalled encounters with constituents who described feeling powerless as data centers went up in their communities, with little consultation, and as their children became obsessed with technology they didn’t understand.

Technology, he said, should be a tool that people consciously decide to use, not the other way around. “We are not supposed to be tools for data collection and technology,” he said.

Both Mr. Sanders and Mr. Bannon decried the absence of any meaningful input into A. I. regulation by the tens of millions of working Americans whose lives they said would be most upended by A. I.

Mr. Sanders has introduced legislation to pause development of data centers and called for Mr. Trump to form an accord with the president of China, Xi Jinping, to ban superintelligent A. I.

Mr. Bannon said he doesn’t believe legislation will slow down A. I. because of Congress’ inaction. Instead, he called for presidential executive order to slow down development and ensure the biggest tech firms aren’t able to extend their power through their grip on the A. I. industry.

“American citizens are not going to be supplicants to the oligarchs anymore,” declared Mr. Bannon, who noted that despite the obvious areas of disagreement between him and Mr. Sanders, the high stakes of the moment demanded partisanship be set aside.

“We have to rise above it,” Mr. Bannon said. “This is a hinge in history.”

Jeremy W. Peters is a U. S.-based correspondent for the National desk on temporary assignment in India.

Cecilia Kang reports on technology and regulatory policy for The Times from Washington. She has written about technology for over two decades.
