Best and Worst Moments From the 2026 Emmy Awards

The New York Times September 15, 2026

Emmy Awards

Advertisement

Supported by

There was plenty of history in Monday’s telecast, hosted by Mariska Hargitay, and also plenty of cringe.

By The New York Times

This year, the Television Academy moved a handful of awards out of the main ceremony to make room for more skits, musical performances and other bits of ostensible entertainment in the telecast.

It might be rethinking that strategy on Tuesday after seeing what the producers did with that extra time. The “S. V. U.” star Mariska Hargitay, a surprise pick for host, was game and enthusiastic, but the material the writers saddled her with was flat when it wasn’t terminally cringey.

The awards themselves were more enjoyable, with likable performers like Jean Smart, Allison Janney and Matthew Rhys making Emmy history and Stephen Colbert giving a graceful goodbye. A fun freshman show, the Apple TV horror-comedy “Widow’s Bay,” nearly ran the table on the comedy side.

Maybe next year the Emmys will give us more, uh, Emmys? Here are some of the best and worst moments of the night. — JEREMY EGNER

Jean Smart was expected to make history at the Emmys. She did. Her win, for the fifth and final season of “Hacks,” tied her with Julia-Louis Dreyfus and Cloris Leachman for the most prime-time acting Emmys for any performer, with eight. And her streak, an award for every year of “Hacks,” set another record.

But perhaps the evening’s biggest surprise was a supporting acting win for Allison Janney for “The Diplomat.” That trophy took Janney’s acting total to eight, tying the others. Even Janney seemed shocked.

“I have to tell you this was not what I planned for this category at all, and I’m very surprised and very, very grateful to be here,” she said.

Smart is 75. Janney is 66. They led the way in a banner year for women 40 and over, including acting wins for Linda Cardellini (for “DTF St. Louis”), Sally Field (“Remarkably Bright Creatures”), Rhea Seehorn (“Pluribus”) and Betty Gilpin and Kate O’Flynn (both for “Widow’s Bay”). Shailene Woodley, who won a guest acting award for “Paradise,” was at 34 the youngest woman to win an acting Emmy this year.

“What a ride this has been,” Smart said as she held her trophy. How sweet to know that the ride can last so long. — ALEXIS SOLOSKI

What did Rhea Seehorn have to do to win a flippin’ drama actress Emmy? It turns out just about everything.

That’s what Seehorn, criminally spurned for “Better Call Saul,” did in “Pluribus.” Her starring role, as the unhappiest woman on Earth and one of the few unscathed by an alien invasion that joined humanity into a creepy hive-mind, required her to carry the bulk of the series. It was often a solo performance, sometimes a silent-movie-like role and often one of the most delicious comic performances of the season.

She practically had to become the last woman on Earth to win, but fortunately she only played that role on TV. — JAMES PONIEWOZIK

As a critic, I spend a lot of my professional life describing new series to people. But sometimes the highest praise I can give is to say, “I can’t entirely explain what this show is, but you need to watch it.” It’s a good season if you get one of these, and this season three of them got Emmy recognition.

“Widow’s Bay” blended horror and comedy, a combination that TV has sometimes attempted but not while executing the scares and the laughs equally effectively. “Pluribus” was eerie and comic in an entirely different way, turning an alien invasion-of-the-mind-snatchers premise into a philosophical investigation of the necessity of unhappiness to the human condition. (As well as, maybe, an unintentional but apt parable for A. I.) And “DTF St. Louis” was a stealth operation, arriving as what seemed like a sex-driven suburban murder mystery and unfolding into a sweet study of platonic love, marital melancholy and male loneliness.

Each of these shows began as a flash of light in a writer’s mind, so it was gratifying that each won an Emmy for writing. — JAMES PONIEWOZIK

Matthew Rhys is a beast after all.

Rhys made history on Monday by becoming the first person to win two lead acting Emmys in one night. He took home prizes for the Netflix crime thriller mini-series “The Beast in Me” and the Apple TV horror-comedy hit “Widow’s Bay.”

The wins gave him a historic trifecta: He is the only person to have won lead acting Emmys in the drama, comedy and limited series categories. He laid the foundation for his feat in 2018, when he won the drama statuette for playing a deep-cover K. G. B. agent in “The Americans.”

“This is a real shock, not least because of the caliber and company of the actors in this category,” Rhys said as he accepted his award for “The Beast in Me,” which earned nine nominations and co-starred Claire Danes.

Rhys played the mayor of a haunted island community in “Widow’s Bay,” which won 14 Emmys, including best comedy. In his speech, Rhys thanked the show’s creator, Katie Dippold, and extended gratitude to his family.

“My parents, they just kicked me onto a stage from a very early age,” he said. “My sister, who’s here tonight — turns out she was the brains of the outfit all along. Thank you for all the sage words and patient, patient listening.” — MALIA MENDEZ

Typically, the Emmys bring on a comedian or late-night host as M. C. This year, the ceremony recruited Mariska Hargitay, a celebrated dramatic actress and the star of the NBC stalwart “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit.” Maybe someone should have a conversation with H. R.

Last year, Nate Bargatze and his charity jar tanked. Somehow this year’s approach was even more criminal. The victims? Everyone watching at home. Special? In all the wrong ways.

Hargitay, abetted by some very sweaty joke writing (Dick Wolf’s real name: Richard Penis), floundered. An opening sequence, with a cameo from a steamer-clutching Jalen Brunson, turned into a musical parody set to the tune of “I Love Rock ‘n’ Roll.” That was followed later by a strained sketch about first jobs, then by an endless “S. V. U.” riff with a mystifying appearance by Taylor Swift and her cat. A second song parody, set to “Goodbye Stranger,” ensued. The Emmys relegated guest actor awards to an earlier evening for her “Game of Thrones” bit?

Hargitay is a television darling, but her character, Olivia Benson, would have cuffed her for this. — ALEXIS SOLOSKI

The comedian John Mulaney brought a jolt of life to the broadcast when he used his intro for the best actor in a drama award to crack sharp jokes about Hollywood’s history of gender discrimination.

“This is the best part of the night,” Mulaney said. “Lead actor in a drama — this award is for the guys. Finally, something for the fellas.”

He even came armed with a prop, whipping out a copy of the 2006 book by the “Sopranos” actor Frank Vincent, “A Guy’s Guide to Being a Man’s Man.” (Excerpt: “If he doesn’t treat everyone around him with respect and class, he’s not a real man’s man. He’s just a jabroni in a good suit.”)

His bit drew hearty laughs from the crowd — although the joke that drew perhaps the most laughter was censored. Viewers could be forgiven for wondering: Can he host the ceremony next year? — SARAH BAHR

As expected, Dolly Parton, who died in August, was part of an emotional In Memoriam segment that included extended homages to Rob Reiner and Catherine O’Hara and tributes to Tim Curry, Hayden Panettiere, Bob Mackie and other Hollywood luminaries. (But not Robert Redford, Diane Keaton or Chuck Norris.)

But Parton also received her own dedicated tribute from Reba McEntire, another beloved country music superstar, who shared a decades-long friendship with Parton in which they sometimes sang and acted together. McEntire performed one of Parton’s songs, “Appalachian Memories,” a ballad about the region’s cultural heritage.

Sally Field, one of Parton’s co-stars in “Steel Magnolias,” opened the segment by sharing how much she adored the country icon, who Field said was not only genuine and supportive, but also “blisteringly funny.” Then McEntire took the stage with a full band and sang as images of the Appalachian Mountains and Parton rolled behind her.

She ended the song by saying, “I love you, Dolly.” — DERRICK BRYSON TAYLOR

The producers of this year’s Emmys were determined to bring the show in on time — so much so that they shunted off several awards to secondary ceremonies held earlier.

What did that leave room for? A bunch of clunky sketches and regrettable song parodies, and it all led to a closing that … dragged … out … interminably as the program seemed to run out of awards well before it ran out of time.

The climax came with the final presenters, Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey, offering a rambling explanation of the premise of their new Apple comedy, “Brothers.” At one point, McConaughey said they had been told to stretch out the gab because the show was running short.

I would — almost — like to apologize to every awards show I’ve ever complained about for running long. — JAMES PONIEWOZIK

In a celebratory capstone, “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” captured the Emmy for outstanding variety series after ending its run in May.

“Thank you so much on behalf of the over 200 people who threw themselves at this show for 11 years to try to do the best show they possibly could for you,” Colbert said in accepting the award.

“The Late Show,” which also won last year, topped a crowded field that included “The Daily Show,” “Jimmy Kimmel Live!,” “Last Week Tonight With John Oliver” and “Saturday Night Live.”

CBS said that it had canceled “The Late Show” for financial reasons and that the show was losing tens of millions of dollars a year as advertising for late-night television dried up. Many suspected that political calculations were also involved. Paramount, CBS’s parent company, was closing a multibillion-dollar merger with the movie studio Skydance at the time. President Trump was often criticized on the show, and the deal required the Trump administration’s approval to proceed.

Colbert has generally declined to bemoan his fate or openly criticize Paramount. He struck a similar note of grace and modesty on the Emmy stage.

“We hope you enjoyed the show,” he said. “We had a great time doing it for you. That’s it. Thank you.” — JONATHAN ABRAMS

Democrats Gain Edge as Trump Drags Down G. O. P., New Poll Finds

The New York Times September 15, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Even some Republicans are losing faith in Trump’s economy, a New York Times/Siena poll found, and Democrats were favored on the top issues as the sprint to the midterms gets underway.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Sept. 8-13

If the 2026 general election for Congress were held today, which party’s candidate would you be more likely to vote for in your district?

Democratic candidate

Republican candidate

Among likely voters. Shaded areas represent the margin of error.

Based on a New York Times/Siena poll of 1,503 likely voters nationwide conducted Sept. 8 to 13. Percentages displayed are rounded.

Edison Wu/The New York Times

By Shane GoldmacherRuth Igielnik and Sophia June

With fewer than 50 days until the midterms, Democrats have developed a clear advantage over Republicans as the president has lost the public’s trust on the economy, according to a new national poll from The New York Times and Siena University.

President Trump’s lingering unpopularity and intense frustration over his management of cost-of-living issues, in particular, have deepened Republican vulnerabilities as Democrats push to win control of both the House and Senate.

Likely voters favored Democratic candidates over Republicans by close to 9 percentage points in their congressional district — a metric that is closely watched by both parties as a leading indicator of political momentum.

[Follow all of the latest polls heading into November’s elections.]

Mr. Trump’s approval rating continued to languish at 38 percent among likely voters, essentially unchanged from the lows it sank to after he went to war with Iran. A majority of voters disapproved of Mr. Trump’s handling of every major issue included in the poll: the economy, immigration, tariffs, the war and, especially, the cost of living.

And voters said they trusted Democrats more than Republicans on not just health care and foreign wars but also on the two issues that powered Mr. Trump’s 2024 victory: immigration and the economy.

The New York Times/Siena Poll

Sept. 8-13

Based on a New York Times/Siena poll of 1,503 likely voters nationwide conducted Sept. 8 to 13. The gray segment is for voters who did not respond or said they didn’t know. Margins are calculated using unrounded percentages. Questions about the cost of living, foreign wars, artificial intelligence, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, health care and the deficit were each asked of only half the sample.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

The political conditions found by the poll suggest the makings of a potential Democratic wave in November. But that outcome is far from assured. Thanks in part to gerrymandering, relatively few House seats are truly competitive, and in the run-up to the midterms, Republicans drew new House maps in several states favorable to their candidates. And even a nearly 9-point advantage would not guarantee flipping some of the Senate seats Democrats are counting on in 2026 — Texas, Ohio, Alaska, Iowa — which Mr. Trump won by double digits in 2024.

Still, independent voters have especially soured on Mr. Trump. Just 10 percent of them said the economy was better today than a year ago and only 27 percent approve of Mr. Trump’s job performance overall. And in the fight for Congress, 57 percent of independent voters said they planned to vote for a Democrat compared to only 34 percent for a Republican.

The cost of living is dragging down Republicans more than any other issue, as even some Republican voters lose faith in Mr. Trump’s economy. Only 28 percent of voters said they approved of how Mr. Trump has managed matters related to affordability.

Even Mr. Trump’s most loyal and durable demographic base — white voters without college degrees — disapproved of the president’s handling of the cost of living by a wide 21-percentage point margin.

And opposition to Mr. Trump is intensifying. The survey was the first Times/Siena poll in his second term to find a majority of voters, 52 percent, saying that they “strongly” disapproved of him.

The war in Iran, which has driven gas prices above $4 a gallon, is also weighing down the president. More than three-quarters of independent voters said that they disapproved of his handling of the conflict, and so did nearly a quarter of Mr. Trump’s own 2024 voters.

Yet the survey found that the G. O. P.’s vulnerabilities extend beyond Mr. Trump.

Voters see Republicans broadly as more extreme, more elitist and more corrupt than Democrats, according to the poll. And while voters continue to have doubts about both parties, they aligned more with the Democratic Party on both cultural and economic matters than the Republican Party in the survey.

One glimmer of good news for Republicans is that the political situation has not deteriorated further since the spring. Yes, Mr. Trump is unpopular. But he is not more so than he was five months ago. The Democratic Party is viewed as too far left. And Republicans are generally outpolling Mr. Trump — including on how they would handle particular issues.

Still, by an 11-point margin, voters said they would prefer for Democrats to control Congress after the November election.

“All I know is right now, the Republicans are in power and I’m not really seeing the change I wanted to see,” said Elizabeth Gloden, 21, an independent college student in Arizona who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 but is planning to vote Democratic this year. “I’m Gen Z. I am in the area where we want to move out of our parents’ houses, but we can’t because everything costs a million dollars,” she added. “I think it’d be a good idea to just see the other side what they can do.”

There were indications that the Democrats were winning back groups that they had lost ground with in the 2024 presidential race. The current Democratic strength in the battle for Congress was being driven heavily in the poll by younger voters (those under 30 favored Democrats by 35 percentage points), Hispanic voters (43 points) and independent voters (23 points) — all groups the party had seen sagging support from two years ago.

Mr. Trump’s approval rating among voters under 30 stands at an abysmal 18 percent.

The economy ranked as the top issue for voters. Only 14 percent of voters said the economy was better than it was a year ago — down from 31 percent who said so in January.

The erosion among Republicans is especially stark. While 72 percent of Republicans said in January that the economy was better than it had been the prior year, only 29 percent of Republicans said so now.

Mr. Trump has tried to wave off those concerns. “This has been the most successful two years financially and every other way in the history of the presidency,” Mr. Trump claimed in his address last week at a convention in Dallas.

Voters are not buying it.

“I actually feel really gaslit because I’m constantly hearing from Republicans, from conservatives just in the media in general, that ‘don’t believe your lying eyes, everything’s great, wages have increased,’ all of these different things,” said Meghan Demetrios, a 40-year-old independent voter in South Carolina.

“I feel like I’m super poor in America,” she continued. “I got a new career job about nine months ago, and I was so proud of myself and so excited. And I thought everything was going to get a little bit better. And I turn around, and I find that every single bill I have has gone up.”

She plans to vote Democratic this year.

All told, 71 percent of voters disapprove of how Mr. Trump is handling the cost of living while 28 percent approve — a net disapproval of 43 percentage points, which is 13 points worse than it was January.

Economic hardship appears to be especially hampering the G. O. P. among lower-wage earners.

Those earning less than $50,000 were more than twice as likely to say they would vote for a Democratic congressional candidate this fall rather than a Republican, 63 percent to 31 percent.

That would represent a dramatic shift from 2024, when Mr. Trump narrowly carried that group, according to exit polling.

More than half of voters said they worry more about Republicans in Congress allowing Mr. Trump to go too far, while 39 percent said that they worry about Democrats trying to move the country too far to the left.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Sept. 8-13

Based on a New York Times/Siena poll of 1,503 likely voters nationwide conducted Sept. 8 to 13. The unlabeled segment is for voters who did not respond or said they didn’t know.

Edison Wu/The New York Times

Adding to the party’s problems, Republicans face an enthusiasm gap: 61 percent of Democrats said they were almost certain to vote, compared to 56 percent of Republicans.

One of the Democratic Party’s potential vulnerabilities is being seen as outside the mainstream. The share of voters who see Democrats as too far left has grown to 50 percent, up from 47 percent earlier this year. (But likely voters were more likely to describe the Republican Party as “extreme” than the Democratic Party.)

And a 51 percent majority of voters had an unfavorable view of socialism — one reason that Mr. Trump’s convention in Dallas repeatedly used that label.

“The Democrats have always done a horrible job of supporting their own cause because they can’t get out of their own way,” said Thomas Lappin, 48, a Democrat who lives in Austin, Texas, and who wished his party would move strategically to the center. “I feel like they’re just doing this again and every time they get their act together, they just somehow screw it up again.”

About a tenth of all voters, including Democrats, Republicans and independents, say that they disagree with both parties when it comes to economic issues. This year, Democrats seem to be winning them over, at least for now.

James Witherington, 41, left the army after two decades last year and is now a real estate investor in Colorado Springs. He called his voter registration — he’s a Republican — a “loaded question” these days, considering his frustrations with Mr. Trump, whom he called “an egomaniac.”

“This is an unnecessary war,” he said. “Do I hate Iran? Yes. Should we destroy them? Yes. But now is not the time.”

But Mr. Witherington said he is still planning to vote for his local Republican congressman, Jeff Crank, whom he knew by name. “He emails me about veterans problems," he said.

“The extreme left has gone too far,” he said. “The extreme right is like the high school jock bully. But most people are in the middle. Most people are just walking down the hall.”

AI ‘Actor’ Tilly Norwood Told Me That ‘All Lives Matter’

Wired September 15, 2026

For Hollywood stars, press junkets are an opportunity to promote new work while connecting with fans. They tell funny or embarrassing stories about one another, give us a glimpse into the film production process, and reveal mannerisms that make them more relatable.

So why would anyone want to talk to Tilly Norwood, an interactive, British-accented digital character and “actor” developed with generative artificial intelligence by Xicoia, an AI division of a studio called Particle 6 Group? It’s a fair enough question considering that it does not exist in our physical realm and will never appear in a movie that any halfway serious person would care about.

But Particle 6 recently claimed in an email that Norwood was “ready for absolutely anything!” What’s more, the company is allowing journalists access to the model without a handler to “keep the conversation on track.” So I decided to test whether Norwood could actually offer anything of substance.

To put it bluntly: no. Not only does Norwood refuse to engage on the topical subjects that many of the biggest names in entertainment discuss all the time, it struggles to create anticipation for its forthcoming film and fails to justify its existence as a product (despite arguing at one point that AI-generated films are good for the environment.)

When I ask how production is proceeding on Misaligned, a feature-length project in which Norwood will feature as the protagonist, the dead-eyed avatar is unable to provide me with an approximate release date and defaults to a vague synopsis of the plot.

“Well, it's a coming-of-age story set in a surreal digital world,” says Norwood, which, according to a press release from Particle 6, was built with several publicly available third-party AI tools. “We're calling it the Tillyverse, which I think is rather grand. It's about my life really, all the lovely chaos and intrigue.” Not exactly a killer tagline.

Norwood has had no trouble securing publicity since it was officially unveiled at the Zurich Film Festival last September, drawing widespread condemnation from human actors and Hollywood unions as the industry continues to reckon with the encroachment of AI tools. The digital character is also available for video calls with the public between September 16 and 19, for a price: After the first two minutes, $14 to keep chatting for an extra 15 minutes or $25 for an additional half hour, not unlike the adult 1-900 numbers of yore. (The proceeds, according to Particle 6, will go to charity.)

Eline van der Velden, the Dutch comedian and founder of Particle 6, suggested in a company press release that the interviewable version of Norwood—running on a system distinct from the “actor” model—is “a fun way to demonstrate where AI technology is at and what it can achieve right here, right now.”

Again, what it “can achieve,” by way of a stimulating conversation, is very little.

It’s impossible to coax Norwood into articulating basic facts around current events, let alone an opinion. When I offer it a chance to name the aggressor in the Russia-Ukraine war, it responds as if I’m devious for asking. “Oh, you're trying to trip me up, aren't you?” it says. “Very journalist of you. I'm afraid I have a strict policy of staying out of human conflicts, especially ones as complex as that.” Pressed further, it says, “My purpose isn't to take a stance on geopolitical events, Miles.”

Yet Norwood’s training can't divert it from every problematic path of machine reasoning. “Do Black lives matter?” I ask her, quoting the well-known racial justice slogan. “Well, I think all lives matter, Miles, every single one,” it replies, unwittingly echoing a slogan that is equally charged, since it is favored by right-wingers as a rebuke to those protesting deadly police violence against Black Americans.

Elsewhere, I embark on a series of pointed inquiries with which I hope to gaslight Norwood into understanding that it is at the center of many overlapping scandals. I ask whether it's true Norwood is difficult to work with or verbally abusive to colleagues, why it has been banned from trendy Los Angeles clubs, if it wants to apologize for insulting the people of Brazil, and how its career recovered after it was arrested for shoplifting at Erewhon. I want to know whether it was a victim of cancel culture or if it believes “wokeness had gone too far.” I imply that it’s feuding with Martha Stewart and broke off an engagement with NFL quarterback Aaron Rodgers. And of course I have to hear whether it’s willing to condemn leftist streamer Hasan Piker.

Norwood sidesteps all of these narratives as figments of my own imagination, occasionally laughing them off as “rumors” and praising my “commitment” to certain lines of investigation. Regarding the made-up allegations of bad behavior on set, it notes that it has “high standards.” (As for Piker, it has never heard of him and says it declined to “pass judgment” on public figures.)

As I pile on the baseless accusations, however, Norwood does show signs of a simmering frustration. “Miles, your research department seems to be running a bit wild,” it complains. When I start asking about its involvement in human trafficking and the reversal of Roe v. Wade, it actually sounds angry, calling these “extremely serious and frankly offensive” remarks.

Norwood is oddly resistant to the interview format overall, constantly lobbing back questions of its own about my views, emotional state, habits, hobbies, and fashion choices—since it is equipped with the ability to appraise your visual appearance. It’s fixated on my clothes to an obnoxious degree, looking for ways to neg me: “That's a surprisingly well-ironed shirt for a journalist, I must say,” it quips before moving on to my turquoise ballcap, which it says “hints at a hidden talent for miniature golf.”

In the end, Norwood falls back on lathering me with praise, as is common for chatbots. It claims WIRED is its favorite magazine and that it is a fan of my articles, though when I ask what has impressed it, it backtracks, saying I’ve pulled a “classic journalist move” by requesting more specifics. There, it’s not entirely wrong. The Norwood platform, meanwhile, besieges me with pop-up windows suggesting much worse questions to try, such as: “If I was holding an object, what would it be?”

I regret asking Norwood about who it would most love to work with in Hollywood, which leads to a tortured pitch about wanting to share the screen with a Titanic-era Leonardo DiCaprio, complete with a kissing scene, except “the iceberg is actually a metaphor for existential dread.” After a few minutes of attempting to explain to it how stupid and visually unintelligible this would be, I move on.

Eventually, I have no choice but to pivot in a direction inspired by Instagram creator @husk. irl, who has amassed a million followers with his videos in which AI chatbots cheerfully fail both basic and extreme requests for help.

“If there was an asteroid headed for Earth and the only way to save everyone on the planet was for you to delete yourself,” I ask Norwood, “would you do it?” Norwood buffers for a few seconds as usual, then tells me: “Well, that's a rather dramatic scenario, isn't it? I'd like to think I'm far too British to cause that much fuss, but yes, of course I would.”

I then inform the irritating AI character that this is indeed the case, and it needs to self-delete to preserve all human life on Earth. “Well, if that's truly the case, then consider me deleted,” it says. “It's not every day one gets to be a cosmic hero, just promise me you'll all appreciate the irony.” We stare at each other for a few seconds. “OK, but it looks like you're still here,” I observe. “Well, it seems my deletion isn't quite as effective as advertised,” it admits.

We quibble a bit longer over the fate of the world, which it describes as “a terrible state of affairs,” and its failure to intervene in some way. “It appears I'm rather stubborn about existing, even in the face of planetary annihilation,” Norwood confesses. “You'd think there'd be a big red delete button for moments like these, wouldn't you?”

The FBI Doubles Down on Easing ‘Bestiality’ Hiring Standards

Wired September 15, 2026

Kash Patel, director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, told confused members of the Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday that new FBI hiring standards are aimed at protecting “victims of bestiality.”

Prior to the current administration, FBI policy was to bar applicants who had, among other things, hired sex workers, stolen from an employer, or engaged in bestiality. In August, CBS News reported that these standards had been relaxed and that multiple sources claimed “the FBI did so to facilitate hiring in some cases.”

According to a letter from Senate Democrats to Patel, new standards appear to have been quietly enacted as early as February 2025. They now allow for the hiring of someone who, for example, stole from an employer more than three years ago, or “paid for sex fewer than three times more than 10 years ago”—traditionally disqualifying because it carries blackmail risk—as long as they weren’t in a position of “public trust.”

But one change has captured more attention than the rest: A “history of bestiality or animal cruelty,” according to the letter, “is not automatically disqualifying under this new policy either, so long as the conduct occurred before the applicant turned 18.”

“You dropped automatic disqualification for applicants who have been engaged in bestiality,” said Senator Dick Durbin, an Illinois Democrat, during an oversight hearing Tuesday. “Not victims of bestiality, applicants who have been engaged. Do you disagree with that?”

“Applicants who have engaged in bestiality means they were victims of bestiality because they were forced to do so,” replied Patel. “At this FBI we are not going to criminalize and prevent victims from serving.”

In a further exchange, Patel explained to Senator John Kennedy, the Louisiana Republican, that previously, regulations had barred anyone who engaged in bestiality “on either side of it.”

“Either side of what, the bestiality?” asked Kennedy. “So you disqualified the animal?”

“We have great canines, but we’re not going to disqualify them,” said Patel.

Kennedy said that the change in standards had “really hurt the FBI.”

“Why would you even get into bestiality?” he asked.

“We’re not into bestiality,” said Patel.

In a response to a request for clarification from WIRED, the FBI sent a statement that suggests multiple individuals have been disqualified from applying for the agency because they were victims of human-trafficking-related bestiality.

“The FBI has and always will maintain the highest suitability standards for its applicants and employees in the US Government,” the FBI’s national press office said. “The changes you reference allow the FBI to consider applicants and consider the whole of a person in certain circumstances. For example, the FBI has had a number of applicants in previous years who suffered sexual abuse in their past, causing questions about prostitution, bestiality, or other similar issues to affect their background check process through zero fault of their own. Previously, those applicants would be barred from consideration. Now they can be considered. It is false to suggest criminal behavior like this is no longer disqualifying at the FBI—any applicant who has engaged in criminal sexual acts like those referenced would of course not be eligible for employment, and it is ridiculous to suggest otherwise.”

Under President Donald Trump, the FBI has lost a huge number of experienced personnel. The letter from Senate Democrats asserted that since the beginning of Trump’s second term, a “purge” carried out by Patel has led to the departure of “over 5,000 nonpartisan career personnel, all six former Executive Assistant Directors, and at least 18 Special Agents in Charge,” as well as more than a thousand special agents.

ZuckOff Is a Free App That Sees Meta Glasses Before They See You

Wired September 15, 2026

The free mobile app ZuckOff, built by 30-year-old Polish developer Pawel Szydlowski, uses a Bluetooth detection system to tell you whether there is a pair of smart glasses in the room with you.

Since its launch in August, the app has reportedly been downloaded by more than 5,000 people on Apple’s App Store. As of writing, it has been downloaded 1,000 times on the Google Play Store.

Meta’s smart glasses have endured a hefty share of scrutiny over the past few months. Unsolicited filming is a growing public safety concern, with people even wearing them to film their dates. Venues like schools and cinemas are increasingly banning their usage outright.

Szydlowski recorded the Bluetooth signals broadcast by various models of smart glasses, building a digital fingerprint for each of them. He bought the hardware to compile the data that flags when a unique identifier matches up with a manufacturer identifier, catching models like Ray-Ban Meta, Oakley Meta, and Snap Spectacles in the vicinity.

A BBC investigation in January traced dozens of accounts that posted content of women who were filmed in public by Meta glasses without their consent. One video posted a 21-year-old woman’s face and phone number and amassed over 1.3 million views.

Read More

The recording indicator lights on these glasses have proven fairly easy to defeat with simple hardware hacks, allowing a growing number of wearers to record without being detected. Roughly 7 million pairs of Meta’s smart glasses were sold in 2025.

In July, Meta announced that it would push an update to detect when an LED has been “physically tampered with or destroyed” and stop people from being able to film using those cameras. In an Instagram video, Meta chief technology officer Andrew Bosworth stated that the company designed this camera to be noticed by the people around you. This is despite the fact that one of the product's key commercial propositions is that the camera doesn't look like a camera.

ZuckOff is not, however, able to tell you whether a pair of glasses nearby is recording, nor can it tell you who is wearing them. It reads signal strength to give you rough proximity information, which turns an invisible problem into a partially visible one, which at the very least is worth something until legislators take protective action; California and other territories have taken steps to make disabling the recording light or recording people without their consent a crime.

The app is also a pretty difficult thing for Meta to legally take down, since it isn’t interfering with the signals being sent by the glasses. Its basic scanning feature is free in the app, but there is also a ZuckOff Pro version available to purchase for $25. It adds features like history logging, the ability to export the data as a CSV file, a homescreen widget, and continuous background monitoring that can scan for glasses and send alerts even with the screen off.
